Firstly, I have to say that MGS 5 is a good game, at least above average, but it has many flaws that drag it down. The most obvious issue is that this game is half-baked af. In particular, Chapter 2 seems messy and irrelevant to the main plot. The large amount of cut content and the lack of a proper ending make me wonder how they considered this a finished product. The first mission was cinematic and intense, so I was super excited—then 50 hours of side quests began. Don't get me wrong; I enjoyed them because of the mechanics, but the missions felt repetitive and clearly weren't designed as story missions. Most of the time, the story goes like this: 'Boss, we have a mission to eliminate this guy,' 'Boss, we have a mission to extract this man,' and so on. When I say repetitive, I mean it—there are only seven unique missions in Chapter 2, with the others being harder versions of Chapter 1 missions. [spoiler]The true ending is the prologue mission with a new cinematic.[/spoiler] This is disappointing, but it's clear the game's development was a disaster. I still recommend it because it probably has the best stealth mechanics and optimization. However, don't expect anything special in terms of story; it's one of the most basic revenge stories ever made, and they couldn't even get that right. It had a lot of potential, but it's clearly wasted—a real shame. 

P.S. Chapter 1 missions in Chapter 2 can be progressed through by playing side quests and listening to cassettes, but it doesn’t make it any better.

This game truly leaves you with a strange feeling, close to phantom pain. In terms of plot, it starts like a common spy thriller, with an abviously evil antagonist and a bunch of guys, who are not saint either, but who certainly look better. The first chapter's plot is pretty much predictable and does not offer anything surprising. The second chapter though... At the first look, it appears to be half-baked and unfinished. But the general mood and the messages differ drastically from what we could see at the beginning of the game. When I finished the story, I truly felt deprived of something. Like there was something I really wanted to maintain, but lost it forever. I'd say that, in terms of the main story, what starts as a plain and simple revenge tale, ends up as a manifest of grief, pointlessness of war, and dark shades of loneliness of those who see the world through the scope of the rifle. I still don't really know, how to perceive the ending of this game. It feels unfinished, it looks unfinished. But in the end, this emptiness and understanding of what comes after this in the general MGS storyline, truly creates an odd feeling of loss.

When it comes to gameplay, it really delivers. The amount of various stealth and combat mechanics really allow you to approach your missions differently. I truly loved the concept of being forced to adapt to fast-changing circumstances. At first, I was savescamming, trying to be the sneakiest guy ever. But the more I played, the better I understood, that this game wants you to improvise, because due to the open world model, every plan can go downhill in a fracture of a second. The sheer amount of gadgets and various weapons you can choose from make me feel like I can really experiment with my playstyle. When I got tired of sneaking around and just wanted to do some optional missions and blend some action in, I just changed my equipment to machine guns, missile launchers, ordered tanks from above, and the game never punished me for playing shooter.

At the same time, sooner or later, I reached the point of understanding the main flaw of this game. Progression. The local system of base building and staff extraction takes a long time to reach a considerable progress. If you want the best guns, the better suits, and generally if you want to make your gameplay smoother and perhaps adjust it to your personal style, you will inevitably reach the point, when you'll have to grind the optional missions for money and resources. I personally did not find the local open world annoying. It's empty, and there's literally nothing to do except for clearing the outposts in search of high-grade staff and resources for expanding the Mother Base. However, those missions are truly a sandbox and can be completed in numerous ways. Nevertheless, at some point, your base reaches the limit of personnel, so you will be forced to expand it. In order to reach high levels of all units you need for unlocking the top-tier gear, you will have to spend a lot of resources. But it's not the problem itself. The problem is that they need to be "recycled" first, and this recycling, as well as the actual platform building, is done live, when you play the game. And it takes hours. So I ended up in a loop: I needed to wait, say 2 hours, until my platform gets built; in the meantime, I completed side missions to kill time; The enemies get stronger with each mission, but your gear remains the same, so you need more staff to raise your HQ level; so you need recources and money; so you wait and grind, wait and grind.... And I really was stuck like this until, at some point of the plot, a secondary base is unlocked, and the process of farming speeds up dramatically. But the thing is, when you really make your build and get the gear you always wanted, the game will probably be nearing its end. Not like it's a bad thing, but the grindwalls they put a lot of good stuff behind can get really annoying sometimes.

As for the main missions, I really enjoyed most of them, except for a few of those that made me fight in the open, which truly makes this game a third-person shooter, whether you wanted it or not. However, making you replay the same main missions during the second chapter seemed weird. It seemed weird because those were literally the same missions with slight difficulty alterations. It looks like they needed to fill your playthrough with something, but they either lacked time, or budget to make it more unique. 

In general, I really liked this title. It's also important to say, that I never really played any other MGS games, and only played Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance before this, so this is my first Metal Gear Solid experience, aside from watching some lore videos. And it was really a fun to play through. I think this game introduced me to this great franchise, and for that I'll always be grateful.

Let me start by saying, that I played most of this game on the Steam Deck and it runs as smooth as butter! easy 60fps with mid or even high settings. Just amazing to be able to run a game that looks this good on the steam deck.

The game starts with a story portion, a very dark one at that (not my personal preference however I've played most MetalGear games so I was already used to it)
After the start of the game that also is a tutorial to get you started with missions and objectives etc. You are set free to work through the main missions and do any side missions available to you as well however you see fit.

I do want to highlight the structure of this game and something that I've seen in many negative reviews.
The entire game is played on 2 open world maps. You only have access to one at the start. While going through the main story missions you will unlock the second map at some point, then you will have missions on both. One map is in a desert area (many reviews are like: it's all sand and mountains what is that all about. Well that is where it is supposed to be!!). The other map is green. The maps are based out of different countries and therefore the map design is based on these locations.

The open world with missions is just brilliant as a world design:
So you start a mission: you get choppered in and ride your horse to the mission location. Do the mission and then? If you are not doing a story mission. You basically are free to roam the open world freely after completing the mission!
Why you might ask? Well you can simply drive to the other missions location and do some resource gathering on the way. Or even scout for new soldiers to "Recruit" for your personal army. You can even effect the next missions you start by getting rind of something in the area that might put you at a disadvantage. 
The whole sandbox nature of this open world is just crazy, and you appreciate it more and more as you continue playing and start to see how the enemy responds to your growing power. Yes the same locations that you visited before will start having new types of soldiers, equipment, air support, and tons more variety. That makes playing any missions like a new experience even if it's at a location you already did other missions in. The objective will be different, the enemy locations and patrols, other military units in the area of that come visit can create a very different game play loop. 

Getting stronger and the story gets better:
When you start you are weak and have limited weapons and tools, as you grow in power you unlock so many new weapons, weapon customization and attachments, and entire army base with facilities that you upgrade with resources you acquire while out on missions, that will allow you to research even more crazy weapons and tools.
You can take pretty much anything of value while out in the open world, to build and expand your base! you see enemy base weapons, take them, you see containers with resources! Yes take them. You see high skilled soldiers! you guessed it! just take them for your own army. See a tank, car, something that moves! take it!
This part of the game is also just so cool, because as you progress and do harder missions you will find more resources, and more highly skilled soldiers, these are the key to progress further as you need them to increase your ability to get specific support while out on the open world, and find people who can increase your ability to research items in the various labs you will have. This makes any soldier a person of interest for you as they can be of great value to you.

You cat get pretty much anything delivered to you while out and about:
One other simply amazing mechanic of this game is that while you are out and you just did a mission, you want to free roam and want a different load-out, companion or anything you have in your arsenal? Your army will deliver it to you by helicopter in a few seconds. You can do this as much as you want (it costs some cash, but nothing to actually worry about too much).
You can pick a place for your airdrop to land to make sure it's convenient for you, even if it means that is on the head of an enemy who is in a tough spot and you can't easily get by them. So the airdrop will land on their head and know them out! This really never gets old!
Also you have limited ammo capacity and your weapon attachments like silencers wear out, so you will be calling in supply drops every now and then during long missions to make sure you are stocked up on ammo and attachments etc.

After playing for a while you will really see your base grow from a small rig to a massive network of rigs in the ocean, see all of the soldiers you "recruited" walking around your base, it's really a great thing to see when you fly back after the missions.

The weapons and your entire arsenal is also just great all round, this is something that has always been the case in MetalGear games and here it's even more varied and gives you the freedom om taking whatever you want on missions, Even this is it's own game mechanic as everything you take has a cost, and if you want to build up cash. You could run a mission that can help you steal some expensive equipment while barely taking anything with you on a mission and then selling your expensive goods to gain cash. You also have to kind of manage your money as research and such also cost money and you should avoid going bankrupt as your soldiers will start to leave if you can't pay them. This is easy to manage generally, however it also adds a layer of depth to the game and makes you really want to take everything you can while out on missions.

MGS5 is a very flawed game, a game that feels like it came so close to being a masterpiece but failed to go the distance.

Much of its failings can be attributed to making it a live-service always online title, tacking on a mind-numbingly unnecessary progression grind to what is otherwise an impeccably crafted stealth sandbox.

at a mechanical level, MGS5 is insanely well made. INSANELY. WELL. MADE. controls are crisp, snappy, responsive, intuitive, the moment-to-moment action goes from tense to brutal in the blink of an eye, customization and player choice are out of this world. The weapon customization system alone stands out. The camouflage capabilities, CQB/hand-to-hand combat, lethal-or-non-lethal combat and takedowns, holding people at gunpoint, human shields, there's almost no limits to what you can pull off with a bit of cleverness.

Sadly, it has systemic problems.

The story, for starters, is an acid trip that wobbles between brilliance and ridiculousness. It has absurd plot holes and contrivances contrasting to an exceptional exploration of a character descending into hell despite mostly good intentions, and it absolutely feels like it had a vision that was undercut and interfered with by studio politics and drama, as this was famously the game that resulted in the schism between Hideo Kojima and the publishers of MGS. 

Other problems coming from these strange choices end up polluting the otherwise pristine experience. A particular issue I have is how harmless most enemies are, where you're encouraged to be stealthy, but in reality you can for the most part run directly at enemies making your presence known and they simply never have the firepower to easily stop you from doing so. There was a flop on my part early into playing this game when I tried holding a guard at gunpoint, and I made a mistake, and the guard pulled out a knife and stabbed Venom Snake, knocking him on his ass and pulling out a makarov. and it was fun. I ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up, I laughed, and just stood there. "aight, GG, I deserve this loss". And so, the guard starts shooting.

and keeps shooting.

an entire mag, point blank, into Snake. And my screen wasn't even flashing red. what the heck? reloads, continues firing. I'm still alive, somehow, after a chest stab and two pistol magazines point blank. This, in a game where you are in control of an engagement 90% of the time, get first strike almost on every encounter, and typicaly neutralize a target (fatally or not) in a single well placed headshot, even once they start having helmets (the neck is still easy to hit) just deflated all sense of urgency or threat from otherwise exciting scenarios to sneak into.

The bosses are also not enjoyable, with the Skulls being extremely bullet-spongy mostly harmless enemies.

So much wasted potential, when the moment-to-moment gameplay is incredible. My best experience with this game was using some mods to lock Snake to a maximum of 10% the usual health, doubling enemy vision range, and halving my ammo capacity, while also removing all the ridiculous grind and deployment costs that first keep you from upgrading your tools, then prohibit you from fielding them because you'll go BROKE for daring to put an underbarrel grenade launcher on an M4, despite somehow having an entire PMC with attack helicopters at your beck and call, what the hell, game... Modded like this, you get an extremely tense and demanding stealth game with a sandboxy feel that can be extremely challenging and fun to complete.

but look, if I need to spend 4 hours testing third-party mod combinations just to ♥♥♥♥♥♥ the game's bloated grind systems and poor balancing... I can't recommend it.

As a long-time fan of the Metal Gear series, Metal Gear Solid V left me with mixed feelings. I’m someone who absolutely adores Peace Walker but can’t stand MGSV’s approach to certain elements. And yet, here I am, surprised by how much I actually enjoy playing it.

The gameplay is undeniably fun. The way MGSV plays is fluid, and the freedom it offers with different strategies makes every mission feel customizable. The fights against Quiet, Skullface, and The Man on Fire stood out as my favorites. I came prepared, whether it was with my trusty sniper rifle, homing rocket launcher, or—yes—even a water pistol. These bosses? Easy. Seriously, Reddit overhyped their difficulty. But their impact? Massive.

Miller and Ocelot are the best part of the game. It’s like having two dads with totally different parenting styles: Miller, the strict one who’s against everything cool, and Ocelot, the chill one who’s like, “Yeah, do it, sounds awesome!” Their dynamic is one of the few things that keeps the more serious tone of MGSV tolerable.

But let’s talk about what doesn’t sit right. The Side Ops. Boring. Peace Walker had ridiculous missions and even a Monster Hunter collab—here, it's all so serious. And the way you handle GMP and development in real-time? That’s just tedious compared to Peace Walker’s approach, where GMP wasn’t a permanent loss. MGSV's realism sucks out some of the charm that made Peace Walker goofy and fun.

That said, the buddy system is a major win. D-Horse, D-Dog, and Quiet? So much fun to experiment with. D-Dog, especially, holds a special place in my heart—what a good boy. He’s probably one of the most useful and lovable companions in the entire series.

In the end, Metal Gear Solid V isn’t bad. It’s just tedious, a different kind of game that doesn’t fully capture the spirit of the series. It reminds me a lot of Final Fantasy, where each entry brings something new but still keeps enough familiar elements to connect it to the rest of the series.

Would I recommend MGSV? Sure, but only if you’re ready for a shift in tone and pacing. It’s not the Metal Gear we grew up with, but it’s still got some redeeming qualities.

(TL;DR: MGSV is my favorite Metal Gear game. The gameplay is incredibly fun with unmatched freedom and dynamic mechanics. While some story points were left unresolved, I love its themes and how it complements the gameplay. Despite cut content, it’s a masterpiece and the ultimate Metal Gear experience.)


Metal Gear is consistently in my top five favorite game series, and there have been moments when I’ve even called it my favorite series of all time. The combination of complex storytelling, memorable characters, and innovative gameplay mechanics has always resonated with me, but Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain (MGSV) takes things to a whole new level.

Without hesitation, MGSV is my favorite entry in the series. The gameplay is incredibly fun—it's a masterclass in open-world stealth, providing players with near-limitless freedom to approach missions in their own style. The controls are tight, the variety of tools and tactics is immense, and the game rewards creativity in ways that few others do. Whether you’re sneaking through a base in the dead of night, scouting with Quiet, or using the Fulton system to send anything from soldiers to animals back to Mother Base, every mission feels fresh and exciting.

But what truly elevates MGSV for me is the story. While I know it’s divisive among fans, I absolutely love it. Sure, it's more understated and fragmented than previous entries, but that subtlety works in its favor. The themes of betrayal, loss, and identity resonate deeply throughout, and even though some plot points were left unresolved (like Eli and Sahelanthropus), the game's narrative still packs an emotional punch. I appreciate how it complements the gameplay by reflecting the grueling, morally ambiguous life of a mercenary.

The open-world design allowed the story to unfold more naturally, making me feel like I was inhabiting the world as Big Boss rather than just playing through a linear narrative. Some may argue that the story isn't as tightly crafted as earlier games, but I believe it’s a perfect fit for what MGSV set out to achieve—a sandbox of infiltration where the player is Big Boss, shaping their legend through action.

While the lack of closure with Mission 51 and other cut content remains a topic of debate, it doesn’t detract from the overall experience for me. The sheer depth of the gameplay systems, the polished mechanics, and the dynamic AI make MGSV a masterpiece in its own right. Every session brings something new, whether it’s refining strategies, unlocking new gear, or simply enjoying the freedom the game offers. Even years later, I still find myself coming back to it because it’s one of those rare games that never stops being fun.

In a series known for its intricate plots and over-the-top set pieces, MGSV stands out as a bold, ambitious evolution. It may not have the traditional linear story some fans expect, but for me, it’s the ultimate Metal Gear experience—a perfect blend of engaging narrative and unparalleled gameplay.

The kind of game that when you finish it, you want to just start over again, as much for the gameplay and replayability than for its iconic scenes (some more cringey than others), music, and setpieces.
MGS3 is everything I love about the series. Effective, charming, powerful, meaningful. It's a journey. Snake's journey, that would define him, leave him scarred and make him the man we know him to be; Big Boss.

Now take The Phantom Pain. It's the antithesis of MGS3. The story, from A to Z, is alienating the player with incomprehensible plot, extremely fragmented storytelling and gameplay, and a story that overall amounts to almost nothing in the grand scheme of things, lore wise.
Putting aside the gaping plot holes and very blurry overarching story (that feels more like a fever dream transcripted by a madman through damaged video and cassette tapes than anything), one of the main issues of this game remains the god-awful repetitive missions.

As much as you feel extremely connected to Snake in MGS3, due to the fact that you're literally dropped in the forest and the game and narrative will go from there, creating a real sense of continuity and overall plot and mission at stake, in TPP, there is absolutely none of that. 
On the contrary, the game is literally a HUB simulator with small set pieces of missions in an open zone where you get deployed and extracted from, hundred of times, online mode-style, with very little explanation and very little MEANING as to why you should care about this story at all. Diamond Dogs is not even Big Boss' organization, you just play a mute that joins a mad Kaz and stuff happens, and some bad guys do things I think, there's a parasite or some other BS reason for stuff happening, and that's it. Absolutely non memorable plot, no emotions whatsoever.

Don't get me wrong. There are SOME ideas. The concept of Quiet was good, but executed poorly and comes off as super cringe in my opinion (more cringey than EVA constantly and clumsily jiggling her boobs at Snake in an effort to charm him, while their real bond happens, in fact, through some other story beats. But I digress)

Anyway. I'm gonna stop there, cuz I'm tired. But I still recommend the game because it's an interesting experience, from a mechanical perspective it's really not that bad of a game. It's just a terrible story, and a terrible Metal Gear Solid game in my opinion.

Just be aware that you're gonna see Hideo Kojima mentioned more times in this game than there are actual lines of dialogue from Snake. 

"Written by Hideo Kojima", "A story by Hideo Kojima", "A Hideo Kojima original game". Every. Single. Mission.
The guy is clearly a narcissist, and he lost himself in that project (but in the end, he got a serious reality-check delivered by Konami, so there's that). 

The result is a shell of what MGS is supposed to be about. Delivering a good SF plot, with some weird, sometimes awkward but loveable twists and good gameplay. 
Well, we're clearly missing some ingredients in TPP to make it "Snake Eater level" legendary. It's not even close.

I can't help but return to this game every year or so for another playthrough, and each time it's just as brilliant and addictive as the first playthrough. 

There really is no game quite like it, providing an open-world military sandbox where you have absolute freedom in what you can do. It has the perfect blend of classic and evolved stealth gameplay combined with a plethora of loud options to mix up each mission. And underneath all of this, there is an intricate base-building system that adds satisfying progression to make each of your actions meaningful. Also, the game just feels nice to play. The controls and movement are responsive and the gunplay is fantastic for a third-person shooter. 

The only place where this game falls short is in the story department with a huge amount of cut content (blame Konami, not Kojima) and lacklustre story in general, especially when compared to the narrative masterpieces that preceded it. Nevertheless, I've played each MGS multiple times (MGS2 was my entry into the series), and MGSV is easily my favourite. I'll take gameplay over story any day of the week.

Many have tried to emulate it, fully or partially, but none have succeeded. A game that was thought out fully in all ways, and represents the full potential of the military shooter genre as a paragon of it's own caliber.

A title released when it needed to be, and the final chapter in an anti-war series with a long and storied history.

Truly an iconic title made by Hideo Kojima; unparalleled in all ways. Stands the test of time consistently; time after time.

I only wish that the title was fully finished before release, and I hope that the MGO3 servers stay live long after the heat death of the universe.

Out here, there’s no such thing as eternal allies or unyielding enemies. That’s the first lesson you’ll learn. Friends become foes, and sometimes, the hardest choices you’ll make are the ones that turn you into the executioner of those you once swore to protect. War twists everything. It tears apart what you thought was unbreakable, and no matter how much blood you spill, you’ll never wash the guilt from your hands.

You’ll meet a wolf in this journey. D-Dog… a companion like no other. He’s fierce, loyal, and he’ll be there in your darkest moments. He won’t ask for anything but your command, and he’ll give you something you’ve forgotten—a reason to smile amidst the chaos. But don’t get too attached. War doesn’t let anything stay pure for long. There’s always a cost to companionship on the battlefield.

And then there’s her. Quiet. She won’t say a word, but she’ll speak louder than anyone you’ve ever known. A sniper, yes, but also a mystery wrapped in silence. Her presence will haunt you. She’ll be the ghost that fights by your side, the one who saves your life countless times… and yet, you’ll never truly know her.

You’ll start to feel something for her, even if you don’t realize it at first. Call it love, call it connection—it doesn’t matter. What matters is that it’s there, deep inside, waiting for the moment you’re ready to admit it. But by the time you do, by the time you understand what she means to you, it’ll already be slipping through your fingers. Maybe that’s the cruelest thing about love—it comes too late, or not at all. And then you're left wondering… maybe, just maybe, it’s never truly over.

The battlefield does that to you. It gives you something only to tear it away. But even knowing that, you won’t stop fighting. Because you’ve got a mission. You’ve got a duty. And in the end, that’s all that’s left. You, your memories, and the choices you made.

You’ll feel the weight of every decision, the sting of every betrayal. And when it’s over, you’ll ask yourself if it was worth it. You’ll ask if you could have done something different. But let me save you the trouble, soldier—there’s no going back. You’ll live with the ghosts you create, and you’ll carry them with you to the end of your journey.

The phantom pain? It never really fades. It’s the price of survival.

So, go on, soldier. Make your choices. But don’t forget—nothing in this world is forever, not even the silence of those you love.

New York styled Pizza:
Pizza dough:
14 g instant yeast
617g water - 95F
950g all-purpose flour
19g fine sea salt
25g granulated sugar
American Pizza Sauce and Toppings:
1 tablespoon (14g) butter
1 tablespoon (9g) extra virgin olive oil
6 cloves garlic, rough chopped
2 teaspoons (4g) red pepper flakes
28 oz (794g) can of crushed tomato
2 teaspoons (2g) dried oregano
1.5 tablespoons (21g) granulated sugar
salt and pepper to taste
Splash of olive oil
2 cups (227g) low moisture mozzarella, fresh grated
2 cups (200g) Monterey jack cheese, fresh grated
1/2 cup (26g) parmigiano reggiano, fresh grated
American Pizza Dough:
Preheat the oven and a baking steel or pizza stone at 500F for 45 minutes before utilizing it.
Whisk yeast and sugar into your water, and allow it to sit for 5 minutes. In a separate bowl, add flour and salt and mix by hand to combine. Pour your water mixture into your flour and mix by hand until you get a rough dough, then transfer to a work surface and knead until it starts to pull away from the work surface and is relatively smooth.
Place your dough in a greased bowl, then cover with plastic wrap and let rise for 1 - 2 hours at room temperature or until double in size.
Punch down your dough and dive into 300g pieces. Form those pieces into balls and place them in a floured proofing pizza box, cover with a lid, and proof at room temperature for 3 - 4 hours. (If you do not have a proofing pizza box, you can use a floured baking sheet, cover it with an inverted baking sheet and wrap it in plastic wrap.)
American Pizza Sauce and Toppings:
In a medium sauce pot, add butter and olive oil. Set that over medium-high heat; once the butter melts add garlic, cook until fragrant, add pepper flakes, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the garlic begins to brown on the edges.
Add crushed tomatoes, oregano, salt, and a splotch of olive oil, boil over medium-high, reduce heat to low, and simmer for 12 minutes, stirring occasionally or until thickened and viscous—season with salt to taste and let it cool down.
Assembly.- Place one of your pizza doughs onto a floured pizza peel, and flour your dough generously.
Punch your dough down in the center, working your way out to create a ¼” wide. Pick up your dough, place it over your closed fists, and rotate it around, gently stretching to 13” to 14”.
Place a couple of spoons of your sauce, starting in the center, spreading in little circles, and working your way to the edge until it gets evenly spread out.
In a medium-size mixing bowl, place mozzarella cheese, Monterey Jack, and Parmigiano; mix until combined. Sprinkle your cheese mixture to your desire and place in the oven onto your baking steel and bake for 5 - 7 minutes or until the edge gets golden brown and the cheese melts.
Enjoy.

Title: “The Phantom Pain: Or How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Cardboard Box”

If you ever wanted to experience the thrill of being a one-eyed, bandana-wearing, gravelly-voiced soldier with a penchant for hiding in cardboard boxes, then Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is the game for you.

Gameplay: Imagine being dropped into a vast open world where your best friend is a horse that poops on command and your worst enemy is a goat that refuses to be Fulton extracted. The game gives you the freedom to approach missions however you want, whether that’s sneaking around like a ninja or going in guns blazing like Rambo. Just remember, no matter how stealthy you think you are, there’s always a guard with the eyesight of a hawk and the hearing of a bat ready to ruin your day.

Story: The plot is classic Kojima – a mix of deep philosophical questions and moments that make you go, “Wait, what?” One minute you’re pondering the nature of revenge, and the next you’re watching a flaming whale fly through the sky. It’s like Inception meets Animal Planet.

Characters: Big Boss is back, and he’s grumpier than ever. He’s joined by a colorful cast of characters, including a sniper who doesn’t believe in clothes and a dog with an eye patch. Yes, you read that right. A dog. With an eye patch. If that doesn’t scream “Game of the Year,” I don’t know what does.

Graphics: The game looks stunning, with realistic environments and detailed character models. The only downside is that you’ll spend so much time admiring the scenery that you’ll forget you’re supposed to be on a mission. Pro tip: Don’t get distracted by the beautiful sunsets when there’s a tank rolling your way.

Sound: The soundtrack is a mix of 80s hits and epic orchestral scores. Just try not to get “Take On Me” stuck in your head while you’re trying to sneak past enemy guards. And the voice acting? Let’s just say Kiefer Sutherland’s grunts and growls are Oscar-worthy.

Final Verdict: Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a wild ride from start to finish. It’s a game that doesn’t take itself too seriously, and neither should you. So grab your cardboard box, put on your best sneaking suit, and get ready for an adventure that’s as ridiculous as it is fun. Just watch out for those goats.

MGSV mixes sneaking and action really well, letting you choose how to play. The open world adds a lot of freedom, and the story has some great twists that keep you hooked. The graphics are top notch, making the game world feel alive and realistic even now. The sci-fi stuff, like the advanced tech and supernatural enemies, add an exciting twist. Plus, the Fulton extraction system is a blast to use, letting you airlift enemies, vehicles, and even animals. Even after 9 years, it still holds up as an amazing game. I highly recommend it!

The Phantom Pain is a one-of-a-kind game. Gameplay wise, you are getting a lot of bang for your buck and a lot of hours well spent traversing deserts, forests and infiltrating into the enemy's base. There is a lot of content here, so much in fact that 60+ hours of real playtime still isn't enough to fill even half of the game's total completion percentage. And how you choose to play is up to you; 90% of the missions are up to your experimentation and playstyle. The masterpiece status that TPP has received over the years by critics and gamers should be reserved for the gameplay only, because, to be honest, the story is quite overcooked, confusing and some of the Chapter 2 missions Venom Snake goes on have little to do with the plot. Also it is annoying that there is no cutscene viewer and you have to replay some of the older missions from Chapter 1 (except they are harder now) in order to progress. It is basically Metal Gear Solid 4 with more gameplay and a lot less focus on the actual story. It just requires your knowledge of previous MGS titles to understand what's going on and who's who. Definitely not made for a newcomer, in my opinion. At least the cutscenes aren't over an hour long. Despite that huge complaint, I actually love the idea behind Venom Snake and a lot of the themes of carving your own path, erasing your history and "selling the world" to change everything. These themes tie in well with the character, gameplay and the player, it's wonderful. You will see what I mean when you beat the game. Last thing: imagine if this was truly finished. The Phantom Pain is it's own unique perspective on the series, another prequel with goals to inspire the player to do things in their own way, and if this was the unfinished version and this is what they offered, could you imagine how much further this would have pushed the series? It's a tragedy. A lovely tragedy, in hindsight. Farewell, MGSV, hopefully Delta doesn't suck.

Alright, so I just nearly finished Metal Gear V. I want to preface this by saying that I have never played a previous Metal Gear game, although I’m a huge fan of stealth games in general. I played the 31 main missions, as well as a large number of side-ops.

[h3] Gameplay [/h3]

I need to start this review with what is undoubtedly the crowning achievement of this game: the stealth gameplay. You’re given an overwhelming amount of choice in most encounters, and are given an insane number of unique tools to complete your objectives.

The stealth is finely tuned so that many of the systems that underpin the gameplay are opaque. Meaning, you’re never truly able to predict exactly how enemies will respond to a certain input from the player. Sometimes an explosion will cause every enemy in an outpost to go running guns-blazing to its position; sometimes they’ll take cover and prepare for a firefight; sometimes they’ll send a couple of men to check it out while the rest defend a prisoner. When someone catches a glimpse of you, it’s often very difficult to tell if they’ll trust their vision and go check out what they saw, or rather forget about it and go back to their routine. You usually aren’t sure exactly how camouflaged you are from enemies. This sounds like it could feel random or unsatisfying, but it never does, and you’re encouraged to play closer to what a stealthy soldier sneaking through a base would actually probably be like, rather than just learn the systems of the video game and work past them accordingly. It truly is phenomenal to play, and never gets boring across the entire main story.

The mission design wonderfully compliments the gameplay. The missions start off fairly simple and linear, as you’re still getting used to how the systems of the game work, and have relatively few tools available to you. As the game progresses, your objectives become more obscure, and less guided. Near the end of the game, you’re given very simple objectives, such as to assassinate a person before they leave a certain area, or to rescue prisoners as they’re moved between outposts. This is where the genius of the game comes into play, as you’re able to creatively figure out solutions to problems.

If you’re trying to rescue the aforementioned prisoners moving between outposts, you can choose to rescue one or both of them at either outpost, or in transit between them. You can work out distractions to separate the trucks they’re being moved in, or to move the guards away from where they’re being held. There are dozens of ways you can solve each encounter, and I’ve only scratched the surface.

TLDR: the gameplay is very likely the best stealth-action gameplay ever in a video game, easy 5/5.

[h3] Story [/h3]

Alright, so I find it hard to really review the story of this game, as I haven’t played any of the previous games. All I’ll say is that the plot is serviceable even if pretty convoluted, and the characters are decent. I won’t say it’s awful, but it definitely feels like there were some internal troubles at Konami that lead to the story being pretty inconclusive.

Overall, the game feels like a small part in a very large story, which I’ve tried my best to understand, but can’t seem to work it out enough to appreciate this game fully. When the game tries to make big twists and plot developments happen, it stumbles and doesn’t execute what it feels like the developers were going for. Additionally, the game is glacially long and the major story moments are often too spread out to get meaningfully invested in.

I will add that the game’s story and world really do shine in the smaller moments. Rescuing a stray dog, or seeing a group of child soldiers for the first time are examples of moments where it feels like the developers took a break from trying to tie this game into the hopelessly convoluted plot they have set up, and rather focused on creating an interesting world to exist in. I only wish these moments weren’t so often overshadowed by the lacklustre main plot.

[h3] Other Quirks [/h3]

There are some very, very odd game design decisions in this game. Most weapon upgrades are very small and incremental, but are set up so they take real-time for your R&D team to develop. Meaning, I might want an upgrade for a weapon or vehicle, but it’ll take 36 minutes of real-time in-game before I can use it. I’ve heard many of the later upgrades have truly abysmal time-gates on them, as well. This is an incredibly strange choice for a AAA game, and works against the overall pacing and feel of the product. I’ll be honest, this along with many of the upgrades being so resource intensive that they’ll take many dozens of hours past the main story’s conclusion really soured the overall experience for me, and made it feel cheap compared to other major games today.

The base-building and staff management felt like a mixed bag. It was fun to extract high-quality soldiers and watch your base grow, but it’s locked behind an incredibly tedious grind, that I can imagine only hard core fans enjoyed to its conclusion. It killed the game’s pacing for me, and eventually I got so bored with this that by around mission 25 I decided I was happy with the equipment I’d developed, and completely ignored the base-building/development stuff until the end of the game.

[h3] Conclusion [/h3]

Despite all the grievances I have with the more tedious aspects of Metal Gear Solid V, I really did enjoy the game, even if it’s just because the stealth gameplay is so damn engrossing that it kept me hooked until the end. I’d recommend this to anyone who enjoys stealth-action games, and isn’t afraid to wade through a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game design to get to the incredibly open and innovative missions, as well as the occasional good world-building moment.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is an outstanding game that offers a unique blend of open-world exploration, tactical gameplay, and a gripping narrative that is both deep and complex. 

What I Liked:
- Gameplay Mechanics: The game shines in its open-world design, giving players an incredible amount of freedom in how they approach missions. The stealth mechanics are top-notch, and the variety of tools and strategies you can employ keeps the gameplay fresh and engaging.
- Graphics and Sound Design: The visual detail is stunning, from the landscapes to the character models, all brought to life by the FOX Engine. The sound design, including the voice acting and soundtrack, adds an extra layer of immersion.
- Story and Characters: The narrative is both intriguing and emotional, with a focus on themes of revenge, loyalty, and the cost of war. The characters are memorable, particularly Big Boss, who is one of gaming’s most iconic protagonists.

What I Disliked:
- Story Pacing: While the story is compelling, the pacing can be uneven at times. Some players might find the second half of the game to be a bit slower and less satisfying compared to the first.
- Repetitive Missions: There are moments when the game can feel repetitive, especially when certain missions are rehashed with added difficulty instead of offering new content.
- Ending Controversy: The ending has been a point of contention for many fans, as it leaves some plot threads unresolved, which may feel unsatisfactory for long-time followers of the series.

Recommendation:
I highly recommend Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain to fans of the stealth-action genre and to those who enjoy deep, narrative-driven games. Despite some minor flaws, it's a masterpiece in many respects and provides an experience that is both engaging and thought-provoking. Even if you're new to the series, the game offers enough context and excitement to be enjoyed on its own.

Imagine being dropped into an open-world sandbox where your best friend is a horse and your arm is a Swiss Army knife. 

You play as Big Boss, aka Venom Snake, aka the world’s most stoic action figure with a killer mullet. Fresh out of a nine-year coma, you’re on a mission to rebuild your private army, which was blown up because... reasons.
The story is pure Kojima, which means it’s a blend of deep philosophical questions, political intrigue, and moments that make you question whether you’re playing a game or experiencing a hallucination. Trying to explain the plot of the previous games is like trying to summarize a soap opera written by a conspiracy theorist. 

The beauty of MGSV lies in its gameplay. The game hands you a bag of tools, silenced pistols, cardboard boxes, decoys that blast 80s pop hits. The result is a series of missions that can be completed in a million different ways. You can go full Rambo, or you can stealth your way through without anyone knowing you were there.
There’s the Fultoning system. Need more soldiers for your private army? Just attach a balloon to their unconscious bodies and watch them soar into the sky. Cows? Helicopters? Wild animals? If it’s not bolted down, you can Fulton it. By the end of the game, you’ll have a floating zoo that would make Noah’s Ark look understocked.

When you're not out in the field, you’re back at Mother Base, a floating fortress where you can hang out with your pet wolf. It’s also where you can develop all sorts of crazy weapons and gadgets, like rocket-punching arms and inflatable decoys of yourself. Plus, you get to watch as your base fills up with people and animals you’ve abducted, uh, I mean recruited-along the way.

It’s a game where you can spend hours meticulously planning the perfect stealth mission, only to have everything go hilariously wrong when a guard spots you hiding in a cardboard box. But that’s what makes it so memorable.

As far as stealth combat sims go, the Phantom Pain is good, but it has several downsides that you might want to consider before picking it up:

For one, it appears like the gamedevs gave up designing the campaign half way through development and then threw in repeat content for filler. However, this is me just trying out Metal Gear for the first time and don't know if it has always been like this. And the story is kind of hard to follow with how crazy it is.

Second, the menus and controls are insanely complicated for when combat breaks out and you need to make split second decisions. There are 3-4 fully custom drop down menus, and 3-4 ways to pickup and put down items, dive, crouch, etc - which can mean that you might accidently dive out into the middle of a group of soldiers when you meant to crouch - or when you goto hide, accidently end up throwing a grenade because there are so many actions that do similar things, that it gets confusing when ♥♥♥♥ finally goes down.

Third, like the menus and controls, the environment can make your character glitch out and kill you. For instance, when riding the horse or running, you can sometimes get stuck on a bump in the terrain for a moment and wind up killed, and worse still, an automatic quicksave is made when it happens. When climbing ladders, walking into booths, picking things up and down - there are so many overlapping controls that you might be putting down a soldier that was knocked out in a stealth mission and accidently pickup an automatic rifle at the same time, thinking you still have your pistol / silencer and then sound the alarm, simply because the game decided you wanted to. So there are a bunch of quirks that you can run into like this.

Finally, the pacing of the game and story with base building and management minigame is poorly thought out and almost not worth doing. There are so many interruptions, you might have 3x back to back to back cutscenes in a row before being able to play the game again, the worst of these took 30-45 minutes. Then the base building minigame is setup like a cheap mobile simulation game, where it kicks off a timer for 5min, 10min, 30min, 60min, 1day or more, while your workers "go do something," so the feature is ultimately just trash. However, it's still worth passively engaging in while you run stealth missions. So there are definitely some questionable features put into the game that seem to have no real purpose other than just to piss away your time for no real good reason.

So if there were ever a mixed review option, the Phantom Pain would certainly fall into that category - so unless you're planning to play the game for the stealth combat sim, there are some parts of the game that would definitely be hit or miss with some people.

While the story isn't as quirky as the past entries, it's still good. If you can't look past that, the gameplay definitely makes up for it. I probably wouldn't sell the world for this game, but only time will tell. 
Also D-Dog is a good boy, best MG character.

MGSV was the last major publisher game with soul. 

A lot of people who have negative opinions of the game (I interpret) have clouded judgement based on the mess that was behind the scenes, and the drama feuding between konami and kojima; what we could've gotten vs what we got. The perspective is understandable and fair, but the game we got is still extremely good, and forever unique. 

The general gameplay loop is its most unique and fun aspect. It scratches the kleptomaniac itch. Scout for soldiers, find the best, crawl across landscape planning a way to abduct the ones you want, build stronger merc group and lead raids or do mercenary missions, repeat. This is what'll keep you going for hours. Not to mention your soldiers upgrading over time, and other activities like collecting animals, equipment, and materials. It's simple and effective. 

The stealth gameplay is one of the most player attentive i've experienced. Every move and decision impacts the outcome of a mission. The examples to give are too many, but some include soldiers being alerted by sound, being alerted by lights being shot out far from them, being alerted by missed shots, haze acting as a cloak, FOV changes based on time of day. Its not all, and maybe sounds very basic at face value, but very few games tend to get those all simultaneously right, while being fair to the player.

In regards to the mainstream opinion, I feel the story and concepts are not as overly serious as people claim it is. The main story definitely has darker moments when compared to prior metal gear games (GZ beats it, though), and less personal funny interactions with side characters, but it balances out with its a fair share of comical and "rule of cool" moments throughout the game. Diamond dog, finding a cassette tape of a guy with diarrhea (you can use in port-a-pottys, and soldiers will walk away), prisoners yelling "ya ha hooo" when fulton extracted, inflatable soldiers traps, and a sonar arm that makes a matrix sound for some early game examples. It isn't too depressing, and has that metal gear charm.

I don't want to brush under the rug the stuff that is/ went wrong. It's not a flawless game by any means. Lonely sandbox at times, reused levels, bad vehicle controls, predictable NPC pathing, environment's bumps may toggle you out of crouch, and enemies can (rarely) see you at impossible angles.

I will reiterate, it could've been better, but what is provided is over all a very solid and fun game.

Being an open world game was also an odd choice, and it does make you wonder how much different it'd be if it had a more linear structure. There are a few common things that people bring up when talking about Metal Gear Solid V: the nigh untouchable gameplay (fine-tuned to perfection), the exceptional music (both original and older), and how bad the story is - bar from a few standout moments. One of these things is a lie.

The unfinished story is brilliant; it is largely well told, emotionally poignant and resonant, and fundamentally powerful.

There will be spoilers from here on out.

The only thing I’ve seen praised is that it has standout moments—like the one referenced above—but standout moments are only possible with a strong underlying plot that leads into them and gives them emotional weight. If you give these scenes yo other games, which don't have the same foundations as Metal Gear Solid V, then they are ruined. Quiet's emotional goodbye rendered unto an apathetic audience and the 'phantom pain' rendered powerless/

Yes, the story is unfinished—BY A MISSION—but one should prioritise judging it first by what is there, and what is there is a genuinely impressive anti-war story. The key ideas, themes, the main bulk of the story, and especially the characters are fully developed and it leads on well to the following metal gear games - even if its current state lends itself more to a sole experience than a sequel (which is probably how most people enjoy it, considering in the present day it is the most popular starting point into the Metal Gear franchise).

Sure, it’s no MGS3 or MGS1, but Christ, those are amongst the best stories in gaming. Saying it’s not the best metal gear story means absolutely nothing. It’s still a brilliant game story.

No, it’s not flawless. Personally, I would introduce Code Talker earlier and have that development spread out more so the second chapter isn’t so full of cutscenes compared to the first. Some plot moments feel weak, but these are generally isolated instances.

Then there’s the discussion of the pacing. This has no merit whatsoever. To give an example, first consider Macbeth - which increases its pace past Act 3, especially as that is the point that Macbeth's fate is sealed. From that point on, he had no autonomy and was speeding towards his doom. A similar case can be made for the diamond dogs. In fighting skull face and Cipher, they had engaged so thoroughly and on such a large scale with warfare and the parasites - themselves a symbol of warfare - that a slower, more plotted development like that in Chapter 1 would feel utterly nonsensical. To give a metaphor they dove head first into the deep raging sea and now have to face the consequences - liberties are curtailed, the staff expanded, as the diamond dogs speed towards their ‘end’. The ‘Big Boss is watching you’ is just one sign of this - although one does think this is pretty weakly introduced, the idea and the prerequisites are certainly there. It just needs more exposition. The similarities to Macbeth don't stop there. The Diamond Dogs and Big Boss are losing control in chapter 2. The missions revolve around fighting a war they aren't even in, forever prolonging this state of war to ease a phantom pain, and trying to understand what is happening to them after it has happened.

MGSV is quite literally a story of a destructive spiral of warfare and vengeance. This is perfectly embodied in the parasites - whom to fight you quite literally have to resort to oppression, which spirals out of control, and the complete sapping of all liberties. It is no coincidence that the cure requires forgoing one’s last link to reality - a family. Quite literally, to fight and win a war, one must sacrifice their all and bring in more soldiers, endlessly enslaving them in a cycle of vengeance. This includes the children, who are, and the game made this clear, continually trained. They don’t try to rehabilitate them or send them to the relevant authorities whom they have contact with; they train them as soldiers, they sack their freedom, and they rebel. To win a war, they inspire more vengeance and the destructive cycle is furthered. 

Even the omission of mission 51 is interesting from a storytelling perspective. It leaves it far more open - the mother base and the diamond dogs are weakened by the parasite, repeated losses, a fall in morale, and the overall cycle of vengeance. What we have left is the threat left in the open; there is no absolute conclusion; it does not go away or is not in any way resolved. This cycle of vengeance goes on, the phantom pain persists, and warfare as the ultimate result is brought closer to hand. To put it simply, the endless war is the interesting idea here - and the open, truncated ending furthers that. That being said, I've seen the unfinished cutscene and played the other Metal Gear games, and the better outcome would still have been actually to be able to play this mission. And this isn't just some tenuous conclusion drawn to make the story sound stronger, this is basically Skull Face's objective, unleashing Sahalanthrapus to facilitate this endless cycle of revenge - this phantom pain - and prolong the cold war. There are even multiple audio tapes that tell you what the outcome of this could be. And by eaving it in the open it almost makes it far stronger.

Then there’s the second parasite - itself a consequence of the cycle of vengeance hatred and war that they have furthered because of this ‘phantom pain’ - a parasite that causes them to seek freedom and escape, which is punished by death. The end result is that the only way out the soldiers truly know or want is an honourable death itself. If this isn’t a metaphor, then I don’t know what it is.

I mean, look, the final level is kind of poorly placed exposition, but it can be understood through the rushed development, and even in its current state its not like this exposition came out of nowhere. The main revelation in this was hinted at throughout the game, most prominently with Volgin, with some obvious but good foreshadowing that the player is not actually Big Boss. Could it be improved: yes. But don't pretend that the other Metal Gear games don't suffer from similar story-telling problems.

And this doesn't even begin to cover the full breadth or depth of the story, including the successful character arcs of Miller, Huey, and especially Quiet, or even the importance of the abundance of Moby ♥♥♥♥ allusions to building and completing this story.

So then, with exceptional music, gameplay as perfect as it is, and a story far more successful and far less messy and incomplete than people claim, the game really is the best Metal Gear game.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a game that leaves an indelible mark on the player, a testament to Hideo Kojima's vision and Kojima Productions' mastery of the gaming medium. This game isn't just another entry in the beloved Metal Gear series; it's a genre-bending masterpiece that offers a truly unforgettable gaming experience.

The game's immersive quality is immediately evident, pulling the player into a complex, interactive adventure that combines elements of hard science fiction, dark psychological drama, and surreal horror. Kojima and his team have woven these diverse threads together, creating a narrative tapestry that is as emotionally powerful as it is intellectually stimulating. It's a game that doesn't just entertain; it challenges and provokes thought, pushing the boundaries of what a video game can be.

From a design perspective, The Phantom Pain is a remarkable achievement. Its rich sandbox environment allows for emergent gameplay, letting players craft their own stories and experiences. The open-world design is expansive and meticulously detailed, providing a vast playground for players to explore and conquer. The inclusion of a wide array of gadgets and weapons adds layers of strategy and customization, ensuring that no two playthroughs are the same. This is all set against a backdrop of captivating storytelling, filled with challenging bosses, beautifully executed cutscenes, and those classic fourth-wall-breaking moments that Metal Gear fans have come to love.

Technically, the game is near flawless. The production values are sky-high, delivering outstanding visuals and a phenomenal soundtrack that complements the game's tone perfectly. The controls are tight and responsive, making even the most complex maneuvers feel intuitive. The voice acting is top-notch, with each member of the cast delivering performances that bring their characters to life.

In summary, Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a visceral, emotionally powerful masterpiece that transcends the medium of video games. It's brilliant, innovative, and undeniably true to the roots of the Metal Gear series. While it's a must-play for fans and newcomers alike, I recommend waiting for a sale or seeking out a used copy due to the full price in the PlayStation store. Either way, it's an experience that will be remembered for years to come, a shining example of what video games can achieve when ambition and artistry meet.

It's an okay open world third person shooter. Lacking in story, especially for a Metal Gear game, and what is there isn't particularly good. Level design feels worse than Ground Zeroes, likely because they needed to design different bases to fill the open world. Speaking of which, the open world has the classic problem of feeling empty and static. Weapon acquisition is largely the same as MGS: Peace Walker, but many of the weapons that were fun to use there aren't present here. No co-op either, so forget about co-op weapons. If you're a fan of classic Metal Gear Solid games and their challenge, you'll probably have the most fun trying no-traces runs of missions, rather than following the more loose intended experience. Not all missions can be run that way, however. Side ops don't track how you completed them, unlike main ops, so there's not much point in restricting yourself while playing them unless you plan on being your own ref. They also feel repetitive. You're forced online when you start up the game, and you'll be forced to make your staff vulnerable to being stolen by other players via making a FOB unless you go offline every time you launch. The offline resource cap is minuscule, and the game actively steals most of your resources and moves them to the online-only FOB whenever it has a connection. The mod Infinite Heaven has options to fix some of the issues here, like random patrols in the open world, custom difficulty, automatic offline launching, and support for community side ops. Grab it on sale if you need a solo third person shooter/stealth game. Avoid if you want something like prior MGS games.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain - A Masterpiece with a Haunting Void

(Introduction)

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain, released in 2015 by Konami and developed by Kojima Productions, stands as a remarkable entry in the legendary Metal Gear series. Renowned for its exceptional gameplay mechanics and intricate storytelling, it’s a game that excels in many ways but leaves players with a poignant sense of loss and incompletion. The emotional weight of Snake’s journey, coupled with an unfinished narrative, makes The Phantom Pain both a triumph and a tragedy in the annals of gaming history.

(Gameplay Excellence)

The gameplay in The Phantom Pain is nothing short of phenomenal. Set in vast, open-world environments, the game offers unparalleled freedom in how players approach missions. Whether sneaking through enemy lines under the cover of darkness or orchestrating elaborate tactical assaults, the variety of strategies and tools at your disposal is staggering. The advanced AI, dynamic weather, and day-night cycles add layers of depth, ensuring that no two missions ever feel the same.

The introduction of the Fulton recovery system, allowing players to extract enemies, vehicles, and even animals back to Mother Base, adds a unique strategic element. Building and managing Mother Base becomes an integral part of the experience, fostering a deeper connection to the game’s world and characters.

(Emotional Storytelling)

The narrative of The Phantom Pain is rich and complex, delving into themes of revenge, loss, and the cost of war. Playing as Venom Snake, players witness the harrowing journey of a man seeking retribution while grappling with the ghosts of his past. The game’s storytelling is delivered through a combination of in-game events, cinematic cutscenes, and cassette tapes, creating a layered and immersive experience.

However, it’s the emotional weight of Snake’s journey that truly stands out. The pain of having to kill former comrades, the heartbreaking departure of Quiet, and the haunting aftermath of the incident that shattered Mother Base all contribute to a narrative that is both powerful and devastating. These moments resonate deeply, leaving players feeling the profound sorrow and emptiness that Snake himself endures.

(A Haunting Void)

Despite its many strengths, The Phantom Pain is notorious for its incomplete story. The game ends abruptly, leaving many narrative threads unresolved. Chapter 2, in particular, feels rushed and fragmented, with crucial plot points left hanging. The infamous "Episode 51," which was cut from the final release, provides a glimpse of what could have been a more satisfying and complete conclusion to the saga.

This sense of incompletion is a significant source of frustration for many fans. The game’s potential for a truly epic and cohesive story was evident, making its sudden halt all the more disheartening. The unfinished nature of the narrative leaves a void that lingers long after the credits roll, overshadowing the brilliance of the gameplay and storytelling that came before.

(Conclusion)

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a masterclass in game design, offering an exceptional gameplay experience and a story that is both captivating and emotionally resonant. Yet, it is also a game marked by profound sadness and a haunting sense of incompletion. The pain of Snake’s journey, the loss of comrades, and the abrupt ending leave players with a deep sense of emptiness, reflecting the game’s title in a very literal sense.

While The Phantom Pain stands as a testament to Hideo Kojima’s visionary talent, it also serves as a poignant reminder of what might have been. It’s a game that deserved a complete and fitting conclusion, and its absence is felt keenly by all who have experienced its highs and lows. Despite this, it remains an essential play for any fan of the series, a brilliant yet bittersweet chapter in the Metal Gear legacy.

[h2]The Best Worst Game I Have Played[/h2]

MGS 5 is a game I have [b]very[/b] mixed feelings about, but I still am leaning towards recommending it in the end. There are several key areas I would like to write my opinion on, such as:

1) Great but unfinished story 
Putting the most conflicting stuff out of the way first – the story. If you’re a fan of the older Metal Gear Solid games, you might expect a deep, twisty plot with huge amount of cutscenes and dialogues. Sadly, MGS 5 doesn’t quite hit the mark here. Don't get me wrong - what we ended up with is still good: the directing is awesome, the story events make you feel and care for the characters, even for the tertiary staff on Mother Base at some points. I won't go into the conflict Hideo Kojima had with Konami, but the story in this game had the potential to grow into something truly brilliant. Hearing [i]"I won't scatter your sorrow to the heartless sea. I will always be with you. Plant your roots in me. I won't see you end as ashes. You're all diamonds."[/i] in that one cutscene literally sent shivers down my spine at that very moment. Unfortunately, in the second half of the game it really feels like the game was abandoned halfway through. Makes me very sad for what we could get but did not.

2) Awful Online Mechanics
Now to the horrible part – the grindy online mechanics. I don't know whose idea it was, but it's bad, very bad. The whole Mother Base and the Forward Operating Base stuff management gets pretty tedious and annoying. Building up your base and staff, dealing with online invasions and constantly managing resources becomes a grind. I think it takes away from the otherwise stellar gameplay experience by forcing the player to do things that are objectively inferior to the main focus of the game, which is stealth action. 

3) Awesome Gameplay and Stealth Mechanics
Where the game really shines though is the gameplay. The open-world design, the addition of Fulton, the addition of different buddies and Pequod fire support really spiced up and improved the already great formula of the previous MGS games by adding the freedom of approach to your targets. The sheer amount of gadgets and mechanics to play with makes even grinding same side ops fun. 

The game gives you a lot of control and variety but at the same time constantly pushes you to explore new tactics by reacting to your playstyle. It adapts and expects you to adapt. 
- You sneak like a ghost and complete your objectives without interacting with enemies? At some point expect more cameras around checkpoints and bases;
- You headshot enemies to sleep with the tranquilizer pistol a lot? Expect more enemies to wear helmets and put up decoys to confuse you.
- You blast your way through with brute force and air support? Expect more soldiers to wear body armor and have RPGs etc.

Even with the undercooked story and the absolutely abhorrent online grind, the stellar gameplay totally makes up for it. I lost hours upon hours just experimenting and having a blast.

So yeah, Metal Gear Solid 5 might be a very mixed bag of a game, but I still recommend it. For all its shortcomings it's still one of the best stealth action games out there.

P.S. Special thanks to the Duran Duran band and their song "Invisible" which resonated with me so much that I came back to play the game again and decided to write this review. Thanks guys, you made the best Metal Gear song that never was.

I never understood the hype about this game, but now I get it.

[h1] Technical performance [/h1]
This game looks incredibly good and runs smoothly on maximum settings. I run the game on Linux using Vulkan and it is rock stable with great performance.

[h1] Technology [/h1]
Looks great. The modern technologies like DLSS are not available, but this game is 10 years old and looks incredible. The developers used a variety of good optimization techniques, such as dynamic LOD, dynamic resolution/sharpness (e.g. objects become blurry with the distance) and I imagine - simply a good game engine. 
The engine has got incredible shadows and realistic weather system. In fact, it's one of few games with such realistic weather system, where the daytime changes and the climate follows with its peculiar conditions. I can only imagine this game was insanely competitive in 2015.
The models are detailed, the animations are well crafted. The game has got many unique gameplay loops, such as building your own base, developing your own weapons through the crafting system. On top of that - items and blueprints collecting, animal catching (lol) and of course the well-known "Fulton" system.

[h1] Gameplay/bugs [/h1]
Absolutely nothing. EVERYTHING IS WORKING. 10 years later I can still log into the servers!
I can get the daily rewards and it seems that the game also receives patches. There is nothing to complain about and the fact that I can run this game on Linux with absolutely 0 issues is a big deal to me.
Lots of respect to the studio for providing such long lived support.

[h1] Genre [/h1]
I never understood Metal Gear Solid series. I always perceived them as some kind of eccentric game series created by a weird game studio. I did not understand the story, the gameplay, the lore.
Honestly, I still do not, the difference is - I have played the game and now I get the general idea. It's absurd, it's sarcastic. It is immersive, realistic, yet also abstract and unpredictible.
I have hard time pinning down the "genre". It is one of the kind.

What does it remind me of? In terms of combat and the game's world - it does remind me of Far Cry 2. Far Cry 2 was one of my favourite games at the time and mostly due to very innovative technologies in the game, as well as very good AI, large map and tons of items/quests to deal with in spare time (the diamonds are 1:1 the same mechanic).
MGS 5 is Far Cry 2 but better. The map is large, quests are pretty interesting, realistic but also abstract. The enemies are very smart and the game's difficulty is demanding. I really like how balanced the game is.
It does not approach the story seriously, but yet the simulation in the game is very satisfying and gives you off the vibe of being a real mercenary.

You can also choose from many different styles, weapons. There is no pre-programmed route of actions. I catch myself playing stealth just to mess things up by not noticing a hidden soviet soldier, who raises the alarm and calls the entire base on me. What do you do in that case? Exactly, it's challenging and fun, you need to think fast and forge your own way out. 

[h1] Value [/h1]
Currently the price is more than fair and I got the game on a discount. I can't wait to buy the other Metal Gear Solid games, including the newest one that is announced in the Store.
I would put this game next to Devil Mary Cry, Elden Ring, Cyberpunk, Thymesia. One of few games that is fun and knows what it is about.

There was a time in my life where I would rate every Metal Gear game a 10/10 on video game sites and pretend to myself that I was being objective. After all, it had to be perfect - it was Metal Gear, one of my favourite series. Reaching the age of maturity (which, it seems, was 25 in my case) and playing through The Phantom Pain a second time forced me to accept something. It isn't perfect. The series isn't perfect. The first Metal Gear has to be played on mute because its 8-bit sounds are aural torture, navigating the Big Shell in Metal Gear Solid 2 can be frustrating at times, and The Phantom Pain is unfinished. This doesn't mean it's not a great game, just like Metal Gear is still a great series.

Hell, it's the greatest unfinished game ever made. It's among the few games that define the eighth console generation. But, on my second playthrough, it also left me feeling empty.

Much has been made of Konami interfering with the genius of Kojima, so much so that anything I try to write feels trite. This game wasn't developed in ideal conditions, and the publisher shoulders a large portion of the blame for that. But I also feel that Kojima made some missteps too, as I'll explain.

Before that, however, we must laud the Phantom Pain where it's deserved. It is an absolute masterclass in sandbox stealth. There are so many ways to carry out missions, limited by your imagination. The simplest way to explain MGS V's gameplay is, "If you can think it, you can do it." If you've got to take out a tank battalion, you can do it explosively with landmines and rocket launchers. Or, you can let them reach their station, wait for a sandstorm and attach Fulton balloons to them - in and out, like the storm itself swept them away.

If you've got a hostage to rescue, you can invade the camp where he's being held and interrogate the guards about where they're holding him; free him, and be on your way. Or you can wait till they're transporting him, lie down with a sniper rifle on the opposing mountaintop, shoot the jeep driver, and then move in for the rescue.

If you're feeling lazy in a seek-and-destroy mission, you can just call in multiple airstrikes and be done with it. There really is a lot you can do in MGS V.

The enemies aren't complete idiots as well. They take note of your tactics. If you prefer infiltrating at night, they'll start wearing night vision goggles. If you're a headshot junkie, they'll be issued helmets. As the enemies adapt, you're obliged to too.

Few games are optimized as well as MGS V. This game worked perfectly even on my old craptop, which lacked a GPU. There is no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ way this game should run so well on seventh-gen consoles and 2010-era computers, but it does. Whoever programmed this, I love you.

Unfortunately, around the time MGS: Peace Walker was being developed, Hideo Kojima's son did something terrible. He told his dad, "This is ♥♥♥♥! All the cool kids are playing Monster Hunter now." Kojima took this to heart, and decided that from now on, MGS would also be a mission-based series. This, I feel, is to its detriment. For all the banal jokes about its cutscene length, MGS was originally conceptualized as a relatively short game that adults could play - they didn't have to care about levels, or collectibles, or multiple objectives.

MGS V is the exact opposite of that philosophy. A lot of time is spent deploying and taking off in helicopters, and if there's one thing that you can think but can't do, it's that I wish the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ helicopter could fly me across the open world from side mission to side mission, rather than having to go back to the level select menu or make the long trips manually. Base management is gratifying, but also tangential to why I play Metal Gear games. You spend a lot of the game on the verge of brokeness, and have to be very selective about the items you develop. You also have to wait for raw materials to process before you can do so - which means you could have all the fuel, metal and GMP needed to build a new platform, but can't because SOMEBODY back at Mother Base is this close to getting fired.

There are things I love and hate about the plot of MGS V. The foremost of the former is that the cutscene direction is award-worthy: this game really consolidated what would become Kojima's signature style in the coming years. Almost all cutscenes are 'filmed' from a single camera in one continuous shot, lending the game its grit. On a second playthrough, it's incredible how in-your-face the plot twists are, yet I didn't spot them the first time.

Hideo Kojima has never shied away from wearing his influences on his sleeve, and he sure incorporated some classics into this one: 1984, Brave New World, Lord of the Flies, Heart of Darkness and Apocalypse Now... There are nods to all of them - some subtle, some not. Watch out for the pig's head and the 'Big Boss is Watching' posters. The music selection is great too.

However, there's no getting around the fact that this is very much an unfinished game. The pacing of the story is completely off, with the beginning and end of Chapter 1 being the most substantial portion - by the last few missions, I was thinking, "Boy, they're really speeding up, aren't they?"

After that, the game's basically over. In Act 2, you're handed a collection of already-completed missions to repeat under specific conditions, with the odd story bit nestled here and there. It's immensely unsatisfying. The cutscenes are great, but half their context has been ripped out. The number of story-heavy cassette tapes also jumps up, which I assume was Kojima trying to finish fleshing out the plot in whatever way he could once development ground to a halt.
