**Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain – A Detailed Review**

*Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain*, developed by Konami and directed by Hideo Kojima, stands as a monumental achievement in the stealth action genre. Released in 2015 for multiple platforms, this game marks a significant evolution in the series, set against the backdrop of the 1980s during the Cold War.

**Plot and Setting**

The story follows Punished "Venom" Snake, also known as Big Boss, who awakens from a coma to rebuild his private army, Diamond Dogs, and seek revenge on those who destroyed his previous organization. The game’s expansive open-world environments in Afghanistan and Central Africa serve as a compelling stage for this tale of revenge, loss, and the futility of war.

**Gameplay Mechanics**

*The Phantom Pain* breaks new ground with its open-world design, offering players unprecedented freedom in how they approach missions. Stealth remains a core element, but the game provides a wide array of tools and tactics. Players can use vehicles, weapons, and gadgets like the Fulton recovery system to create a playstyle that suits them best.

The game introduces a dynamic, real-time world where enemy bases adapt to the player’s actions. For example, if you frequently use headshots, enemies will start wearing helmets. This adaptive AI ensures that each encounter remains fresh and challenging, encouraging players to continually adapt their strategies.

**Base Management and Development**

A key feature of *The Phantom Pain* is the management of Mother Base. Players can recruit soldiers and prisoners of war to expand their base, unlocking new technologies and capabilities. This adds a strategic layer to the game, requiring players to balance resources and manage their growing army effectively.

**Graphics and Sound**

Powered by the Fox Engine, *The Phantom Pain* delivers stunning visuals. The open-world environments are richly detailed, with realistic weather effects and day-night cycles that influence gameplay. Character models are exceptionally lifelike, and the motion capture performances enhance the game’s cinematic quality.

The sound design is another high point, featuring a soundtrack that blends iconic 80s tracks with original compositions to heighten the game’s tension and emotion. Voice acting, led by Kiefer Sutherland as Snake, is superb, adding depth to the characters and the narrative.

**Legacy and Impact**

*Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain* has left an indelible mark on the gaming industry, redefining the possibilities of open-world games. Its intricate gameplay systems, compelling story, and rich world-building set new standards for the genre. Despite some controversy over its development and the game's incomplete narrative, it is celebrated as one of the greatest video games of its generation.

In conclusion, *Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain* is a testament to Hideo Kojima’s visionary approach to game design. It offers a masterful blend of stealth, action, and strategy, cementing its place in the history of gaming. Whether you are a series veteran or a newcomer, *The Phantom Pain* is an essential experience that exemplifies the pinnacle of gaming artistry.

As a long-time fan of the Metal Gear Solid series, I had high hopes for Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain. Unfortunately, the game fell short of my expectations in several key areas.

Firstly, the story, which has always been a cornerstone of the MGS series, feels fragmented and incomplete. The narrative lacks the depth and intrigue of its predecessors, leaving many plot points unresolved and characters underdeveloped. The abrupt ending and the sense that content was cut or rushed further detract from the overall experience.

Gameplay, while innovative with its open-world design, quickly becomes repetitive. Missions often feel like variations of the same objectives, lacking the creativity and variety that previous games in the series offered. The expansive world, although beautiful, feels empty and devoid of meaningful content, reducing exploration to a chore rather than an adventure.

Moreover, the base management aspect, which initially seemed like a promising addition, becomes tedious and feels disconnected from the main gameplay loop. It often feels like busywork rather than a compelling feature.

In conclusion, Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain fails to live up to the legacy of its predecessors. While it introduces some new ideas, it ultimately feels like a missed opportunity, lacking the depth and cohesion that fans have come to expect from the series.

As far as being a Metal Gear game goes, MGSV fills the gap between Big Boss' story and Solid Snake's story pretty well, albeit it certainly has its flaws. Hideo Kojima claims the game isn't unfinished, but playing it makes it pretty obvious that isn't true.

Gameplay wise, the open world is a nice addition. Granted theres only so much to explore and the camps can look kind of  samey, but going to each one and doing whatever missions that apply is fun. While you have way more weapons and tools to choose from than other games, if you either opt to go in loud or sneak around you'll be using the same stuff 90% of the time. Trying to sneak without killing? Fulton and tranquilizer pistol. Trying to cause as much destruction as possible? Whatever the most powerful weapons you have are. That being said, there's different angles and methods to get into bases, but that's really where all the variance is. A big plus is mother base. You don't just get thrown into the open world, but you get to collect all sorts of things and even have the added mechanic of fultoning certain soldiers you come across.

The most negative aspect of the gameplay, though, is how repetitive it is. Since the game was unfinished a lot of things are reused. A huge chunk of the second part of the story involves repeating missions with extra attributes, or revisiting locations over and over again with a few things changed around. Even upgrading mother base, as fun and beneficial as it might be, gets tedious as getting the resources you need to upgrade everything correctly would take countless hours of grinding. It's not quite as bad as Ground Zeroes but my God it's lazy. Blame Konami.

That all being said, the game is very good at immersing you in everything. The aesthetic combines 80s mercenaries with the class Metal Gear look perfectly. Honestly, gathering up funds just to get some new armor or paint is worth it for the looks. But the best highlight is collecting casette tapes and listening to Kojima's music taste while traversing Afghanistan and Africa. It puts a really nice spin on everything and just makes the game that much more fun.

As far as the story goes it is extremely unfortunate that Kojima couldn't finish the game. It's easily one of my favorites in the series, aside from Skullface being a pretty underwhelming villain in the end as wasted potential for a character. The game comes to a pretty abrupt end, and even with the extra information we can find online it's still pretty clear that there's more to the story missing between that and Solid Snake's mission in Outer Heaven. Additionally, while I understand Venom having a different voice and behavior, he's way too quiet. And as much as I love them Ocelot and Miller talk too much, although that's moreso when you're out in the world than during the story. The first part of the game was formed in a great way, but the second one just seems like a mishmash of confusing main plot points. With the way it forms up, the whole storyline of Venom getting twisted by revenge falls flat on its face. The story of MGSV is full of potential and great characters, but didn't get the time and effort it deserves.

Despite it's clear unfinished attributes and sometimes repetitive gameplay, MGSV is still a very fun game to play, even grind to an extent, which really speaks on the quality of what was worked on, regardless if it made the final cut or not. Enjoy it as the last truly good and faithful Metal Gear game, even if it doesn't live up to some of its predecessors.

If you want to play what is arguably the best sandbox third person shooter then play this game. You have a ton of different ways to complete missions no matter if you want to do them loud or in stealth. Just keep in mind there is a real-time timer on researching new gear and the higher tier the gear the more it'll cost you to use it. But, if that frustrates you then you can easily mod around it.

Now, as for why I originally didn't recommend this game. If you want to play this game mainly for the story then you're going to be very disappointed  by the ending, because there is no ending. The game got released before the story was finished so you end up with an abrupt plot twist out of nowhere after playing a few missions that you've already played, but with challenges added to them.
Don't get me wrong, this game has some great moments of storytelling. But honestly that just adds salt to the wound since there's so many interesting ideas and plots that don't get answered and sadly never will now that Kojima is no longer working on the series.
This game is essentially the death of a franchise, even if Konami has decided to bring it back from the dead.

Let the hum of the AC chopper wipe away your thoughts and enter the hypnogogic blindness of Venom Snake. I sunk 200 hours into this on PS3/PS4 before buying this copy.

Это будет тот самый негативный обзор легенды от душного токсичного геймера, критикующего ЛУГЕНДУ.
Потому что легендой он был 20 лет назад.
В игре всё работает =) Но при этом в какой-то момент перестаёт работать или так напрягает, что сил терпеть это нет. Как говорил один пухляш "Хватит это терпеть!" Итак, по порядку подгорания стула под тактической попой:
1) Не рабочий стелс. Супердиверсант Снейк, будучи профессионалом проникновения, во всех кат сценах бегает с оружием без глушителей, а вне сцен нам даётся 1 глушитель на одно оружие. Но нюанс в том, что он отлетает после первого же магазина. Почему нельзя таскать с собой запасные - загадка уровня Нибиру. Как и загадка, почему нельзя таскать с собой, например, метательные ножи. И вообще ножи, чтобы можно было сразу убивать пешек, а не брать в гача-захват. Оружие с глушителем, кстати, надо изучить =) Почему нельзя просто купить глушители на чёрном рынке - брат прошлой загадки. Кроме оружия, стелс руинит сам Кодзима. Правила у него рабочие, а вот сюжет он вписать в них не может, поэтому регулярно подкидывает игроку детей в калашами, у которых радиус обзора больше чем у взрослых (и точность как у спецназа ГРУ, лол), суперсолдат которые плевать хотели на урон от пуль и которые видят как коты ночью пачку вискаса, а так же обычных пешек, которые уже по второму выстрелу всем городом точно определяют, откуда стрелял снайпер и лупят по игроку так, словно с пелёнок учились стрелять. В те моменты, когда стелс работает (то есть когда миссии самые не сюжетные и Кодзима не вмешивается) игра через стелс приятная, окей. 
2) Не рабочая боёвка. Зачем оружию параметр проникающей способности, если вне зависимости от калибра каску и броню оружие не пробивает с первого выстрела? =) Даже вплотную. Условный парабелум и 7.62 равны =) Каски из адамантия наверное. Или вот, почему ИИ с пулемёта очередью в 5 выстрелов на 150м попадает точно так же метко как и автоматчик с калаша на 150м? Параметр кучности знает что он в игре есть? А параметр дальности? Или они, традиционно, только для игрока? Да и в целом стрелять из оружия...ну не то чтобы комфортно. Даже скорее просто нон-стопом чувствуешь себя бездомным, который оказался в дорогом ресторане. Ты крутой, купил нефтяную платформу под базу, воруешь танки с помощью воздушного шара, покупаешь вертолёты и имеешь на счету миллионы шекелей, но не можешь купить оптику на свой ПП, сдвоеный магазин и пачку глушителей, гоняя с одним, потому что Кодзима решил что изучать приблуды для оружия будет прикольней. Как итог - вражеские снайперы бегают с ЛЦУ, а я нет =)  Спустя 40 часов я этот вопрос решил, но блин, хороша ложка к обеду. Перестрелки в играх Юбисофт и то приятнее (Прости меня, Господи, что похвалил юбиков всуе, но они правда в кой-то веки выглядят неплохо). А ещё у нас есть вертолёт, который летая кругами на точке эвакуации, имея полную пачку ракет и авиационную вольмидулку, не отбивается от наземных аборигенов =) Как они с калашей вертушку сбили?.. Я не знаю...
3) Сюжет. Я прошёл 30 эпизодов обязательных миссий и почти все доступные доп задания. И знаете что? Пейн, я сюжета не чувствую. Лишь изредка Кодзима вспоминал, что у него сюжетная игра, а не "стропильня" в открытом(нет) мире и подкидывал откровенно кринжовые референсы в стиле "ауф, два волка сила, вынесите всех красиво". Серьёзно перестаёшь воспринимать происходящее уже к серединке Афганистана, ибо кринж, господи. И семья во все поля. Форсаж с этими моралистами даже рядом не плавает.
4) Титры. Да-да, они самые. Первый раз за 25 лет игрового опыта жалуюсь на титры. Кодзима в начале КАЖДОГО эпизода напоминает, кто его (эпизод) создал =) И иногда в конце. ЧСВ выше МКСа. Если сложить стопкой каждую строчку, где Кодзима упоминает себя, то можно построить лестницу в рай.
5) Дизайн мира. Почти всегда это прямая кишка. Встречаются участки местности, где можно пообходить, но передо мной так часто стелют прямую дорожку, окружённую "НЕПРОХОДИМЫМИ" скалами, на которые и ребёнок залезет, что я часто задавался вопросом - зачем было городить большую карту? Просто сделай отдельные локации, не мучай ж**у. Но больше всего меня порадовал особняк, в котором почти все двери были закрыты, чтобы СОВСЕМ НЕНАВЯЗЧИВО подсказать игроку как ему стоит идти.
6)Нулевой сторитейлинг. Что за герой? Кто они такие? Что вообще происходит? Ответа нет. Не у всех в этом мире были все серии плоек. У меня вот была только первая. Чё там было между первой и пятой? Даже банальной внутриигровой справки нет. Зато есть 100 миллионов аудиокассет. Надеюсь, мои дети когда-нибудь их дослушают(нет).

I have played MGS 1,2,3,4, and Peacewalker and was excited to see the final game in the series. I have never been more disappointed in a game. 


1. Time: This game greatly suffers from being an open world game. The travel takes a very long time, and there's nothing to do along the way, except kill the same 4 station guards every time (if you don't, and they spot you, you lose fame). EVERYTHING in this game takes WAY longer than it needs to (travel, scanning enemies, etc). Even exploring the HOME BASE takes a few minutes to get from one section to another (not that there's much to do there anyway). 

2. Level layout: In the other games, despite most of the game taking place in the same facility, the rooms are all very different, making you actually think about where to go. The movement is very precise, and there are many ways to handle encounters.

In MGS5, every "level" is a small facility with very similar level layout. They are either a set of 10 one or two room buildings (where 8 of them are empty, one of them has a little cash, and the last has your objective) or a small facility such as a courtyard prison with a wall with a few rooms in it. This leads the game to have a very repetitive loop of sneak up on one guard to find which building has your objective, sneak over to the building, and then leave.

3. Enemy AI: In previous games, the AI is smart, it is actively trying to kill you. If you do get spotted, you have to get out of sight and hide away until they lose track of you. This leads to the player having to think through their decisions and when they do get caught, find a place to fall back to regroup. 

In MGS5, the enemies are incredibly stupid. They almost go out of their way to get killed (standing out in the open, or revealing themselves when they spot you). When they DO see you, you get about 10 seconds of slow mo to take them out before they alert the others. If you waste your slow mo, the game encourages you to run and gun your way out, but the enemies rarely miss, and if you try to sneak away, the AI can almost always see you behind cover.

Honestly don't know how to feel about this one, I had such a good time in the first half of the game to the point where I feel (similar to many reviewers) that this game more than deserves a perfect rating. Prior to this review, the only game I felt justified a perfect 10/10 was The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild; however, once I had finished the first half of Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain, I was almost convinced this title stood at the same level as BOTW. 

Now, I'm not sure, without spoiling anything the second half of MGSV: TPP feels more than forced, not only was the story given to me in bite sized chunks that felt like I had to work towards any bit of story progression, but the work I had to do to progress was literally EXACT repeats of previous missions with different gimmicks (such as maintaining perfect stealth or not taking a single hit.) I'm not going to sit here and argue about the idea that Kojima was forced by KONAMI to release the game because I simply don't believe this to be the reason for the repetitive nature of the second half's missions. I would've much rather had an incredibly short second half than to have replayed missions with the hope that I would get new story content. I cannot stress how insulting it was to repeat some missions, complete with their original cut scenes. Imagine you were watching a movie and during the second half of the movie a random scene from the first half was inserted, you would think it was a mistake, right? Well, this is exactly what happens in TPP after defeating the main boss. 

With that being said, up until mission 30, I really enjoyed my play through of this game, I still recommend it to anyone reading this interview, just know that the second half will let you down and not to let yourself get invested or hoping for more content within the second chapter.

e.g. if there is no direct line to enemies, when you shoot, and enemies have to rely on echo - they will be confused as to where the shot came from.
e.g. you can approach an enemy from behind (or from the front if they are unprepared) and if it's clear to them they would be shot, they will surrender, and answer some interrogation questions. 
some, however, will pretend to surrender (reading body language can help you detect which ones pretend), and attack you with a knife if you're close.
e.g. superior going-prone / crawling mechanics. you can actually make use of a little natural undulation of the ground to get a full cover in very unassuming places.
e.g. if you're quick you can disarm the enemy on hand to hand combat, and redirect their weapon at them (they will surrender if it's not full all base against you combat, otherwise they might produce a sidearm after a fraction of a second of a hesitation after disarmment)
e.g. you can lunge forward to a prone position, max payne style though without slo-mo (e.g. to quickly jump behind cover, or to tackle an enemy to the ground on collsion.
e.g. if you space it well and execute it right you can avoid getting shot even once during full combat exchanges. engaging when they are running, reloading, turning around, communicating, or otherwise occupied for a moment, or even in between the burst of shots that they are sending, if you space it right.
e.g. during an attempt to capture a base stealthily you basically have a choice per each enemy you neutralize - kill (contributes some bad karma points resulting in the main character changing appearance); strangle or beat unconscious (weakness - after an amount of time specific to what made them go unconscious, they will wake up and go on the radio to raise alarm, however they will not immediately go to combat if someone else in the base spots you and raises camp to red alert); capture and force to surrender and stay quiet (they will not get up after a certain amount of time, but they will immediately join their peers if the base goes on red alert after you're spotted). So a mix of pros and cons.
Leaving a body somewhere will also cause problems XX mins down the line. Someone will spot it if you don't think about body placement, and optimal body placement is not easy or at all possible a lot of the time, because of how base is packed, and virtually everyone moves or turns around in inconvenient directions, often. (which is perfect for the type of game that this is). but then removing a body (e.g. by fulton extraction, possibly should be stayed up until the base is all cleared, cause other enemies will spot it if employed to get rid of a body) (which again, is fair for a stealth / military game).

performance - a potato computer will give perfect performance. No frames dropped ever.

cons - level design is not at all what it  should be.
every single enemy base is basically a few shacks and ruins thrown together, surrounded by kilometers of wasteland.
there're  unreasonable amounts of empty space in between them too, with nothing going on.
an occasional patrol (super duper rare) will be exactly where you expect it. I expected way more ambushes in between bases. 
the world feels horribly empty, bleak, dead, and uneventful.
it's supposedly open world but there will be a lot of areas artificially blocked off. cliffs forcing movement through certain corridors. bases walled off by untraversable cliffs, etc. a lot of fake-looking, unscallable cliffs.
level, world, base design pales in comparison to ghost recon wildlands (which has such a big world but full of life, events, multiple factions' interactions, enemies at every turn, bases full of weaknesses to exploit and being approachable from every angle, etc.) so badly there is virtually no competition here at all.

Story and dialogues are so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stupid, you'll lose brain cells every time you don't skip a cutscene.
lots of heavy terms thrown with clear lack of knowledge of what do they mean or how it actually works.
everyone speaks in breathy, overwhelmed way. so full of themselves, and so full of emotion. dragging on and on and on. 
glints in the sunglasses. pompous bullsh**

missions are so stupid, it will hurt. e.g. magical enemies jumping from in front of your iron sights to behind you, off-screen. repeatedly. for an hour or so.

open world gameplay (against normal, real-world enemies, none of the magical or super duper sci-fi imaginary characters) however, is superior.
it's very, very, very challenging (in a desirable, logical, and fair fashion).
That is to say, I play with reflex turned off (slow mo which turns on when someone detected you to give you one last chance to pop a quick shot in their dome), markers turned off (hud indicating enemies and following them around visually above their heads, or letting you know when they're suspicious, so it is more life-like when turned off), no silencers (they are literally unfairly silent in stealth games, here too) etc. for a more realistic challenge.
And the game is probably the most real stealth/military simulation I've had on my plate, game-play wise.

Another con, however is that there is no co-op, gameplay. Not really a game to share with a friend.

MGS V: TPP is easily my favourite stealth game of all time. It’s a type of gameplay we don’t see much nowadays. Most blockbuster AAA games have stealth mechanics, but they’re almost always optional and not very fleshed out. The Phantom Pain is a game that’s all about stealth, and I wish I could play it for the first time again, and then again, and then again.

Let’s get the [b][i]bad[/i][/b] out of the way first. To start with, it’s not the best PC port. The Metal Gear games started on console, and it’s clear Konami didn’t quite have PC in mind when developing this game. Prompts showing the controls show controller inputs by default, which is partially fixed by changing a key binding, but some prompts still show controller inputs. The controls screen always shows controller inputs, which was very confusing when you first got to use the walker gear.

There’s also an issue where under-hand throwing grenades is extremely difficult with keyboard and mouse. You have to hold left click for a second – not too short and not too long – or Snake will throw that sucker way farther than you expected.

Another issue I had with the game is the inability to skip through certain parts. For instance, every time you start a mission, you [i]have[/i] to sit in the helicopter for about a minute without being able to do anything. It’d be nice to be able to skip that part, especially if you’re replaying the game.

There are also a few strange mechanics that don’t feel necessary. For example, the virtual PF battles and PF points feel totally pointless. Combat deployments aren’t very interesting either and could’ve been implemented in a much better way.

[hr][/hr]

Most of my gripes with the game are, thankfully, not [i]huge[/i] deals. However, there are notable aspects of the game that I wish were designed differently. The AI in this game is absolutely fantastic, but it definitely feels like it’s too easy not to get spotted. Despite the AI being intelligent and conforming to your behaviour, all the enemies still seem to really need glasses. You can go prone a couple metres in front of an enemy in broad daylight and they won’t see you.

It would be great if the game had an optional, harder difficulty that made enemies more perceptive, as well as stronger in combat. That brings me onto my next issue: going in ‘guns blazing’ is far too easy. For a game that is all about stealth, it’s not at all difficult to just shoot everyone like you’re Rambo once you get spotted. Snake shouldn’t be as powerful in combat as he is, when he’s up against five, ten, or more enemies. He can easily survive plenty of gunshots, grenades, and missiles. I wish being spotted was more of a threat than it is.

MGS V: TPP has a very interesting mechanic where enemies learn and adapt to your behaviour. If you often headshot enemies, they’ll start wearing helmets. If you often infiltrate at night, they’ll start using flashlights and night vision goggles. Some enemies will also start using heavy armour, shields, and rocket launchers later in the game.

While this is a unique mechanic that adds a lot to the game, it doesn’t entirely fulfil its purpose. The intended effect is to disincentivize the player from using the same strategies without ever trying something new, but it doesn’t have as big of an impact as you’d want it to. Enemies with helmets can still be headshot if you just aim at their eyes or necks, and they can lose helmets from headshots. And enemies using flashlights or NVG barely has an impact.

I found myself using mostly the same loadout and strategies for the entire game: a silenced assault rifle with a silenced tranquilizer gun – and, once I obtained it, a silenced tranquilizer sniper rifle. I never felt like I had to change my strategy aside from the few missions that require you to use heavy weapons.

Now, I want to discuss what I consider to be my biggest gripe with the game, and that is the fulton. The fulton device lets you extract enemies immediately, making it all too easy to get rid of bodies. The game world has lots of toilets and dumpsters you can hide bodies in, and part of previous MGS games was hiding bodies in bushes or whatnot, but in this game, once you obtain the fulton (early in the game), you can simply just fulton every enemy, and they’re gone. I would’ve much preferred the fulton to have fewer uses, giving more importance to upgrades, or some other downside to prevent constant fultoning of enemies. There’s no negative to fultoning an enemy or prisoner other than other enemies potentially hearing or seeing it, but they have to be very close for that.

I also want to mention that I think this game shouldn’t have been open world. The two maps you get to explore are mostly empty, with small to medium-sized enemy outposts scattered about. There’s not much to find and explore outside of side-ops to do, flowers, and resources within outposts. While Kojima always wanted to make an open world Metal Gear game, I think the game would’ve benefited from being a traditional, less open game.

Another negative I have with the game is certain missions and enemies. Some missions have ‘the Skulls’, which are unique enemies that can’t simply be one-hit tranquilized or stunned, and you have to use heavy weapons, such as a light machine gun, to take them out. I never found these to be very interesting. In one mission, where you are surrounded with Skulls, I just stood on a rooftop the whole mission and shot at them. There’s no way to Skulls missions stealthily, so it feels weird for the game to take away the stealth aspect and force you to use heavy weapons.

The last issue I’d like to discuss isn’t something that pertains to gameplay. Rather, it’s the sexualization of female characters. It doesn’t ruin the game, and not everyone has an issue with it, but it did make me a bit uncomfortable seeing Quiet and the other female Skulls be so sexualized. For example, when the female Skulls are first introduced, the camera pans up, showing their asses and cleavage. And Quiet is sexualized throughout the entire game. Out of all the games I’ve played, this game definitely has the most sexualization. Do with that information as you will.

Once upon a time, in a quaint little farm nestled in the rolling hills of the countryside, there lived a farmer named George. George was a hardworking man who tended to his land with care and dedication, but he had one prized possession that he cherished above all else – his prized cow, Bessie.

Bessie was not just any cow; she was a gentle giant with a heart of gold and a penchant for mischief. George had raised her from a calf, and together they had formed a bond that was unbreakable.

One sunny afternoon, as George was going about his chores, he noticed that Bessie was acting a bit peculiar. She seemed restless and fidgety, mooing loudly and pacing back and forth in her pen. Concerned for his beloved cow, George approached her cautiously, trying to discern what could be troubling her.

To his horror, George soon discovered the cause of Bessie's distress – she had somehow managed to eat his suppository! It had fallen out of his pocket while he was tending to the crops, and Bessie, ever curious, had mistaken it for a tasty treat.

Panicked, George frantically searched for a solution to Bessie's predicament. He knew that if he didn't act fast, the suppository could cause serious harm to his beloved cow.

With no time to waste, George enlisted the help of his neighbor, Old Man Jenkins, who was known far and wide for his expertise in all things farm-related. Together, they concocted a plan to safely remove the suppository from Bessie's stomach without causing her any harm.

Using a combination of ingenuity and sheer determination, George and Old Man Jenkins crafted a makeshift device out of household items, carefully guiding it down Bessie's throat and into her stomach. With bated breath, they waited anxiously as the contraption worked its magic, gently extracting the offending suppository from Bessie's belly.

And finally, with a triumphant cheer, they succeeded! Bessie let out a contented moo as George and Old Man Jenkins breathed a sigh of relief, knowing that their quick thinking had saved her from harm.

From that day forth, George made sure to keep his suppositories safely out of reach of Bessie's curious appetite. And though it had been a harrowing experience, it only served to strengthen the bond between man and cow, proving that true friendship knows no bounds – not even when it comes to suppositories!

PROS :

CONS :

- The Openworld gimmick gets old fast because it's empty and forgettable.
- The second place you can go to is the awful Motherbase : could have been a simple menu, but devs thought it'd be funnier if it was also big, empty and uninteresting to roam as well.
- Then there is the most absurd idea of this product : Motherbase management. Who give a sh!t ??
 There are so many systems implemented into this feature, that it's not only a confusing mess to understand or keep track of, but it's simply out of place ! You launch MGS for the story, not to manage soldiers specialization, sidekicks equipement, currency/ressources, contracts, advancement research or whatnot.
- You get a loading screen (the chopper) every time you jump from Motherbase to the wilderness. And that is hella annoying because it happens a lot.
- The game has a side missions system, and forces you to go through these repetitive boring chores in order to unlock the main "story" after a quota is achieved, as opposed as a usually organic story driven game.
- Speaking of which, the narrative moments in PP are just scarce and lazy. It barely says anything remotly significant or exciting. There are some big memorable scenes, but it's worth 30min altogether, which is insulting.

I wouldn't try to review this masterpiece in a written Steam review, because I can't do it proper justice and out of fear of leaving something behind. But in light of the upcoming Metal Gear Solid Delta, I finally decided to quickly write up a few sentences here as a thank you note to the developers and to further augment the game's aggregate score.

The uniqueness, creativity and smoothness of the gameplay is something I've never seen before. The controls are smooth user friendly, even arcadey. Every input feels tight and precise with 0 delays.
The game offers an unsurpassed sense of freedom in how your approach each mission and any single situation can be changed on a dime.
The enemy humanoid AI is the best I have ever witnessed in a game thus far and will tear you apart remorselessly if you think you can exploit it.
Both all-guns-blazing action and stealth are so much fun that getting caught doesn't feel like a punishment, although the game encourages you to take the stealthy approach and you'll be rewarded for it.
Be warned the main story is heavy on cutscenes and dialogue, seeing as it is a Kojima game you should be expecting that anyways.
There are 2 multiplayer modes here. A single-multiplayer mode called F.O.B.s where you infiltrate other players Forward Operating Bases and a more ordinary multiplayer mode, branded Metal Gear Online which has all the archetypal Call of Duty style modes, deathmatch, capture the flag and more. Both modes offer a plethora of ranking and biweekly events/challenges that you can participate. I have spent 75% of my playtime in FOBs. They are that good (and if you abhor multiplayer you should give this one a try seriously because it's not what you think) and so long as Konami maintains its servers I'll keep on playing at least on a weekly basis.
A technical marvel for the time it was released and continues on to this date. The game engine used to develop it, the Fox Engine, is the single most optimized 3d engine I have ever experienced. If you're on an NVidia GPU there are some graphical settings you can tweak to enhance them still. Suffice to say it runs good, buttery smooth amazingly good. 
There is also slight modding support which can be leveraged if you're on a not-potato PC to give an extra oomph to the otherwise top-notch gameplay. I wouldn't bother with it though unless I have completed a full run of the main story.
The sound design is immaculate. The score is great albeit a step down from the first MGS trilogy imo.

An immensely deep & replayable game from start to finish. It is as challenging as it is rewarding. A massive game of epic proportions, a game for the ages. A Hideo Kojima game.


PS: I hope Konami takes its time with MGS Delta, because surpassing this one will be the feat to end all feats.

MGSV is not a typical Metal Gear game. However, it is seriously fun to play. Most of the criticism I've seen for this game is issues with the story, but I haven't had any issues with it. Assuming you play the Metal Gear series in chronological order (Starting with 3: Snake Eater), Peace Walker does a pretty good job of bridging the gap between 3 and 5, so the change shouldn't be as jarring playing in that order.
Game-play wise I'd say this is the best Metal Gear has to offer (aside from Rising, but Rising isn't really a stealth game). It has a nice blend of new and old concepts such as the box, stun and kill-based weapons, CQC, hold ups, along with fulton extraction, phantom cigars and the buddy system. There is also Mother Base and the aerial command center that allow you time to customize weapons and manage your resources. When it comes to the buddy system:
D-Horse - mostly good prior to getting D-Walker, but also has the advantage of enemies not attacking it unlike your other buddies. Useful when you have to get near the enemy
D-Walker - Useful for quick getaways and can stun enemies thus saving ammo in the stun gun.
Quiet - gives you covering fire and can save you from being spotted on multiple occasions, highly recommend during total stealth missions because she can draw enemies away from the objective.
D-Dog - helpful for getting stealth take downs
Story-wise I would praise it as highly as the other games, but the overall tone feels much more serious in Phantom Pain. Set in the 1980s, it serves as central meeting point for many iconic characters throughout the series. Including new characters such as Venom Snake, Quiet, Code Talker, Skull Face, and (spoilers) returning and future characters such as Benedict "Kaz" Miller, Huey Emmerich, Revolver Ocelot, Big Boss, Liquid Snake, Paz, Psycho Mantis, Colonel Volgin (sort of) along with mentions of Solid Snake, Solidus Snake, The Boss, and Major Zero. My biggest issue is less with this game, but how past games (set in the future) utilize most of these characters. Venom, the protagonist YOU SPEND 35 HOURS PLAYING AS, DIES AT THE END OF OG METAL GEAR. And Kaz, who this game truly brings to life, is randomly killed off in Metal Gear Solid as the twist. Huey is fairly redundant other than to give backstory to Ottacon, seeing as that Ottacon only ever mentions his step father in MGS2, meaning Huey was never a part of his life. In terms of the larger story, I would call this game along with the original Metal Gear the turning point in the story. Metal Gear is split into two time periods, which I would describe as Big Boss (1964 - 1990s) and Solid Snake (1990s - 2018). This game's role is tying up any lose ends in Snake Eater, Peace Walker, and Ground Zeros, and MG is meant to begin the story of Solid Snake, which extends to MG2, MGS1, MGS2, MGS4, and (to an extent) MGR:R.

This game took me to the highest heights and to the lowest lows.

For starters, I have always appreciated what Kojima produced. He was never meant to be a game director, and it shows, with cutscenes and camera angles that are reminiscent of the greatest cinema productions.

However, MGSV is not it. It's nowhere near the quality that Snake Eater was, and for better or for worse, it's nowhere near what Death Stranding, at least in terms of story telling and character emotion.

I loved how the story unfolded in the first chapter/part, especially how the characters felt extravagant but relatable. I especially liked how mysterious everything was laid out in front of you, and how many things just didn't make sense.
The gameplay is great, with a lot of room for playing "in your own way", that cannot be found anywhere else, in any game. Each mission is approached differently, and enemies learn the ways you approach them and change their defenses dynamically as the game progresses. The customization is top notch and each companion brings something new to the table. The economy back at "mother base" is well put together, adding an extra layer of gameplay (that I was not too keen on trying at first).

That's where the good things stop. The second part of the game is strictly composed of "rescuing children", redoing missions, and completing side ops. Most of the missions are uselessly hard, and if you do not have patience or skill, you will be punished harshly. Only in the endgame, there is more info added to the story, however, even the end is a repeat mission. And you can tell that's when Kojima fell off with Konami. The development is rushed. It feels incomplete, without any meaning or extra information, and a lot of storylines are left incomplete. And not in a good way either, just... incomplete. For the last entry in the series, it's such a shame.

Glad to see that Kojima has its own studio, and managed to recruit some amazing talent to still share his great ideas.

There is no game like Metal Gear Solid, however.

For any fan of the Metal Gear series, this game is the culmination of MG gameplay across the games over the years. The near sandbox approach to the game with total control of Snake in the battlefield along with the aid of Motherbase, truly puts almost everything at your fingertips and helps personalize and humanize your missions as the legendary Snake.  Great characters, engaging story, its very easy to get lost in Kojima's most polished entry in the Metal Gear series.

Fun, fast-paced, immersive—a great stealth sandbox experience. While it's a shame the game wasn't completely finished (you can see the cut content floating around the internet), it's still a well crafted experience, with some over-the-top characters (a Kojima trademark), an interesting premise and a decent reveal at the end (the story's pretty interesting even though it might no be Kojima's most philosophical entry in the franchise, it still offers a lot for the fans). The FOX Engine is still impressive to this day, the game-play is varied enough and allows different approaches, the maps, while not excessively large, offer enough content.

I strongly recommend this game, even to people who aren't fans of the series or don't really care about its characters, as it's some of the most fun I've had in an open-world game.

If you're looking for a review of this game you've come to the wrong place, but if you're looking for an outstanding dinner idea you've come to the right place.

Prep Time:
15 mins

Cook Time:
45 mins

Total Time:
1 hr

Servings:
10

Ingredients:
1 pound pork roast, diced
3 teaspoons minced garlic
1 (15 ounce) can black beans, drained
1 cup Recaito (such as Goya®)
1 (5 ounce) jar pitted green olives
1 (1.41 ounce) package Sazon seasoning with Achiote
3 cups long grain rice, rinsed
2 ¾ cups water, or as needed

Directions:
Spray a large stockpot with cooking spray and set over medium-high heat. Add pork and sauté until browned, about 7 minutes. Stir in garlic and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add beans, Recaito, olives, and Sazón seasoning. Reduce the heat and simmer for about 10 minutes.

Add rice to the pot and stir to coat. Add water and bring to a boil. Cover and simmer for 20 minutes. Uncover and stir rice at the top, avoiding the slight crust on the bottom of the pot. Remove from the stove if rice has absorbed most of the liquid; if not, cook for up to 10 minutes longer.

Tips:
You can use pigeon peas instead of black beans if desired, and any cut of pork will work.
Add water carefully in Step 2. Too much water results in mushy rice while too little will make it dry. You should be able to stir it, and it should look like a dense soup.

Despite having been released a long time ago, the game hasn’t really lost its story impact, nor technical prowess. If as a woman, playing it comes with a certain amount of discontent and ambivalence regarding the female characters (more specifically their artistic direction rather than their script), as a PTSD sufferer, the overall experience still felt weirdly soothing as the story and the pace effectively captures the most dissociative aspects of trauma. As a technical artist, the game never ceases to marvel me at how incredibly well optimized and beautiful it is. Nearly 10 years after its release, it still happily competes with a lot of the stuff that we see now.

As now mental health representation is more of a topic than it used to be, I think that TPP does a fairly good job at representing how PTSD and subsequent dissociative disorders might feel like from the inside. In times where now Dissociative Identity Disorder is mostly (mis)represented by questionable TikTokers, MGSV TPP presents a surprisingly correct clinical aspect of it, even if at times evidently exaggerated and incomplete for dramatic purposes. It does explore the dissociative capacity to gloss over massive internal contradictions while never truly concluding to anything meaningful, as that degree of dissociation rarely resolves itself spontaneously. In that regard, the open world design truly was a good choice over linearity, as the missions come as disjointed collections of events and the past becomes increasingly vapid, buried under nonsense, violence or the rare glimpses of joy of freedom as you ride a jeep accompanied by your silly dog, or your unique incomprehensible and silent friend. The game is a deliberate mess, and that mess feels alive.

As with all Kojima’s games, there is a quality of grief and silence and use of negative space against a backdrop of the quick succession of crazy events that in my sense truly manages to show the nature of trauma, in its brutal stupidity, astonishing scale, and inescapable nature. I’ve never thought so much it was a properly pacifist take, as I’ve read now and again. Something that I do appreciate with M. Kojima work is that despite having many aspects that are irritating, boastful, verbose and full of male self-centeredness, there is a quality of unapologetic sincerity that makes it quite disarming. I do not know if it is sufficient, but there is a sense of establishing a dialogue with the story as if you would establish it with a friend. The game allows for very personal dives into it and personal self-reflection, which is something that I haven’t seen I think in any other AAA game out there.

Not all public will like MGS in general. Its bleakness and verbosity are understandably true deal-breakers for many people. But for all peeps out there that are looking for experiences that bear some true meaning, and perhaps some sense of comprehension in despair, I’d recommend doing them all in chronological order of release, including Peace Walker and Portable Ops, before going through GZ and TPP. It is a series of games that ought to be experienced as they clearly go a step further than mere entertainment. They are imperfect, but to my sense they also are works of art where you can feel how much care and artistic alignment has been given by everyone involved in its creation, not just Kojima himself. It is also very interesting to see how many elements in TPP predate the shift that has been operated later in Death Stranding.

Can this game be fun? Yes. The problem is, if you're a completionist, the amount of grinding and pay-to-win stuff in it will annoy you a lot. If you buy this game on sale, you'll possibly enjoy it unless you like investing to develop your equipment, at which point, you'll realize that you're going to have to sink a couple hundred hours to get what you want.

===Graphics===
Good, especially considering the age

===Gameplay===
Somewhat satisfying. If you shoot somebody in a helmet in the chin or one of the other unprotected parts with a tranq dart, it doesn't count it. That's lazy hit-box making and it's annoying. The grinding means you'll have a lot of repetitive experiences trying to extract quality recruits so you can level up your capabilities and develop new items

===In-Game Economy===
You can beat the game with low-level weapons, mercifully, but you have to wait for real-life days to develop more than half of the upgrades. You have to grind resources for hours to afford them as well. It's an obnoxious experience and a transparent cash grab since you can pay for coins to speed up upgrades for a lot of things. it's like $10 for 1000 coins. You can blow through that pretty quickly

===Story===
Not great, not terrible. Typical Hideo Kojima. "War's terrible, now play my war game." Thankfully, the cutscenes are skippable and not awful, generally

===Online Interaction===
Half the FOB missions are players with almost-impossible defenses. The others are people with no defenses. Never build a nuke or else you'll get a lot of stuff looted.

===Soundtrack===
Not terrible, not too memorable. Lots of 80s tracks

===Closing Thoughts===
It's a moderately enjoyable game that suffers from an obnoxious amount of gatekeeping for unlocks between time to develop things and resources required to do so. In that way, it reminds me of a typical phone game where it's free, but the developer makes it essentially impossible to be anything other than a novice if you don't want to spend money or grind for hours. IA lot of the time, you have to force yourself to "have fun."

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain : By Triple F

"Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain", released in 2015, stands as a landmark achievement in the long-running espionage franchise. Developed by Kojima Productions under the visionary Hideo Kojima, it marked a dramatic shift towards open-world exploration while retaining the series’ core focus on stealth and tactical action. The Phantom Pain isn't without its flaws, but its merits as a gameplay experience and a melancholic farewell to Kojima's Metal Gear are undeniable.

The Phantom Pain takes place nine years after the events of Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes. Players once again assume the role of Big Boss, a legendary mercenary seeking revenge against the shadowy XOF unit who destroyed his mercenary nation, Mother Base. The narrative unfolds in a series of missions spread across a vast open world – a stark departure from the linear levels of previous entries. This open-world, dubbed "Afghanistan," is a sprawling desert landscape littered with Soviet outposts, rebel strongholds, and abandoned villages. It grants players an unprecedented level of freedom in how they approach objectives.

While the open world provides a playground for exploration, the heart of The Phantom Pain lies in its refined stealth mechanics. Players have a vast arsenal of tools at their disposal, from silenced weapons and tranq guns to cardboard boxes and sneaking suits.  The core gameplay loop revolves around infiltrating enemy outposts, neutralizing or avoiding patrols, and completing objectives like rescuing hostages or extracting valuable intel.

The Fox Engine, which powers The Phantom Pain, delivers exceptional visuals and a remarkable attention to detail. Environments are richly detailed, with dynamic weather patterns that can affect gameplay. The (Day & Night) system influences enemy behavior and creates unique tactical opportunities. Raiding a base under the cloak of darkness offers a distinct challenge compared to a brazen midday infiltration.

The Phantom Pain isn't just about sneaking around enemy lines. Players can also choose to go in guns blazing, utilizing a robust weapon customization system to craft the perfect loadout for their play-style. The game doesn't penalize this approach, but enemy reinforcements and helicopter assaults can quickly turn the tide of battle for the unprepared.

Beyond combat, players manage Mother Base, a sprawling offshore platform that serves as their base of operations. Here, they can develop new weapons and gadgets, train soldiers, and even extract resources from the open world using a multipurpose helicopter. Mother Base management adds a strategic layer to the experience, allowing players to invest their resources in customizing their own personal army.

The Phantom Pain's narrative is a complex web of espionage, revenge, and political intrigue. However, it's also fragmented and cryptic at times. Key plot points are delivered through cassette tapes scattered throughout the world, which players may or may not choose to listen to. This fragmented approach can be frustrating for those seeking a clear-cut, traditional narrative.

The game also suffers from a controversial ending, one that feels somewhat incomplete due to a well-documented falling out between Kojima and Konami during development. Despite these issues, The Phantom Pain's story offers plenty to ponder, particularly for longtime fans of the Metal Gear saga.

In a nutshell, "Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain" is a masterclass in open-world stealth gameplay. It offers a vast world to explore, a wealth of tools to approach objectives, and a refined combat system that caters to both stealthy and aggressive tactics. While the narrative may be fragmented and the ending somewhat unsatisfying, The Phantom Pain stands as a remarkable achievement and a fitting farewell to Hideo Kojima's vision for Metal Gear Solid.

I've had this in Steam for a while now, but it took me a while to get around to it.  I hadn't played previous MGS games, but this got a lot of highly favorable reviews.

The first mission was a crawling simulator that ends with a weird dude on fire.  Huh.

The next mission was more straightforward, although the tutorial was a bit skimpy on the things that I imagine are second-nature to MGS veterans, such as how to incapacitate hostiles.  Nowhere does it mention that, when you get within 5m of a hostile, you need to hold the Ctrl key down to crawl more slowly or you'll be heard.  I got a bit frustrated with the way stealth worked, and walked away from it for a bit.

The reason it wasn't working for me was that I was used to games like Deus Ex, Dishonored, and Far Cry, where being spotted can be Very Bad depending on what you're trying to do.  In MGSV, you get a chance to drop your opponent in "reflex mode", which is actually pretty easy to do so long as you're fairly close.  Once I figured out slow-crawling, iron sight shooting, and supply drops, things got better.

One thing that MGSV does that many other stealth-focused or stealth-capable games don't is apply time pressure.  On the main missions, the situation is evolving.  If you're too slow, you can miss out on secondary objectives, or (in some cases) fail the mission entirely.  This was occasionally frustrating, e.g. a prisoner-rescue mission where you're supposed to follow somebody around, but you're not told (unless you complete some secondary objectives) that the prisoner isn't interrogated until after dark.  I spent a lot of time waiting and wondering until I eventually just looked it up online.

Another example of time pressure is that the enemies you incapacitate will wake up after a few minutes.  A few missions in, you get the ability to remove hostiles from the board, but in the early going you need to make steady progress... or just kill everybody and hide the bodies.  The game mildly discourages you from murder, but as far as I can tell the consequences are purely cosmetic.

The story missions are meant to be played more than once.  The first time through, the secondary objectives are hidden, and you can't know what the various triggers are.  If you're a completionist, you'll need to play through a second time to complete the secondary objectives, and a third time to do a "speed run".  (For example, the after-dark prisoner mentioned earlier can be rescued immediately if you happen to know where he is kept during the day.)

I found I enjoyed the side missions and "free roam" more than the story missions, because I could relax more without having to worry about racing an event.

Much of the complexity is introduced gradually, e.g. buddies and management of Mother Base expand over time.  This helps keep a fairly complicated game from becoming overwhelming.

Overall the game is a lot of fun.  Weird story.

A Masterpiece of Stealth and Strategy

I've sunk countless hours into METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN, and I can confidently say it's one of the best gaming experiences I've ever had. From its breathtaking open-world design to its deep and rewarding gameplay mechanics, this game sets the bar high for the stealth-action genre.

First and foremost, let's talk about the gameplay. The freedom it offers is unparalleled. Whether you prefer to sneak past enemies undetected, engage in intense firefights, or employ a mix of both, the game accommodates your playstyle flawlessly. The controls are tight and responsive, making every movement feel natural and intuitive.

The game's open-world environments are stunningly realized, with each location teeming with life and detail. From lush jungles to arid deserts, every area feels distinct and invites exploration. The dynamic weather system further adds to the immersion, as rainstorms and sandstorms can dramatically alter your approach to missions.

One of the standout features of The Phantom Pain is its base management system. Building and expanding Mother Base not only provides tangible benefits in terms of resources and support but also adds a layer of personalization to your gameplay experience. Watching your base grow and evolve as you recruit new soldiers and develop new technology is immensely satisfying.

And let's not forget about the sheer amount of content packed into this game. With a plethora of main missions, side ops, and challenges to tackle, there's always something new to discover. Plus, the inclusion of online multiplayer modes adds even more replay value, allowing you to test your skills against other players around the world.

Now, about the story. While I found it to be engaging overall, I can understand why some might find certain elements to be a bit over-the-top or melodramatic. However, even if the narrative occasionally veers into "cringe" territory, the strength of the gameplay more than makes up for it in my opinion.

In conclusion, METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN is nothing short of a masterpiece. Its unparalleled gameplay depth, stunning visuals, and vast amount of content make it a must-play for any fan of the stealth-action genre. Don't let a few questionable story moments deter you from experiencing everything this game has to offer.

This is an all-time classic of the 2010s, internet memes and Konami aside, this game has stood the test of time as far as its stealth mechanics and gameplay is concerned and rivals even older stealth games that are seen as the peak of the genre. The way the missions are laid out and the open world nature of the game allow you to take on any mission in any way you want. One mission could play out in several different ways depending on how many gadgets you've developed, making this game addicting and infinitely replayable. I've finished the Metal Gear saga back to back many times and I always look forward to replaying MGS V. Though I prefer the storytelling of the older games in the series, the gameplay is uncontested.

The story in this game is unorthodox in many ways. Even if you're familiar with the other games in the series, many things in this game will not be explained to your face, and even after finishing the game you might want to hit up some subreddits or forums to discuss the ending. I recommend listening to the tapes, which are like the Codec transmissions of the older games, except they let you play the game while listening to them, which is an improvement in some ways, but since they are just audio logs they are not happening in real time, meaning the actual story has less dialogue. This being primarily a gameplay experience, is somewhat preferable since no one's chewing off your ear for hours, but this also being a Metal Gear game, this is rather unusual and divisive among fans.

The game covers heavy anti-war themes about nuclear deterrance, obsession with revenge, the inevitable failure of ideals among other things. If you enjoy Kojima's wild ride from the past games, this game will definitely interest you. If you are just looking for a damn good stealth game, this game will keep you busy for a while. I've finished it on PS4 before, and returning on PC was smooth as butter. Yes, I had to start over, but the gameplay is seriously captivating. Even if you're not a Metal Gear Solid fanatic as I am, you'd want to dig into this.

Despite how much I respect Metal Gear's story and legacy over its series of games, it's not even why I love this game so much. I mainly just love the gameplay flow. Building your own military base, recruiting new soldiers, getting ferried by your own personal helicopter, sneaking and/or raiding enemy bases to take their stuff and their soldiers... it's so much fun, and you have a ton of options on how to go about it. if you ever get bored of one approach, try switching things up, using tactics or weapons you wouldn't ordinarily use. It's just great. I wish there were more games of this style with open-ended military combat and NPCs supporting you. Closest I can think of is some of the ARMA games and those go way hard into the difficulty and learning curves for me to get into them.

I also highly recommend Infinite Heaven mod for this game, as it lets you tweak a lot of the game's settings to suit your desires.

Right from the moment you’re told to get on your horse and explore the Afghan countryside, Phantom Pain feels intimidating, almost overwhelming in terms of the freedom its open world affords and the number of concepts it expects you to grasp. It’s almost too much, especially given the relative linearity of previous Metal Gears. But what initially appeared to be an overly dense tangle of features to fiddle with instead unraveled into a well integrated set of meaningful gameplay systems that provided me with a wealth of interesting decisions to make.

The story of this game? Meh. It's like trying to follow a soap opera plot after a power outage - confusing and not all that satisfying. Sure, there are a few glimmers of brilliance in the character moments scattered throughout the cutscenes and tapes, but let's be real, there are better Metal Gear tales out there.

But hey, let's talk about the real star of the show: the gameplay. Now, Venom Snake? That guy moves like greased lightning and his close quarters combat? Smooth as silk. With so many options to tackle missions, it's like being a kid in a candy store, except the candy's armed guards and the store's a warzone. Whether you're a sneaky ninja or a guns-blazing action hero, this game's got you covered. And that's why, despite its storytelling stumbles, it's still the king of the Metal Gear series when it comes to gameplay.

Metal Gear Solid V is obviously a game I spent a lot of hours playing, and yet on balance, knowing everything I know now, I don't recommend it. As you near the end, it's painfully obvious Konami pushed the game out the door when it wasn't finished. The game abruptly ends with several essential plot threads unresolved. Even worse, the ending is the stupidest slap in the face in the history of video games.

The plot would have been terrible even if it was finished. Similar to George Lucas, series creator Hideo Kojima is one of those guys people hail as a genius or dismiss as a crackpot, and at times both sides are kind of right. With MGSV, the latter is overwhelmingly on display. The story is yet another unnecessary interquel that creates way more problems than it solves. Kojima clumsily touches numerous third rails in a failed effort to address humanitarian issues. Characters are mishandled. The story is tasteless and incoherent. Way too much of it is told via audio tapes, and protagonist Venom Snake speaks way too little. I guess Kiefer Sutherland's price was too high.

The gameplay and graphics are easily the game's strongest elements. This is the most sophisticated game engine ever seen in an MGS game, and the amount of gameplay content is orders of magnitude larger than any of the other games. This makes for a really fun sandbox to play around in, and there were plenty of great hours mixed in with the dud ones.

However, some of the biggest changes tend to water down the series' trademark stealth. If you get spotted, just automatically go into adrenaline time and pop the guy in the head before he has time to raise the alarm. If the alarm is raised, it's an open world, so just run offsite until things cool down. No need to hide the bodies of enemy troops or worry about tranqed enemies waking up; just attach a baloon to them, and watch the hilarious animation as your helicopter snatches them away. About to die? Just run around until your health automatically regenerates.

There's also the usual time-consuming bloat that comes with an open world game, not to mention a ton of garbage time managing the Mother Base, tinkering with your personnel, and researching weapons upgrades. It can't be overstated how many of my "gameplay hours" were spent sitting in a helicopter listening to audiotaped dialog, or AFK entirely, waiting for research upgrades to complete. And oh yeah, there are almost no bosses in a series famous for its amazing boss fights.

Ultimately, as awesome as MGSV's gameplay was at its best, 8 years later there are just too many great open-world sandboxes out there to recommend one with this many glaring flaws. If you want one that's story rich, try Witcher 3. If you want one that's stealth heavy, try Horizon: Zero Dawn. But if you want to see the "Kojima style" at its best, try Metal Gear Solid 3 and Zone of the Enders: 2nd Runner.

Only thing I can criticise are the recycled missions, while some can be a decently fun challenge (like the subsistence missions for the Snake Eater nostalgia) most of them are just really frustrating, and definitely going a little hard on the challenge-to-fun ratio, and they do not feel super rewarding. My only gripe with MGSV, and this was also a gripe I had with MGS2, is that the boss fights SUCK. MGS is a stealth game series, and everything in the game is trying to make the player better at stealth. However, none of the boss fights challenge your ability to be stealthy. The fight against the Man on Fire, the Skulls ambush on pequod, and the fight with Sahalanthropus did not use the stealth skills whatsoever, which is a shame in my opinion, because a good boss fight should test the skills you have learned, not throw them away in favour of a gimmick(like the water towers in the case of MoF, or the melee with the skulls, or the tanks with Sahalanthropus). Other action games like DOOM, Dark Souls, etc. all feature bosses that are fun to fight because the bosses challenge the skills that the game has the player learn. The reputation that this game is "unfinished" kept me away from finishing it. Ironic, I know. After researching into what Kojima has said himself about the game and experiencing the entirety of the game's story for myself, the meme about Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain's being "unfinished" is a severe exaggeration. This is a finished game. There is a beginning, middle, and end and it does indeed close the loop of the Metal Gear Solid saga beautifully. The fabled "Chapter 3: Peace" and "Mission 51" and "unimplemented Battle Gear" stuff is blown wildly out of proportion. 

The Phantom Pain, in typical Metal Gear Solid fashion but executed in a much darker tone, is a deeply personal meditation on the nature of war, loss, vengeance, and deconstructions of narratives and so-called truths that give justification to harm others. In my opinion, it is the best and boldest storytelling this franchise has ever done. I doubt it will get the critical re-evaluation that Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty experienced. 

In terms of gameplay, its take on open-world tactical stealth and combat is still unmatched even to this day. This is truly an unprecedented form of freedom and agency within the context of providing the ultimate elite soldier fantasy and the inevitable tragedies that come with it. 

If you're a fan of the series and haven't played this, see for yourself yet another Metal Gear Solid game proving again why thematically, this series remains the some of the best experiences you can have in the world of gaming.

As a long-time MGS fan, I initially had a really hard time accepting this game, as did many. However, after putting it away for a few years, and deciding to appreciate it on its own merits, rather than as the non-existent game in my head I would like to see instead, I did end up immensely enjoying finishing up the story.

One thing I will say is that the second half is a lot stronger than the first, which is rare for a video game. (To clarify, I'm talking about the second half of the story, not "Chapter 2" specifically.) I also find that knowing some of the major spoilers in advance can actually greatly enhance the enjoyment of the experience and make it less jarring or off-putting. (Don't worry, I won't post any spoilers here.)
I would also like to dispel the rumor that this game is unfinished. While some content was cut, as with any game, and while Kojima's ambition knows no bounds, this game and its story is definitely completed in its current state. Especially if you compare the total volume of cutscenes, audio tapes, and gameplay environments to the total volume of cutscenes, codec calls, and gameplay environments in any one of the other MGS games, it checks out.

For those who like to mess around with games or even be completionists, the gameplay speaks for itself. But I would like to address those who like me might feel like they struggle (or would struggle) with some of the sillier or less immersive-looking aspects of the game. So here are some pointers I have found for myself:

- Only fulton enemies with a high rank. If you fulton everyone, it can get repetitive and a little cheap. But fultoning select enemies is actually kind of fun.

- Ignore the "demon points" feature. While the game doesn't talk about it, most people I think know about it: Kill too many enemies and eventually your "horn" will grow and you'll be permanently bloody. But this is unlikely to happen unless you mow down every single enemy and make some obviously morally questionable decisions later on that I won't spoil. Trying to tranquilize every guard severely hindered my enjoyment. So with this relative leeway in mind, I suggest throwing a suppressor on a .45 and making use of your knife whenever necessary like in the other games.

- Every couple of missions, go into the staff management, look for staff with the troublemaker attribute, fire them, then select to automatically sort all staff into what roles fit them best. Next, go to combat deployment (will be unlocked relatively early on) and keep sending the teams on missions that give a good amount of GMP and resources like fuel, metals, and "biological materials." Lastly, develop your base platforms whenever you can. Doing these few things will ensure that you can pretty much unlock/develop all the weapons and items you want, and that you'll unlock all the important sideops that can become available toward the end of the game.

- This point will be controversial, but I find locking the framerate to 30 makes me play more slowly and methodically, like a real stealth game. 60 fps really encourages me to run around and just kind of play like a headless chicken. And yes, it's a meme, but 30 fps does look more cinematic, and where has that ever been more appropriate than in an MGS game? But this is up to personal taste, obviously. I felt "forced" to play it at 60 for the longest time but switching to 30 increased my enjoyment immensely.

- Don't do "free roam." Seriously. The best tip I can give is that when out in the mission area, you can open the menu (*not* the iDroid, the game menu) and there will be an option called "Return to ACC." I use this as often as I can. Doing random side missions and just traversing around the map in general really burned me out on the gameplay and overall atmosphere, and made the story feel "thinner" than it needed to. Just do main missions and a few sideops with relevant rewards or progression. Don't free roam and capture random outposts, you're going to revisit them enough as it is. Unless you don't mind all that, of course. For me, it helped to cut out as much downtime as possible.

- LISTEN TO AUDIO TAPES AS SOON AS YOU GET THEM! The audio tapes should be seen as the new codec calls/"power point" cutscenes. The yellow ones are the crucial ones, but all of them are what constitutes the story and are obligatory in my opinion. I made the mistake of treating them as kind of side content and, honestly, not fully appreciating them. The fact that they're optional certainly didn't help. So, basically treat them as if they were not optional. Then you will also find that this game actually has an amazing story and some of the most original and well-thought out ideas in any MGS game, far from having a "bad" story.

- There are guides online about making some graphics tweaks which really help the game, mainly activating HBAO+ in your nvidia control panel and turning off the ingame AO. Depending on your graphics card, locking it at 30 fps can also free up power to bump up the resolution, which helps with aliasing. The latter is a night-and-day difference for me visually.

Good luck and have fun! As a long time MGS fan, it helps not to treat this game as the big series finale. That's MGS4. And it's objectively also not the most "MGS"-MGS game, that's MGS3 in my opinion. It serves as a great sort of "interquel," sandwiched between Peace Walker and Metal Gear 1. All in all I'm really glad I gave this game another chance. Yes, it's very different, by design, but it's still a wonderful game in its own right and a worthy addition to the Metal Gear series.

The Phantom Pain is an absolute overall masterpiece. The only downside is how the story does not have a proper ending while having so much build-up, it's quite sad what happened with the director and that we might never get any MGS with his vision behind it going forward. 

The Gameplay:
The gameplay and mechanics are some of the most perfected that any game has ever focused on. The character movement is very smooth, which is up there with games like Control and even Watchdogs where you can play around with the left stick and there are different in-between animations for your character in comparison to games like The Witcher where the character's movement is stiff when changing direction. Not to mention there are different stances which all have great movement although I find that moving backward while in a prone position can somehow cause forward movement. 
There are mechanics such as day/night which you can choose when to infiltrate enemy bases during a mission and tools to help you do so depending on what you choose. The Enemy AI is also on the clever side in that they can start wearing helmets when they find they are mostly killed by headshots and will also equip night vision goggles when you mostly infiltrate at night. You are equipped with options to choose certain partners which can be a dog, Quiet the sniper, and a walking gun machine. Then other items are choosing the form of transportation such as vehicles or a horse for traveling the open world, although it's not quite as open but each deployment gives you freedom of how to approach the enemies.  

The Story:
I'd be lying if I said that I understood the story of the game, but I sure enjoyed some twists as this was my first time playing a Hideo Kojima game, I just wish I could have an ending to it in order to have a more clearer understanding of the whole thing.

The Controls:
The controls of this game are great and modern, I know there was only one button which was a problem for me and made no sense, especially on horseback( I shall come back to this when I remember exactly what it was). But with a game that gives as many tools which all have their own control schemes, it is something that is bound to happen. 

The Sound:
The sound of this game really encompasses you in the world, and the fact that it changes depending on if you're using binoculars is also a great detail. The only issue is how I found the sound too hard when running or have your horse galloping it is a bit off for me, I would not be surprised if that was intentional as I believe it could've been to enhance the experience to show the sound distortion when running almost like what they did with the crosshairs when shooting becoming double as a way to give an experience of a character that is blind on one eye. 

I made the mistake of playing Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain before playing Ground Zeroes( as I thought it was some sort of an online multiplayer thing) which is another thing that made the story confusing for me but I found the experience of this game way too perfect that it could stand with the most modern titles and even best them when it comes to the mechanics and even the graphics although it does not have RTX. This is one of the greatest gaming experiences in history in my opinion, you could even say Red Dead Redemption 2 is one of the only ones that worked hard to dethrone it.
it has very realistic stealth and options , open world is quite wide but leaves it like that for sake of story . lots of interesting gameplay elements and best expectations on a hideo kojima game.

If you want something that is like MGS 1, 2, 3, 4, or even Peace Walker, this isn't it. It's now multiple open world maps with gameplay that feels like it has taken inspiration from past MGS, along with other games like Assassin's Creed. 

Mother Base and missions with side missions returns from Peace Walker but done in a way that expands upon it and feels like it's what Peace Walker should have been. 

The movement and gunplay is great, but it feels easier to just gun your way through if you want whereas I feel that was much harder to do in past Metal Gears. No radar this game but you can spot enemies and then they'll stay highlighted and appear on the map, similar to how it works in Assassin's Creed, it's a good way of not being completely blind and not having the radar considering lore-wise it shouldn't be made yet. Although some of the technology shouldn't, the iDroid is a hologram handheld with GPS and can scan documents and quickly download mission data, given the year this shouldn't exist. (Yes I know it's MGS with psychic's and stuff, but this was a big argument for why MGS3 was radio instead of codec, no radar, etc, so it continuity wise it feels like it's off)

For the story, it's got it's MGS twists and turns but definitly feels different, like there is something missing compared to past titles. 

Graphics look great for a game from 10 years ago, up close you notice models and textures can look a little dated but overall the game looks fantastic and even runs at 60fps on Steam Deck! 

Overall it's a great game, plenty to do and explore, definitely recommend

As my first Metal Gear game I went into it blindly, and came out quite impressed. Despite its repetitive missions and activities in the open world, rather weak writing for the antagonist and some of the supporting casts, lots and lots of exposition over radio and not as animated or interactive as you might have expected from a AAA game, and the abrupt and unsatisfying ending, it somehow still manages to always remain fun and interesting. When most other games have the above mentioned problems the game end up being mediocre at best. But in Phantom Pain the gameplay, the amazing visuals which is still better than most new games, and the music makes for such a grounded experience that I know it will stick in my mind for years.

Getting all the achievements is also fun, albeit impossible without a guide for some of the collectibles. Another top tier game for the golden year of gaming in 2015!
