In five hours I adopted a wolfdog pup, kidnapped a spetsnaz officer, got mauled by a bear, repainted a helicopter, used the Fulton Recovery System on a passing goat, and sniped a spetsnaz recon team while She Blinded Me With Science played on cassette.

Yep, it's a Hideo Kojima game.

PROS
- Who's a good boy? DD's a good boy! DD is a good boy, yes he is!
- The Fox engine is excellently optimized. This game should be playable with beautiful graphics even on middle-tier systems. If you can run Ground Zeroes, you can run this.
- The open world is well-done. It's also huge, but it feels dense enough that you're never more than a few hundred meters from something to Fulton. Environments are somewhat varied.
- There are multiple ways to approach any enemy installation, ranging from the obvious to the easily missed. It's encouraged to find a perch a couple hundred meters away and scout ahead.
- The world itself is well-done, too. There are weather changes, a day/night cycle, and these actually affect gameplay by making stealth easier or harder.
- You can Fulton extract anything. Anything. Soldiers? Of course. Cargo containers? Yes. Jeeps? Sure. Emplaced machine guns, mortars, AA guns? Definitely. Tanks? Yep! Bears, sheep, goats, and buzzards? Absolutely. I'm surprised you can't fulton-extract the freaking buildings at this rate.
- Mother Base management is like a more fleshed-out version of Peace Walker's. In many ways, this game is Peace Walker 2, and I definitely put that in the "pro" category.
- Good soundtrack full of 80s pop and rock hits that you can blare out of a helicopter. Also, you can upload custom songs and have your helicopter play them.
- I have 24 hours in the game and am at 17% completion - needless to say this game is not wanting for content. There are tons of missions and side-ops to do and hundreds of items to research, upgrade, and customize.
- Speaking of customizing, you can customize the base's paint schemes, your unit's emblem, your helicopter, various vehicles, and hand-pick your loadout for every mission.
- Mission checkpoint system generally means missions are neither too hard and frustrating, nor too hand-holdy.
- 24 hours in, I haven't felt a pressing need to grind. I've progressed perfectly well just by doing all the missions and new side-ops, without going back and repeating old missions (except for on several occasions just plain wanting to replay missions!). There may be more grinding ahead, but it certainly doesn't beat you up with it early-on.
- There are some surprises, even in the open-world. Without spoiling, I at one point unexpectedly walked right into a sniper duel while on my way to do a side-op. The weather changes often quite rapidly, creating unscripted emergent situations. I've had a sudden, unexpected sandstorm screw up an attempt to snipe a base full of enemy soldiers, leaving me running to salvage my plans when a body was discovered before I could finish. Fortunately, this can help you as well.
- The gameplay itself is fun. I find myself going hours at a time without actually doing missions or progressing the plot purely because it's fun to attack the hundreds of outposts and bases in the open world.


CONS
- While the AI isn't entirely stupid - and they're capable of surprising you from time to time - in general you'll learn pretty quickly how to pick guards off one at a time, thus making actual sneaking unnecessary.
- This problem was also true in Peace Walker and MGS4 - you'll have hundreds of different firearms, but have a reason to use maybe five of them. Fortunately, there is some sense of progression, as you can upgrade guns over time.
- Kiefer Sutherland doesn't talk as much as David Hayter's Snake did. Most of his talking is done over cassette, too. I miss Hayter's "commentary" in the world.
- The box may not say it, but this is a Hideo Kojima game, and it will remind you of this. Again. And again. And again. And again.
- Mother Base is explorable this time around, but it's a little empty. The game encourages you to return to it frequently, but there isn't really much to actually do there - at least so far.
- Microtransactions buy stuff that can accellerate and skip build timers. The good news is I've yet to feel punished or forced to use them, but they ARE present and I'm not buying them on general principle. However, I have gotten some MB Coins for free.
- The ending, without spoiling things, is rushed. It's painfully obvious content was cut. Some plot threads are mostly unresolved. You should search online for the cut content, there are some videos from the collector's edition of an unfinished mission that tied together a major plot thread at the end.


Other Notes
- MGS fans might find the game as a whole, and especially Kiefer Sutherland's Snake, very quiet. After the opening chapter, gone are the intrusive, hour-long cutscenes. Most are a few seconds or minutes long. There are no extended Codec conversations either. However! Much of the story and the content that used to take up long Codec calls is now found in cassette tapes, which can be played any time you want. This ends up being a good tradeoff, as you can listen to the long diversionary rants on random topics while still doing stuff in the game. Do yourself a favor and keep up on new cassette entries while you're out in the world.
- Reflex Mode is back from Ground Zeroes. This is, to put it mildly, controversial, with some people thinking it makes the game far too easy. If you're in that camp, it can be disabled.
- The story is shaping up to be significantly darker in tone compared to past games. If you've played Ground Zeroes, this isn't a surprise. However, I find it hasn't lost that Metal Gear charm.
- Lots of reviews, previously including this one, complained about long commutes and lack of fast travel. There is a fast-travel system, every enemy base has a fast-travel point that you have to unlock by finding it and picking up an object that lets you use it.


Conclusion
It's only September, and I've found my GOTY already. This is more than a worthy entry into the franchise; it is easily competitive for the title of Best Metal Gear Solid Game. If this is to be the last real MGS game, it's a worthy sendoff of a beloved franchise. 10/10.

I would say that MGSV was both one of the best stealth games and stories I had played recently. Whereas previous MGS games were very linear, MGSV decision to go open world paid off very well imo. It made the world feel more liveable, and giving the player freedom to infiltrate and exfiltrate enemy outpost from any direction within the greater context of an open world map, along with choosing weapon/gear loadouts before, made the experience of sneaking into enemy territories more deliberate and planned. The story is also much more clear and shorter cutscenes in this game than the previous MGS4.

There are quality of life improvements to make the fail state not so damning, like smoking cigars to speed up time to reset enemy AI from alert to regular patroling, and allowing players to literally balloon enemies out of the area to clear enemies without having to leave them asleep or killing them. There's a lot of incentives to go 'extreme stealth' throughout the game, but gun gameplay is pretty good if you want to go on a rampage as well.

My only gripe with the game is that around 3/4 of the first chapter, level design is pretty lackluster in comparison to the rest of the game. But that's just a couple of missions, and it's not enough to knock it down, it was just a complaint I had.

So in conclusion, really great game, highly recommend to others, just don't look up info on the story as it is easily spoilable, from experience :(  just play yellow casettes and yellow missions and you should unlock everything!

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom orthodontist is a stealth game and the ‘finale’ to the metal gear solid series. I have not played any metal gear games before so playing this one is what has gotten me into the series for the first time. This game is heavily story driven and serves very good writing and characters to the players. The gameplay of the Phantom Pain is excellent and provides some of the best stealth gameplay you’ll ever find in a stealth game in general. Hitman Blood money is often seen as the stealth game which set the bar for the genre’s mechanics in general, with dozens of ways that a mission can pan out. The Phantom Pain expands on this freedom given to the player in how they tackle their objectives. When I was playing this game, my brother who had played this before me, told me that “everything in the Phantom Pain is possible, if you think it is possible, you can do it”. I was stunned that you can turn out lights in this game with your silenced weapon if a watch tower is giving you trouble or using a cardboard box to get by enemies who are proving to be a pain. I especially love the items you are given such as the active decoy which always fools the enemies making it easier to get by them, or leave their guard post with a prisoner while they get angry over a decoy you threw at them. The possibilities in this game are endless.

The Phantom pain is also open world with two areas that you can explore, Afghanistan and the Angolan – Zaire border as much of the game is centred on the 80s events of the cold war. What I really liked about the Phantom Pain and its prequel Ground Zeroes, is that it ties into real world events very well which allows for more historical understandings in the game especially for events like the Angolan civil war which not many people know about. Whenever something like this is present in the game, I’ll start searching up about the historical context just to understand it a bit more. The environments in the game are very well detailed and offer nice views, especially those in Afghanistan which are surrounded by mountains and a lot of nice scenery. Since the game is open world, there are multiple side quests which are worth doing to extract resources. A lot of the game is focused on extracting these resources in building your very own “mother base” while also arming a private militia. You’re not only extracting resources but you’re also extracting army soldiers, animals, vehicles and weapon emplacements. 

I enjoyed the mother base aspect of the game as you always want to unlock new things such as weapons, items and just seeing your base develop overtime. It’s a really good addition to the game and actually stuff like this should be present in more open world games. Other games that do a good job at management of a base of some kind were Saints Row 2 and Scarface: The world is yours. Obviously, they weren’t as detailed as they were in The Phantom Pain, but it gave players a lot of customisation to play with as well as giving the player a sense of accomplishment. I really did enjoy the mother base aspect of the game and taking resources to see my base grow.

Obviously, the soldiers you extract also have an impact on this, and you should always use the analyser function on your binoculars to see which soldiers are best at what. There are facilities at your base such as medical, research & development and intelligence (to name a few) which are important in developing better gear for the missions that you can partake in. The Phantom Pain is really good at giving dozens of content to the player to experiment with and I can see why some would want to do a 100% run on this game just to get the best out of the content that is on offer.

I also really enjoyed the story to the Phantom pain as it is well crafted and emotionally connecting at times, especially the arch between the character Quiet and the protagonist. This arch at the end game becomes extremely emotional as it makes you feel sorry for Quiet and what she must deal with. Characters in this game are well acted and have a lot of character in them. What you are looking at here is a solid story worth investing your time into, especially the end game where things just go crazy.

The Phantom Pain is split into two parts, part I and part II. It should be noted that the true ending happens in part II, so there is more to play in the game after beating the main story. 

However, the phantom pain does have its share of problems. The first issue I want to bring up is the checkpoint system because it is dam awful. I was playing Dark Souls 3 the same time I was playing the Phantom Pain and I had trouble deciding what frustrated me even more, the camera in dark souls or the checkpoint system in The Phantom pain and I reached the conclusion that both are equally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awful. The checkpoint system in the phantom pain decides when it wants to save for you and sometimes it can be at the stupidest points possible. You may be heavily invested in an infiltration in a soviet base, extracted the best soldiers and materials, then you get spotted by some guy and sends the whole base after you and you either die or restart at a checkpoint because you know you’re in trouble and there goes dozens of minutes of progress. The system is very punishing in the early parts of the game because you have the lowest tier equipment, making things much harder for you. What they should have done is include a save system that works similar to how Hitman handled this. In Silent assassin, contracts and Blood money, saving worked by giving the player 7 saves per mission as they progress through the level. This should have been in the Phantom Pain to avoid bs checkpoints that aren’t saving progress properly, I would have been happy to have 5 saves per mission or something of the sort that accommodates for the mission length. 

The second issue is the re-playable missions in part II. Some of these levels are just ridiculously difficult and tedious. Whoever thought this was a brilliant idea is a bit of a ♥♥♥♥. You shouldn’t need to do them just to progress the story, especially when they are at a high level. A lot of people online say that the devs just “gave up on part II” which I disagree with a bit since part II expands on the story very well. However, they should have introduced more new missions rather than re-playable challenges which are just tedious and frustrating.

My last issue was that the antagonist, skullface, barley appears in the game. I think Skull face could have used more scenes since he isn’t really that much of a hateable antagonist. He’s just there really, it’s his militia which are more hateable than he is. It’s a bit disappointing since his voice actor did a really dam good job on him.

In conclusion the phantom pain is a really good game and in fact, people who aren’t that fond of stealth games should play it as stealth isn’t always required to succeed. It’s a logical game that makes you think of what you can do in each mission. Get this and the prequel, ground zeroes.

Do you want to know a secret? Do you promise not to tell? It took me five years to finally play this game. And it's the first - and so far the only - "Metal Gear" game I've ever played. I had bought it for my account a long time ago, but as I occupied myself with other games, I kind of forgot about it in my library. So in 2020, I finally brought myself to play it - and the timing couldn't have been more awkward, with the whole epidemic thing that happens later in the game.

By the time I played it, I was already familiar to a lot of it through the memes, the fan arts, the YouTube videos and so on. As such, there wasn't much that was revealed to me in the game. But by playing it, I finally understood the reasons for all the backlash it received. As some of you might know already, "The Phantom Pain" was not unanimously praised like "Arkham Asylum", "Witcher 3" or "Skyrim" were. Because for all its accolades and public recognition, the game also had its detractors, who were not such an insignificant minority. And now, I know why.

The game is too big for its own good. I'm not saying that it should have been over at the end of its first part, but its second part is filled with missions you've already played, but harder. It feels incredibly lazy for a game so rich in story and obsessed in continuity. And don't even get me started on the side ops: skip them as much as possible. They're the same thing over and over again. You'll come across some important side operations which are essential for the story, but as for the rest, don't bother with them; play the main missions and be happy. Unless you're in severe need for money.

Speaking of which, money is a big thing in this game: everything you do will cost you money, which you acquire by completing the missions and selling your resources if necessary. With this money, you can upgrade your tools, craft new weapons, make new attires and expand your base. This managing aspect of the game was a very nice touch, but some upgrades take time to finish - real, actual time. In-game days can pass by very fast, but when the game informs an upgrade will take a hour to complete, it really is a hour, so just wait for it. That sucks.

Each main mission is presented as a chapter, and each chapter has its own opening and closing credits. I have to admit I felt it was a bit egocentric from Hideo Kojima's part to have his name so flaunted during the whole game, but it was like if the game was being presented as a television series. Often times, the cutscenes can get massive, as the story just unfolds itself and we just stand idle and watch - again, like a TV show. But they can be skipped, so that's not much of a problem.

The real problem however - and one that made me infuriated at first - is that this game has a horrendous user interface. Now, I hate when PC games don't have the proper keyboard and mouse prompts - specially when the game itself is a shooter. But the thing about "Phantom Pain" is that it does have keyboard prompts - it's just atrociously bad. It actually combines keyboard and controller prompts: the mouse and the WASD keys are signalled as the controller sticks, while the 1 to 4 keys are signalled as the D-Pad. But for the rest, all the other keyboard promprs are there intact. The menus have no mouse input as well, so you can see this was a lazy port.

There are three maps for you to play in. The Afghanistan map where you begin in is mountainous and hard to be traversed, and on top of that, you'll face occasional sandstorms that are much more annoying than helpful. The Angola-Zaire map is more bearable and even more pleasant for navigation. And then there's your base at the Indian Ocean, which is at first this lone platform, but you can expand it so much that you'll end up actually needing a car to drive around it. You'll get to drive some vehicles, but there's no flying or boating. This isn't a "Far Cry" game - or a "GTA" game, for that matter. Fast travel is very cumbersome, which makes things more difficult: you constantly need to call for the helicopter, it can only pick you up at certain landing zones, and it actually takes a lot of your time. There's barely anything fast in this fast travel.

You're equipped with this fulton balloon that you can use to transport people back to your base (yes: like you saw in "The Dark Knight"), but later on, it can also be used to extract vehicles, animals and mounted weapons. And at one point, you can upgrade it into a wormhole device, which will facilitate extractions much more. By extracting enemies soldiers, they will - for some reason - join your team. Not only that, but as complete critical missions, volunteers will appear. From that you'll build an army which you'll eventually send in dispatch missions around the world.

Now, this is one of those stealth games where the stealth is optional. You can perfectly storm a base with guns blazing and destroy everything in sight. You'll even have the weaponry for such, like tanks, grenade launchers and machine guns. But the game wouldn't be so fun anymore: the thrill of the game is to sneak around and take out guards one by one. Suppressors have limited usefulness, and each shot should count. It's also worthy to mention that the more people you kill, the more you'll fill what I found out to be a "demon meter" - once it's maxed out, Snake will be covered in blood, and it won't wash out until you quit killing people and start making more use of your non-lethal weapons. You don't wanna be all covered in gore... do you?

You'll have four buddies that can be deployed to missions with you. There's Quiet, who is actually not as useful as you may think at first. She can be helpful, but only if you give her suppressed rifles - otherwise, she'll rile up all the base. The D-Horse is a great companion, because he can help you to cross long distances without requesting the helicopter constantly, and can even help you in combat with the right vests. There's the D-Walker, which is your personal combat walking gear in case you don't actually mind being covered in blood. And of course, there's the one you'll find yourself playing with all the time: the D-Dog, who can spot enemies, weapons, resources and prisoners easily, and can help you taking out some enemies. And if you get tired of staring at Snake's ugly face all the time, you can eventually play as different soldiers.

For a game so ambitious, and with so emotional and devastating moments, it also seems to be really self-aware. It winks at you at some points, not taking itself so serious: at one point, you rescue who appears to be Hideo Kojima himself. The story can get convoluted, but you still have a sense of what's going on, even if you're jumping into the lore blind like I did. The voice work is just spectacular, specially from Kiefer Sutherland, Robin Atkin Downes and Troy Baker - the moments with their three characters together are the best in the game. Tara Strong is also there, but her character barely appears in the narrative.

And the soundtrack is amazing: the original score is wonderfully arranged and produced. The game also implements several 80's tunes that you can collect as tapes throughout the world, and you can play them during missions like your own mixtape.

All in all, "Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain" is a severely flawed but also amazing game. It will become a grind if you're that completionist obsessed with the 100%, with the achievements. But once you invest in the story and main missions, you'll be in for a treat.

Now I just hope I don't take five more years to play "Revengeance".

Metal Gear Solid is a series about war and loss. Occasionally there will be some witty dialogue put in for the sake of humor and to try not to take the game too seriously. Metal gear solid 5 is considered the gameplay peak of the series but also the story valley of the series and yet it still gets massive praise. I am here to provide my opinion on whether metal gear solid 5 is a great game or not in a pro/con style and ending with my conclusion.

Pro:
     The game is pretty long. Now there are only 50 story mission (probably 15 are repeat missions with specific gameplay limitations), many many side ops, many side objectives in the main story missions, and animals to collect. Now if you want to go out of your way to 100% the game then your looking at a large amount of time to achieve that goal.

         You have a large amount of weapons/ tools to use during missions. You can uses your basic fire arms like handguns, shotguns, snipers, ect. You have access to plantable weapons like c4, mines, decoys, and animal traps. Buddys like a dog, the famous quiet the sniper, and 2 others. An array of vehicles  and the use of your chopper to provide cover fire. To get even more fire arms you use blueprints and materials to craft it which takes specific number of ingame time to make considering the star rating of the weapon.

     Cutscenes when they are in the game are pretty well shot. The camera takes careful planning on focusing on some important details. Really nothing else needs to be said since metal gear solid normally has some fantastic cutscenes in their games and this is no exception.

       The paz side story is very good. That is all....I just liked it and it made doing a few side ops worth doing just to see the conclusion.

Con:
       Like I said the game is the story valley. The game has very little in terms of cutscenes but rather than awesome post mission cutscenes you get a still background with narrative dialogue/ most of the plot is within tapes to be able to listen to while you play but that creates a conflict between focusing on the stealth/ shooting or listening to a large amount of tapes to understand the story. It is easier to watch a video on youtube explaining the story.

         More tools is less fun. Pretty much you have more weapons that are the same or similar but only has minor stat difference. Eventually you will find a gun that you like and you will just stick with it since any additional weapons are too similar to care. To add on top of that you take the time, money, and resources to build this next level gun and you need to pay a good amount of gmp to use it in the field. In the early game that is annoying since you will be using money on all sorts of stuff and now you need to spend a more to just use it. Early game that can be annoying and encourages grinding to have the opportunity to have fun since you will have disposable gmp.

       Some missions do not feel very metal gear solid like. I am mainly talking about the infamous mission 45 which you think your doing a stealth mission maybe but when you get in the mission your locked in it for good without any way to leave other than fulton extracting a container to fly off with it. The game puts you in a small arena fighting off waves of tanks which get progressively more annoying especially one tank can instantly kill you. The way many people do the mission is use the armor parasite. I do not know what the devs were thinking but this is not just cause 3.

       The map is too huge. Now i get it is cool to have a big map that intertwines with each mission area but it dull to look at since it is big as ocean but deep as a puddle. It has no real substance to the open world structure. The world is way to empty to even think this is an ok open world sandbox structure.

Conclusion:
      I want to like metal gear solid 5 but it is a mixed bag. It is a very mediocre dull game but the small amount of store points adds to the whole metal gear saga. Unfortuantly it is a struggle to get through the game and the story is mainly stuck to tapes so it is very visually uninteresting to look at. The cutscenes though few and far far between are nice to look at but does not warrent a playthrough. Just look up the story and cutscenes on the internet since playing the game feels like a rushed and hollowed experience. I can not recommend the game.

If steam had an option for a mixed review this would be one, the gameplay mechanics are great for doing missions the way you like since the options avaliable to the player are so deep and varied but the open world sucks and the plot is severely lacking compared to previous Metal Gear titles; there's no overarching drive to motivate the player like the nuke launch in MGS1 or the Shagohod test in Snake Eater so I ended up losing interest

TLDR: If you want a stealth game with great gameplay, Buy. If you want a stealth game with an interesting and complete story. Wait till a sale.

Jumping in you will be greeted with an opening act that sets the tone as a supernatural thriller set in the peak of the cold war. Then the game lets you loose in its open world, and you think wow this game will be a story driven roller coaster. This is a deception. There is extremely little narrative substance to the game, most of the missions and side quests are busy work. People say that Hideo Kojima’s writing is supposed to be crazy. But that feels like a cover for this kind of totally incoherent story. It’s also an extremely Japanese game, and by that I mean It’s filled with vague white people, It casually objectifies the one woman it has and it has a totally bananas moral compass.

This is also the kind of game that the phrase “ludonarrative dissonance” was made for (when the gameplay doesn’t match the story). Because there's upgrades and progression to weapons and gear, you will solve gameplay situations that you will then watch in melodramatic cutscenes be unsolvable. You will lose a companion hiding from a lone soldier, even though you just wiped out an entire mechanized company with tanks and a gunship. The good:

-Easy to learn, challenging to get perfect
-Kojima Productions has put a staggering amount of attention into details, like the chatter between soldiers, armies responding to your strategy both short-term and long-term (and chatter about that).
-Storyline keeps you hooked (especially when listening to intel tapes). Playing earlier MGS games (especially MGS1 and Ground Zeroes) before or after makes the universe even clearer. This despite the massive plot holes which are described in 'The Ugly'. It's like literature, in a sense.
-Multiple ways to complete a mission
-Excellent optimization, runs a solid 60fps on a 1050 Ti with an i5-3450.
-Good graphics (for a 2016 game)
-Good soundtrack (collecting music tapes becomes addictive)
-AI feels intelligent, and forces you to rethink your plans (while allowing a failed plan to still work in your advantage when you react quickly)
-Good voice acting
-Fun to play
-Many hours of gameplay

The bad:

-Snake feels eerily quiet. Almost makes one think that they could only afford Kiefer Sutherland for a limited amount of sessions
-Controls feel somewhat clunky, as if they just decided to map the PS3/4 controls to the mouse and keyboard. Sometimes making a wrong move makes Snake stand upright without demanding it, causing him to be detected.

The ugly:

-Chapter 2 feels botched, would have been an extra option on the main menu like in re-releases of earlier installments. Repeat missions can be avoided by doing a few side ops, though. I mean, without spoiling, recycling content is something that MGS1 (very recommended, PlayStation 1) did, but not as blatantly as this game did. I'm inclined to blame Konami's urge to get out of home video games for canning a proper chapter 2 and possibly the entirety of 3. Also a very likely canned mission (although Konami furiously denies it) which causes a massive plot hole between this game and MG1/MG2/MGS1. Kind of sad, actually.

Annoyances:

-Credits after every single mission. Yes we know Hideo Kojima made this game, Konami should have allowed him to put his name on the box as usual instead of this.
-Online functionality can be at the detriment of the singleplayer experience.
-Occasional lack of autosave checkpoints can be very frustrating when one gets killed right near the end of a boss battle.

Verdict:

I recommend this game wholeheartedly, and definitely when it's on sale.

Hideo Kojima (小島 秀夫, Kojima Hideo, born August 24, 1963) is a Japanese video game designer, director, producer and writer.

Regarded as an auteur of video games, he developed a strong passion for action/adventure cinema and literature during his childhood and adolescence. In 1986, he was hired by Konami, for which he designed and wrote Metal Gear (1987) for the MSX2, a game that laid the foundations for stealth games and the Metal Gear series, his best known and most appreciated works. The title that consecrated him as one of the most acclaimed video game designers is Metal Gear Solid (1998) for PlayStation. He is also known for producing the Zone of the Enders series, as well as writing and designing Snatcher (1988) and Policenauts (1994), graphic adventure games regarded for their cinematic presentation.

In 2005, Kojima founded Kojima Productions, a software house controlled by Konami, and by 2011, he was appointed vice president of Konami Digital Entertainment

In 2015, Kojima Productions split from Konami, becoming an independent studio. Their first game was Death Stranding, which released in 2019.[5] Kojima has also contributed to Rolling Stone, writing columns about the similarities and differences between films and video games

On November 10, 2019, Kojima was awarded two Guinness World Records for most followed video game director on Twitter and Instagram

Kojima was born the youngest of three children in Setagaya, Tokyo, Japan. His father was a travelling salesman. His family moved to Osaka when he was about four years old. They watched movies every night and he "wasn't allowed to go to bed till the film had finished".

The family moved to a small city of Shirasaki. They soon moved to Kawanishi, Hyōgo in the Kansai region. He was 13 years old when his father died and Kojima has commented that early on in his life he had to deal with death. Kojima was a latchkey kid, often having to look after himself when he came home from school. Staying at home by himself in isolation still affected him as he stated in a 2004 interview, "Whenever I travel and stay at a hotel I put the TV on as soon as I enter the room, just to deal with the feeling of loneliness".

He wanted to be an artist, filmmaker or illustrator, but felt discouraged by the pressure of social norms favoring a stable, salaried job over creative pursuits, and also because his uncle was an artist who struggled to make a living. The death of Kojima's father, which left the entire family poorer, was another reason. Kojima began studying economics,[8] while writing short stories in his spare time; he submitted some of these to magazines but was not able to get anything published. He cites that his stories were often 400 pages long while most magazines wanted their short stories to be around 100 pages.[10] Eventually, he shifted his creative focus to making films with a friend who had an 8mm camera.

In an interview on G4's TV series Icons, Kojima revealed that while studying economics in university, he found himself playing video games during his free time, mainly on the Nintendo Famicom. In his fourth year in university, Kojima surprised his peers by announcing his intentions to join the video game industry, despite initially having ambitions of becoming a film director. He felt a career in video games would be more satisfying. The majority of his friends and peers strongly discouraged Kojima from pursuing video games due to it being a new medium that was not as respected or financially secure. His mother, however, remained supportive which gave Kojima the confidence to go ahead with his dream. He would later reflect positively upon his choice, stating, "The industry was full of dropouts, people who felt like games offered them another chance. I met many people in that same situation; we bonded together through that in some sense". Kojima has cited Shigeru Miyamoto's Super Mario Bros. (1985) and Yuji Horii's The Portopia Serial Murder Case (1983) as the games that inspired him to make this decision. He cited Hydlide's open world game design as an influence. His literary influences include Kōbō Abe, Ryu Murakami, Yukio Mishima, Kazuaki Takano, Project Itoh, Yasutaka Tsutsui, Seicho Matsumoto, Richard Levinson, William Link, and Paul Auster.

Metal Gear Solid 5's development history is a modern day tragedy in gaming. Hideo Kojima's departure from the title's development basically turned what could've been one of the best games of 2010s into merely very good. 

First the good: 
+Gameplay - The shooting and stealth mechanics are blended perfectly. Everything controls and feels nice, and as your arsenal improves, so do your options in how you tackle missions. Combined with an addictive base building mode and you have a rare single player title that's gameplay loop can stand alone. 
+Graphics/Performance - Game still looks great and runs well.  
+First half of the story - If you're a Metal Gear fan, it's very engaging and builds up to a lot of big moments, including tying in Cypher/The Patriots to the plot as a whole. But....

The Negatives:
-Second half plot - It's clear that after "Chapter 1" Hideo Kojima was no longer working on the project. The missions are repeats of the one's from the first half, and plot threads are just left dangling.
-Music - Less of a negative and more of a meh-ative. From "The Best is Yet to Come," to "Snake Eater," the MGS franchise has always had a few more memorable soundtracks. "The Man Who Sold the World," is a great song, but that's about it. 

Overall: 9/10

This game really is quite bad. The opening sequence will take up half of your life. The constant spamming of credits between missions is pathetic (hubris anyone?). I'm honestly quite disappointed. Coming from a long time Metal Gear fan, this game just isn't what I though it would be. I'm quite displeased with this game, but only because I have such a high regard for the MGS franchise. I like the game, but I can not leave a positive review with a good heart. I have many problems with this game, namely:
- the gameplay,
- controls,
- movement,
- the story,
- the open world,
- mother base minigame,
- the multiplayer feature

The greatest problem with this game is that the gameplay doesn't support the Metal Gear franchise. One of the most prominent stealth game franchise. In MGSV, you can't finish the game without killing anyone. In MGSV, if you snek into a large enemy base without anyone noticing you, YOU ARE ACTUALLY PUNISHED FOR IT. Since the in-game tech research is tied to the number of people you take down and abduct, you are actually forced to take enemies from their posts. In MGS4, you could DECIDE to help one of two militias fighting, or sneak past the frontlines and ignore them all together. The choice is nice, but as one of the most prominent stealth game franchise, ditching the "ghost" style gameplay, where you aren't interacting with enemies other than sneaking around them is quite frankly appalling.

The PC controls are whack. It is very clear that as a controller has limited amount of buttons, some buttons need to have multiple purpose. These are directly mapped onto a keyboard, rather than split up onto multiple buttons. The control scheme shows a bloody controller, and the only way to figure out the controls is to look at the list of bindings. In game hint messages that tell you to push x button to do y shows controller buttons/sticks, even when no controller is plugged in. This really goes to show that the PC release wasn't a priority.

The movement is absolutely garbage. Since the player can not jump, all climbable ledges have a climb action that is shown to be available when the player is near a ledge. This system causes many many frustration. Some ledges that look like a small stairway step can not be climbed. Even if it looks like you could just walk right up on them. Some ledges have miss-placed climb action zones - that is, you can climb a ledge on the left side of it, but not the right side. Another way movement is absolute garbage is that when you push wasd, your character goes running. If you enter a door this way, enemies get alerted since you just bashed the door in. In order to open a door silently, you have to hold ctrl, and your character would move slower that a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ snail. This is obviously not a problem with a controller, where the player can move the thumb stick only halfway forward. Splinter cell solved this problem by thinking about how many extra buttons PC has and added an option to open doors slowly, when you push another button. It isn't really rocket science.

The story is butchered like pig. On youtube, one can see all the cut content, cutscenes people have extracted from the game files. There should have been more to Eli's story. But the story that did manage to stay in the game is really watered down. Coming from MGS4's long winded, movie like cutscenes, MGSV realy under delivers. Ocelot, who appears in MGS games more than any Snake, is reduced to a wikipedia. If you care at all about the crazy story of MGS, you have to sit through optional voice recordings. So what used to be hours long, cinematographic, popcorn grabbing, intense cutscenes, is now nothing but unlockable easter egg void recordings.

The open world is not open at all. The main missions have designated mission areas on the large open world map. That means is that if you wish to get from A to B on a different rout that what was designed, you are leaving the mission are and are failing the mission. What's the point of a open world, if the player can decide how to get from A to B? If the open world is cut down to small, linear sections? Between main missions you can roam the open world without these restrictions, but what's the point? I want to get clever during the main missions, not playing around between missions. Honestly I'm sure the game would play much nicer is these restrictions would be removed. However, I wouldn't oppose if it was a linear game either. MGS4 is quite a linear game and is twice the masterpiece than this not-so-open world mess. Not to mention that the episode based mission list really destroys  your immersion into the open world of MGSV. Just crashed in a helicopter and are surrounded by enemies? Who cares, go ahead and do 5 side mission before returning back to this crazy moment and dealing with this situation. lol.

Mother base is a disaster. I understand that many survival games where popular at the time, collecting, crafting stuff, building a base. But mother base and the resource collection in this game is terrible. The man who sold the world, the man who steals nukes, who f*cks with the soviets, with private armies, with secret services, magic burning people, zombie teleporting snipers and giant nuclear mech Metal Gears is picking flowers. Picking flowers, collecting shiny boxes with materials to develop mother base. Big Boss picking flowers is the single most ridiculous feature in this game and in a very bad way. Just like abducting enemy soldiers, picking flowers provide a resource that is necessary and completely destroys the gameplay. Mother base requires such a high level of micromanagement for negligible gains, it's actually just a pain in the a**. The micro management, the terrible UI, the lack of mouse support in UI all just add up to a simple question: why on earth is this all implemented? Why do I have to do this? In my opinion, it's great to see mother base growing, but it shouldn't have been something the player has to micro all the time. Moreover, mother base can't even be entered. You can't do anything while at home. I think if it was much smaller, but enterable, explorable it would have been much more interesting.

The multiplayer is just plain stupid. The whole FOB mission just feels repetitive, and useless. Thankfully you can opt out, but makes you think why single player games are willing to sacrifice longer story and more missions in favour of trying to squish in some form of multiplayer. Moreover, timed missions are always, always a unwelcome & hated feature of stealth games. Timed missions and forced multiplayer feature in a single player stealth game? Thank you, I'll pass.

All in all, I'm not happy with this game, but only because the previous MGS games where such gems. I don't understand why so many game review articles call this a masterpiece. The previous games were twice "tactical stealth action" games this is. MGSV lost it's connection with it's predecessors.

Farewell, Metal Gear.

So, I'm not recommending this game, but NOT because it's a horrible time (it's not... entirely). 

As of writing, I've put 77 hours in and plan to do more because it's an excellent game to play on your brain's autopilot once you get good at the core gameplay loop of sneaking into bases big and small in two big wide ole' sandboxes and wreaking merry havoc in both fatal and not-so-fatal varieties.

The game is certainly fun inasmuch as you sneak around and stick balloons on things, but the game is horridly grindy, full of arbitrary time gates and unpolished edges, and notoriously unfinished. 

It's also tonally inconsistent, going from "damn the whole world and let's tunnel the whole way to  h e l l  because we're already demons" to chiding you if you do anything vaguely villainous, which can range from a stern talk on heroism from the otherwise always ready to F*** S*** UP Miller (who undergoes a fair amount of character reversal between this game and Metal Gear 2) to outright giving you a straight up mission failure at worst. For a game where that was advertised around the whole point of "watch Naked Snake finally give up on the world and turn into infamous war criminal Big Boss from Metal Gear 1", the whole heroism points system from Peace Walker included here totally clashes with that advertised premise.

And that's fundamentally what's wrong here: [i]this isn't the game we were promised.[/i]

Whatever epic story you imagined watching the trailers is ten times more interesting and fulfilling than the one you'll get here. Whether characters are poorly written or just poorly used, the cast is a disappointment. Kiefer Sutherland would have been better off passing up this job offer as, despite offering a sufficiently darkened and world-weary Snake on the cusp of becoming the Big Bad of the first two games, he barely gets to speak in cutscenes, with Venom Snake reduced to Heroic Mime status in the vast majority of cutscenes. Those scenes tend to be short, by the way, going from 20 seconds to 2 minutes on average, and there aren't a lot of them -- if you play this game even close to the way it wants you to, the cutscenes are very widely spaced. A worthy successor to Metal Gear Solid's historic fusion of video game and movie, this is not. It's not even close. I hope you enjoy listening to radio dramas, because cutscenes have been replaced with [i]cassette tapes[/i]. Oh boy.

Plot threads go nowhere, and that's when they bother to try to go anywhere at all. Would have been nice to see  ̶L̶i̶q̶u̶i̶d̶ ̶S̶n̶a̶k̶e̶ Eli have some sort of relationship with Big Boss beyond simply smacking the tar out of each other. Would have been nice to see Big Boss have a relationship with most of the characters, honestly. I mean, his relationship with Quiet is about the only one handled sort of well (just please don't think about the age difference!).

None of that is even approaching the subject of the missing final chapter, the fact that there's no final boss, that the story just goes "I guess we're ending here now. Bye bye!", or [i]that[/i] plot twist. You know the one I mean.

Semi-forced PVP mechanics don't help, nor do the microtransactions which exist for no other reason than to force you to pay very real money in exchange for fake money to get your newly developed gear now, rather than in a few hours to a week.

If you play this game on PC, for the love of god, use Cheat Engine if for no other reason than to cut down on this time-gated grinding BS.

There's a good game under this title's laundry list of defects, but sadly, it's not a very good Metal Gear Solid game. It has far more in common with [i]Ghost Recon: Wildlands[/i] on just about every level than it does with Metal Gear Solid. If you liked Wildlands, I have good news! If you came hoping for the grand finale to Metal Gear Solid, or even just a well executed Metal Gear Solid game... my news is not so good.

Buy this game on sale, and play it with a cheat table active so you don't spend 6 hours waiting for your R&D team to deliver you an overpriced pistol that's [i]slightly[/i] better than the one you already have. 

Sorry Boss, this ain't the finale we were promised. That's still, and probably forever going to be (whether you have issues with it or not), [i]Guns of the Patriots.[/i]

PROs:
+ The overall production value of MGSV is ridiculously high. I don't think I've played a game this polished before; it's truly astounding.
+ Despite being an open world game set in the Afghanistan desert and the South African prairie, the level design is fantastically detailed and lovably made.
+ The graphics are fantastic. Even in AAA games, I usually stumble over a low-poly model or a low-res texture, but in MGSV I didn't find any flaws. The physics for hair and clothes are a very welcome addition that does a lot for immersion!
+ The voice acting is excellent, as is the soundtrack, and the overall sound.
+ The cinematics are fantastic. 
+ The playtime is high. It took me about 56h to complete all the story missions (see below) and about a third of the Side Ops. 
+ The story missions of the second chapter are so frickin' awesome that I can barely contain myself! Mission 43 ("Shining Lights, Even in Death") is absolutely haunting, and mission 45 (y'know, the Quiet one), is easily one of the emotional highlights of gaming history (at least Aerith doesn't die).
+ The gameplay is excellent. Stealth mechanics, gunplay, even micromanaging your stupid motherbase units. 
+ I'm pretty sure that all the flaws this game has IMHO come down to design decisions.

NEUTRALs:
~ The story consists of 50 episodes, 31 which make the first chapter and more or less complete the story of MGSV. The second chapter only has seven (incredibly excellent) story missions and twelve updated versions of old missions in 'hard mode'. Those weren't exactly fun to me, so I pretty much skipped all of them, with no disadvantage to me. It still strikes me as odd.
~ Apart from Quiet (who incidentally also is the only female character with a significant amount of screen time) the characters weren't all that likeable to me. I mean, they're all cutthroat mercenaries, so I guess they aren't supposed to be likeable, but still...
~ Quiet is an absolutely fantastic character, going for the whole 'badass chick with superpowers' thing, with a truly interesting backstory. Unfortunately, it feels a little as if the backstory is primarily supposed to justify her being all but naked with ridiculously jiggly breasts. Not that I mind having a remarkably attractive model as my sidekick, but c'mon, at least try not to immediately win the Oversexualixed Bingo.
~ Weapon suppressors wear out after about half a magazine. It clearly is a design choice, one which I can even comprehend, but it still annoyed me to no end. Thankfully there's a mod that doubles the suppressor durability (and also doubled the fun for me).
~ A lot of things about MGSV are just kind of... odd. Like the weird focus on glasses at times, or the 'Defecate!' command for your horse enemy soldiers, or the entire thing with the Man On Fire, his Flaming Unicorn, and the Floaty Boy. Honestly, after finishing the prologue, I thought I'd stumbled into some guy's acid trip. 
~ While the open world's two areas are big enough for a wide variety of missions, I pretty much knew it by heart after finishing Chapter One. Capturing/infiltrating the ever same outposts again and again for the various Side Ops did get pretty repetitive after a while.

CONTRAs:
- It's a lazy console port. The control tips the game gave me were for a controller. In quicktime events I was told to tilt my left analogue stick that way, despite me playing on PC with a keyboard and mouse. (Apparently it is a common issue that the many fixes on Google didn't solve for me).
- The jump'n'run controls are atrocious. In about two thirds of my attempts to jump over a gap, I instead fell to my death. That was rather annoying, especially because it always happened when the last checkpoint had been half an hour ago. Thankfully it's barely necessary. 
- While Motherbase is beautiful, navigating it is horrible. Traveling from one point to another involves either driving along mostly straight lines, or sitting in a helicopter for a few minutes. Sure, it's nice to look at your base the first time, but after that? Also, whoever came up with the R&D target practice Side Op... yeesh. I'm half convinced that guy implemented it just so the beta testers would complain about the crappy jump'n'run controls. Thankfully traveling around Motherbase isn't necessary all that often.
- The weird inclusion of Online features for the Singleplayer is hell on people with spotty internet connections (like me). It can be deactivated (though not permanently, I think) but of course I didn't do that. So suddenly my internet broke and the majority of my money and resources were gone until the connection reestablished itself. I'm not sure why it's designed this way but it annoyed me quite a bit. Shouldn't be a problem for most people though.

tl;dr
All in all, this is a fantastic 3rd person stealth shooter and a cinematic masterpiece with a highly polished gameplay. The (to me) only interesting character is uncomfortably oversexualized, the hints for controls were for a console (for me at least), and the very few parkour-like sections suffered from crappy controls. A single playthrough should take about 50h, though I'm sure a speedrunner could make it in less than half of that, and finishing all missions and Side Ops would probably take twice that.
I can easily recommend this game to everyone who even remotely likes stealth shooters. I bought it for 7.50€ (should be the same in $), which included Ground Zeroes, though that tiny short game is kinda useless.

This is a game I've enjoyed a lot. That is, up to a point where the annoyances starts to kick in for real. I've played this game in sessions over a few years, but I've come to a point where I wonder why the heck I've bothered... Read on.

The positives:

- Graphics. A beautiful world set in both Afghanistan and Central Afrika. Fantastic animations. Etc.
- Polish. The game runs flawlessly, and seems to be almost free of bugs.
- Gameplay. Some of the missions are great, and controlling the character works great, he always do what you're trying to do.

The negatives:

- Absolutely ridiculous story. There are so many sci-fi elements here which often doesn't make sense at all, and if you're the roleplaying type, this will be immersive breaking for you.
- The insane jumps in difficulty. Some missions are so easy you could almost do them blindfolded, while others are barely doable. Look up "Mission 20: Voices" on various sites and read the comments to see the best example on this.
- Side missions. There are 157 of these, and most of them is simply about freeing a prisoner or extract a high profile target. Not much else than that.
- Resources. You'll need a lot of these to expand your base, and if you're buying other bases, the costs to upgrade those will get insane. The problem is that you have to to a few tricks to get the RAW resources, then another trick to make them processed, because playing th enormal way won't get you close to get what you need to upgrade multiple FOBs (bases).
- Upgrading your gear. In addition to require insane amounts of money and resources, this also takes a lot of time. Prepare to play for 500+ hours if you want everything upgraded. Seriously!
- Online system. You *can* play this offline, but the moment you lose contact with the server, you also lose access to most of your resources. Because most of these are stored online, NOT on your computer/console. One of the most ridiculous online features I've ever seen.
- FOB missions. Here's my main reason to say "f*ck this" to this game, and the reason why I've had enough now! Other players can infiltrate your base while you're offline, and steal your resources. Yeah, you read that right. I've lost millions of resources this way, and it can't be stopped!

This was my first entry into the metal gear solid franchise. Seeing how this game was just a few bucks and me being a fan of stealth games, i thought i would try it out.

This game expects you to know the events that happen prior. So I looked up the story line and somewhat caught up. There are 2 chapters and a supposed chapter 3 which was cut from the game. While I enjoyed the first chapter, the story in chapter 2 is better for me personally although half of the missions in it are just rehashed missions with a twist from chapter 1 which aren't story related.

What really impressed me were the systems which worked in tandem to give you a new experience each time. You could infiltrate the same outpost a dozen times and each time it would be different. Enemies will react to your play method. Get too many headshots, the enemy will start wearing helmets. Attack at night too often, they'll start using flashlights and night vision.

The stealth in this game is by far the best I've played. I did get spotted once or twice where I feel I shouldn't have. Enemy AI is unpredictable at times. Sometimes they'll check if they see something and other times they won't. You can use the weather to your advantage as well. Such as using the reduced visibility due to a sandstorm or muffled noises due to rain.

The fox engine is optimized to front and back. I had no technical issues with the game whatsoever. And the graphics still hold up in 2020.

As the title may have suggested, there are a few areas I have issues with. While the game is indeed open world, its barren and empty, safe for the outposts and the occasional enemy patrols. Not being able to go from one point to another on the map via the chopper is an inconvenience as you have to return to the ACC and then go back. And for the main issue, the credits before every mission. These are an annoyance and at times spoil certain characters that are going to show up in the mission.

The lack of mechanics that carry over from Ground Zeroes (cameras, actual value to extracting soldiers via helicopter, enemy bases that are more than just a few huts in the middle of Africa). The way the game tried to justify multiple "endings" with glorified cutscenes that have one or two extra cinematics. The infuriating animal collection sidequest.

And yet, behind it all, is one of the best core gameplay loops ever constructed for a stealth title. 

Recon your target. Figure out who you want to nab for Mother Base. Go in with exotic weapons and shoot up the settlement, or sneak in and holdup/choke your way to supremacy. Have Quiet handle 90% of the legwork while you explore the African countryside. Play wallhacks with D-Dog as you try to clear out an XOF-controlled base in Afghanistan. Laugh as a brown bear chases you over hills as it tries to two-shot you. Dress up in Snake's original fatigues and pretend you're replaying the opening of Snake Eater while your tromp through Lufwa Valley. Outrun a flaming man who is chasing you through a burned-out refinery, then freak out when he starts spamming your escape heli with fireballs.

This game has given me more memorable moments in recent memory than just about any other I've played. Whether it's the conclusion to the "secret" sidequest on the Medical Platform, cruising around in a jeep with D-Dog by my side as Hall and Oates blasts over the speakers, frantically backpedaling as I try to avoid being spotted by troops or leaping out of my helicopter as it explodes above me, this game has given me more pure joy than a lot of other games. Yes, it can (and will) wear out its welcome... a hundred-plus hours in. Yet, it remains one of the few games I've gone and played through, twice over (the second being for 100% completion).

I still give this a very strong recommendation, even in spite of its late-game shortcomings. While I will always wonder what the game could have been had Kojima had more time (and I'm not necessarily blaming Konami for the situation - it's far more complicated than what many originally believed) with the latter half of the game, the experience is still one that shouldn't be missed for any player.

Highly-recommended, and well worth a play.

Where to start with this one? Perhaps, with the fact that I've never played a single MGS game before this one, not even 
MGS: Ground Zeroes. I picked it up on Steam after completing it years ago via crack version and I was blown away completely.
My first impressions were: this game definitely has to have at least a thousand mechanics, which it throws at the player at any one time. Saying that I was overwhelmed by the sheer number of possibilities at the start is a huge understatement. It might a while to figure out what's what and what are the best ways to use each gadget. I have to give the game props on how original some of the stealth mechanics are. I don't think I've seen any other game, where you can run around in a carton box or kidnap soldiers from the battlefield. Amazing stuff!

The story is even more confusing for a newbie. The game almost expects the players to thoroughly know the characters and the events that happened before the game. I still have more questions than answers after spending 100+ hours in the game. I guess I'll have to blame it on the lack of experience with the previous MGS games. All I can say is that the cast, the voice-acting, and the cinematics are top in the industry.

MGS V: The Phantom Pain is also an amazing looking and optimized game. I have encountered zero issues during my lengthy playthrough. Some of its environments are photorealistic, especially in Afghanistan. The African levels are just as immersive and believable, if not more.

The one complaint I have about MGS V, which does not concern the overabundance of gameplay mechanics, is the game's monotony. The side-missions are extremely repetitive and get increasingly more tedious to do, once you get to a certain point in the game. It's either: 'Go rescue that hostage' or 'Go blow up this convoy'. It gets boring the more you play them. I haven't tried out the multiplayer aspect of the game, but from what I've heard, it's pretty much dead.

Overall, incredible game, which offers an immersive sandbox experience with literally thousands of toys to play around and experiment with. Use them wisely and don't forget to summon your in-game buddies if you get lonely. They have some cards up in their sleeves (or bras...)!

Edit Update on Review:

I`ve played this game more... A LOT more. And I think I should add more of what I think to this game.

It`s a LOT more indepth than I initially expected, I`ll detail the main bits.

1. The missions are quite varied from the usual stealth to tank busting.

2. The soldier security AI is very good. If take off X-Ray and marking on the soldiers, you`ll notice how good they are. At the beginning they`re relatively relaxed, and you think you can take out a soldier or two which is easy on tiny outposts of 3 men. But any bigger and it`s not that easy. Even if you have a big ambush advantage and take down a few sentries, someone (I guess the section leader), will make a comms check. When he gets no reply, they go on alert. Sometimes they`ll just call for support which will make things even worse. Also when on Alert they usually stop walking about alone where it`s easy to pick them off, they start searching in pairs. Some soldiers are quicker on the ball than others.Even when you take out an area it`s only for a while since you often get these security trucks that come by to check everything`s ok! Very good security measures, though they are still a bit short-sighted.

3.When you blow a situation and they all go into combat mode, life can get really tough, especially in daylight. They`ll mark where you are and gather to attack it, even flanking. You need to get away from that spot fast. I usually have a back up plan like a bomb planted elsewhere to get their attention if I have to run.

4. Pretty much all missions let you do a job how you want. The missions almost never end unless you get killed. For instance, I had to find a prisoner through an enemy  interpreter, but I didn`t think and used a Tranq on the interpreter knocking him out instead of following him. So I sent him to base and they interrorgated him giving me info on where the prisoner may be found. You can even kill the interpreter, but then you have to find the prisoner yourself.

5. As the game goes on you`ll get all kinds of help from a dog (if you want him) to others. You`ll also have access to military support such as artillery. Very useful, but they all cost money.

6.You get a base (an oilrig) that at first seems empty, but then you employ staff, extra stuff and can really expand the base with medic station, R&D, military, etc. There`s way more to it than meets the eye. You can even customise it to your colour pref and even Logo. It`s almost like a 3D version of the Xcom 2 base and I wish Xcom 2 had a base that you could run around like this! 

7.You manage staff, you even manage missions staff can go on.

8.You can customise your Helo and even add music which really adds to flight in and out of missions or around the base.

9.It isn`t feminist/sjw nonsense which I really, really like, ie Quiet and most fighters are men.

10.It has some strange thing like animal conservation on your base and saving animals (but it does help get in money).

11. Weird story, but it`s ok.

12. Very realistic in some aspects (most the military and stealth stuff).

13. Some people said all you do are Afghanistan missions. Untrue. I`ve been doing African ones too, facing a lot of Africans and South Africaners so far and I`m only 12% into the game!

14. No Fast Travelling that I can see, except by realistic means, vehicle, horse, chopper, even on the base. I like as i`ve never FT in any game even when it tried to make me! Very old school.

Neutral:
1. The fantasy stuff, but now I realise why it`s called `Metal Gear Solid`. The fire man, the girl in the gasmask that`s actually a bloke. I don`t mind it, but it can be  `weird`.

2. the naming of things has that weird Japanese Final Fantasy feel, ie the simplistic names for things such as "mother Base" (nobody Western actually calls their base `mother base`) and other names that are just too on the nose at times. It likely sounds better in Japanese.

4. Campaign story is ok so far, but I`m more interested in the `open world` stuff.

5. It`s not really open world. it`s quite open but many mission lock you between impassable hills so you can`t go approach from a different angle.

6. Each mission can be LONG, as in an hour or more, depending how you approach them and I approach realistically.

7. No FT. Some people will probably hate that as they`ve been spoilt by FT.

8. If you keep failing a mission (by dying), the game gives you the option to go easy by wearing a chicken hat- I refuse! But it`s funny and then becomes annoying when it keeps asking me!


Negatives:
1. I still find doing everything in 3rd person annoying. A dedicated optional 1st person mode would make this 10\10. I`m sure I`d be 50% more efficent in 1st person.

2. A few missions are hugely annoying such as the one where I had to find a lost Wanderer. It took me absolutely ages trying to get him. Fortunately they`re the side missions.

3. Sometimes you aren`t given a choice when it looks like you should have one in the story.
4. Where are all the civilians?

I`m really impressed how much this games does, and it really tries to immerse the Player, but it takes its time. It takes quite a while before you start seeing the depth of this game. I`m only 12% of the Campaign in! It`s one of those games you have to play for at least 5 hours before you see what it has to offer.

This game is fast becoming one of the best games I`ve ever played and that`s saying something from someone who almost never touches 3rd person games. Recommended.

Forced PVP, a cynical money-grabbing scheme and no option to save manually ruin what would otherwise be a flawed but amazing game.

The issue here is that 90% of the resources and equipment you gather in your supposedly single-player game are kept 'online' in the cloud where other players can steal them.  Even while you are offline.

Want to protect your investment in time and effort?  You can buy 'insurance' from Konami but only for real money.

Honestly it's a scam worthy of a mobile game, I'm almost impressed.

And of course, even if your stuff doesn't get stolen, you can't access it yourself if you lose your internet connection.  Fantastic game mechanic.  To make matters worse it only really starts to affect you after you are about a quarter of the way through the story and have hours invested, so good luck getting a refund.

Other than that, well, it's a Hideo Kojima game.  Don't worry, you won't forget, he makes sure to have his name up on the screen at least twice an hour while you are playing - writing and level design credits roll after every single mission.  Oh and also before, during the briefing, so you can't skip them.

The first level of the game consists of half an hour of cutscenes, which can thankfully be skipped, and half an hour of crawling along the ground, which can't.  Every time you start a new game.  Make a save point after the intro so you don't have to play it again every time?  Sorry, no manual saves.

That autosave is the other massive drawback of this game.  It's inexcusable in a supposedly open-world game to not allow you to save when you want.  It's unreliable as well: it's not tied to completing missions, or moving to different zones, or even to the passage of time, it just seems to save when it feels like it.  Sometimes three times in as many minutes, sometimes not for an hour.  Which, inevitably, means at some point you are going to lose hours of progress. 

The interminable cutscenes, the constant rolling credits, and the lack of what I guess they considered an 'immersion breaking' save option can sometimes make it feel like you are watching a movie rather than playing a game, but if so then it's a movie aimed squarely at tweenage boys.  Obviously the character of Quiet is well known about these days; I won't go into the dubious lore that tries to explain why she is walking around in ripped fishnet tights and a bikini, I will just point out that every cutscene involving her seems to start with the camera zoomed in on her chest.

As for the actual gameplay?  It's a lot of fun with lots of different options for completing missions, but the mouse and keyboard controls suck.

So I'd never played a Metal Gear Solid game before. It's weird. Not necessarily bad. The gameplay itself is good. Guns, sneaking, the buddies you get to help you, the sheer amount of options on the tale for how you wanna play is awesome. Every variety of lethal or tranquilizer weapons, using balloons to abduct people and animals, bipedal mechs. It has a lot of good stuff, and many beats in the story are pretty good or at the least they ham it up so much you'll chuckle at how serious they take things. 
Positive notes I will say. Sneaking is great, everything about the sneaking feels right. Hiding in darkness, taking cover etc. They give you lots of ways to hide like hiding in toilets, dumpsters or cardboard boxes. There's lots of little bits of polish and mechanics that are neat. You get a recording of a guy having violent diarheaa and if you play it while a guard might suspect you're hiding in a toilet, he gets grossed out and leaves. And you can move around as the cardboard boxes not only to sneak,  but to fast travel. The cardboard box stuff is just great. 
One of the best things in the game is your buddies. You start with a horse. D-Horse is cool. Great horse, comes when you call, can later on poop on command. You can hang of his side and hide while riding. The you get D-Dog. D-dog is amazing because he shows you where all the enemies nearby are. Which is super useful because up until that point, you keep getting caught by dudes who you didn't notice. He also later gets the ability to distract stun or kill enemies. Super good dog. The you get Quiet, who is a sniper. As a buddy, she's probably the best because you have actual backup in the game. In addition she can also scout places. She's not always as efficient as D-Dog, but she can cover your butt when you need it so she's great. Probably wouldn't have made it through the game in the time I did without her. Final buddy is a Walker vehicle. Barely used it but it's neat. Goes real fast, and super all terrain. 

That said it does have a number of negative aspects worth discussing. First off, unless you played other Metal Gear games, you won't know a bit of what people are talking about is, except for context clues. That's normal for a game that's part of a longrunning series but this is some next level stuff where they really don't explain a lot of who people are prior to this game.
Secondly, it starts with this hospital level where everything is really weird and confusing and you have severely limited mobility at first. Now all the weird stuff does get cleared up, but you have to play the whole game to learn why all the crazy stuff in the first level makes sense. A lot of people have also said that the game doesn't have an ending. No it does. They just make you replay the first hospital level. Which is annoying because even though you now understand all the crazy stuff, you're also just replaying the same low mobility tutorial level and all they changed was that there's like 1 little cutscene change. And then there's a bunch of cutscene at the end that end it. 
So yeah, the end doesn't have a boss battle or a clear ending point due to something you did. Which sucks because there are a couple of loose strings that don't get tied up, that they clearly wanted to make into a final boss and didn't. 
It's also really clear everything that happens the way it is, happens just so they can set up the games that already came out, but take place in the future. 

All in all, good game. They just go a weird direction sometimes.

This game is a huge turd. Don't let my playtime deceive you: I hated this game so much that I made sure to 100% it, just so I could feel certain that I'd never have to come back to it again. Let's examine.

#1. Story

Remember, "Nanomachines, son?" 

Well..."Vocal chords parasites, son." 

Receive in this game an exhaustive answer to a question no one was asking. How did the characters in MGS3 receive their magic powers? Vocal chord parasites!

♥♥♥♥ that!

In terms of structure, the story is a disaster. Gone are the days of the Kojima cutscene. There are hardly any cutscenes at all (plus one really long and awkward car ride with Skullface), and the story is a meandering mess. At the end, when the stupidest twist of all time is dropped onto the player, you must completely redo the tutorial mission WITH ALL OF THE TUTORIAL STUFF STILL IN THE GAME--remember that you've played at least 100 hours to get to this point--just to see the one thing at the end that's different. 

The entire third act of the game was cut and there's basically no ending, and most of the missions are copy-pasted with minimal differences. The game has 50 missions technically, but you run out of new ones at 25 and then have to do slightly changed versions over again in order to reach the "true" ending. And once you do reach the "true ending," once you do replay that ♥♥♥♥♥♥ tutorial--which, by the way, everyone raves about; it's boring, linear, and not anything like MGS should be, and it tipped me off that this game would blow right from the get-go--you magically receive a dozen extra audiologs that explain all of the rest of the story to you. That's it. The final chapter of the Metal Gear saga, and its conclusion is a podcast. Not even a cutscene where Big Boss explains everything. Just a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ podcast. 

We were supposed to receive the origin story of Big Boss. If you haven't already been spoiled, that's not what this game is. It was supposed to tell a tale of a descent into darkness, bridging the gap between the idealist of Peace Walker and the warmonger of Metal Gear. Snake even has a horn! Look how dark this'll be!

But MGSV isn't dark. In fact, it goes out of its way to be not-dark. There are child soldiers, but you're not allowed to murder them--in fact, you get a game over if you try to. By the midpoint of the narrative, Venom Snake has basically started his own daycare, and Kaz makes sure to always remind us that the kiddies are being treated well. Huh? What? Aren't we supposed to be evil? Isn't Venom the bad guy? What is this? Is Kojima really this incapable of writing a thematically cohesive narrative, or could he just not stand to be mean to babies in his game? 

If you can't tell, my disappointment in this regard is immeasurable. For years I was desperately awaiting MGSV's release. MGS3 is my favorite game of all time. I love Peace Walker. I like MGS2 and 4 a lot. And even after falling for the scam that was Ground Zeroes, I was still unbelievably excited for V. 

Then I played the game. 

#2. The Gameplay

On the surface, MGSV has an excellent primary gameplay loop. The sneaking has never felt better. It has one big problem, though: 

IT SUCKS. 

The issue is that the primary gameplay loop doesn't feed very well into the base management systems. You can beat this entire game without ever thinking about it, and so you're hardly ever incentivized to actually engage with the mechanics. You will anyway, because everyone likes cool stuff, but the unlocks basically do nothing. Not in the literal sense; literally, they're very valuable, for the most part, but MGSV is too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ easy. You can beat the whole game by shooting everyone to death with rubber bullets. And you HAVE to take rifles every mission! No OSP, unless the game decides it's an OSP mission. 

Every stealth game, and especially every MGS game, struggles with this problem, but you have so many tools in MGSV that it's the worst it's ever been. A sneaking mission? Why not just take a tank instead?

Yeah, you can drive a tank in this stealth game. 

The entire game has been balanced around the slow-mo Splinter Cell alert mode, where you have a free three second window to get a tranq headshot when spotted. This will make even the most inept players feel like a god. It trivializes stealth. But if you turn Splinter Cell mode off, the game suddenly becomes impossible--sneaking just isn't practical over long distances without it, not in a game set mostly outside. More on that later. 

Ironically, Ground Zeroes is the MGSV we really needed. A focus on open-ended stealth action in conjunction with clear objectives and linear narrative. A game that is narratively cohesive, just like MGS 1-4. Peace Walker works because it's, basically, a mobile game. But when I sit down to play a game at my PC, I don't want a mobile game's structure. It's too disjointed. It doesn't work. Every mission in this game ends before it feels like it's gotten started. It's not engaging. 

This, in conjunction with the complete focus on overworld stealth, ruins the game. Sneaking around Afghanistan, which is all brown and tan and ugly, is not nearly as interesting as sneaking around Shadow Moses. Understand that there is basically NO inside stealth in this game. There's a very small number of vaguely urban levels, but most of it is in the desert or the jungle. This is repetitive and uninteresting, and the focus on exteriors means the level design is completely without merit. There's just nothing there.

I'd like to remind you at this point that all of the best parts of MGS3, the game that takes place in a jungle, were actually when you were inside of a Soviet compound. 

And there are just so many other issues. Flying in with the helicopter every mission, seeing Kojima's name over and over and over again, dealing with clunky menus, handling countless bugs (many of which have probably been fixed by now; i haven't played this game in 4 years)--basically, ♥♥♥♥ this game, don't play it.

#3. ♥♥♥♥ this game, don't play it.

In summary, if you want a TL;DR: "Vocal chord parasites, son." That should explain my review. Oh, wait, it doesn't? ♥♥♥♥ YOUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUU
