As someone who's played every game since Metal Gear Solid at release I still love this game although it's easily the weakest of the Kojima made games. The gameplay itself is great although the side quests are very repetitive (go extract/destroy tanks, clear this minefield) but the game lacks the depth of previous Kojima games. In previous games you could call experts who would tell you about guns/equipment but in this game they just state the obvious, telling me what it is and stopping at that. I do love the level design though and how Kojima used the open world to let the player take lots of different approaches to a mission. The story is told mostly through tapes and even then snake barely talks although I do like him when he does, his voice is much better than it was in ground zeroes but still no David Hayter. Enemies are deaf and blind however they can call in reinforcements and a helicopter and they search your last location if they lose you and you can always bump into those reinforcements while escaping. You can of course disable these and it can make for useful distractions, getting certain guards to move out of the way while you go in and rescue a prisoner. The Kojima humour is still present, the funniest thing is having DD on lethal, sending him into a camp and just watching him jump on enemies and slitting their throats. You can also have Quiet snipe an outpost and sit back and laugh as they're picked off or give her a loud sniper and laugh as she comes under fire from the whole outpost and you get to sneak in.
I love that you can drive vehicles in this game, giving you another way to complete objectives, drive straight in and use the armour to tank the shots then quickly fulton a prisoner or attack the base with it while playing 80s hits. If you don't fancy driving you could also have the helicopter transport you, ride on your horse or use a small mech. Speaking of mechs, there is a boss metal gear which is a fun and unique fight and quite tough. The skulls you fight are also very tough. It took me hours to beat both versions the first time through and the sniper battle when you first meet quiet is also fun, especially on extreme where one mistake spells your death. The plot had an interesting story about eliminating languages but skull face is so underused, he was excellent and mysterious in GZ but that goes nowhere. He's so unimportant they gave major characters from other games a comeback and fleshed them out, they all have nice twist endings that I won't spoil. MGS4 had their nanomachines to explain away things and this
game is no exception which is a shame. They have their own version of nanomachines that relate to the eliminating languages thing skullface is trying to do, I tuned out to it though and can't remember why they're in the story, the reason given already makes sense without needing their own version of nanomachines. So while everything is a mixed bag I still easily recommended this.

PROS
---------------------
A game that was incomplete story-wise and yet remains one of the most satisfying gaming experiences to date. Smooth gameplay, breathtaking graphics, seamless controls, awesome missions. Even if you've never played Metal Gear, this one's an absolutely amazing game.

+Phenomenal soundtrack collection that will lead some pretty damn awesome "OH F*CK YEAH, THIS IS SO HAPPENING RIGHT NOW* moments

+Caters to both beginner and advanced stealth gamers- whether you go guns blazing or try to do it the Big Boss way, the fun and the challenge remains the same.

+Just amazing CQC-Animations-Feeling of take downs

+Great Gunplay

+Amazing details & Easter Eggs + Costumes + Characters

+The whole concept behind vocal parasites I found to be mindblowingly good (even tho greatly unrealized into actual gameplay-story progression)

+Awesome open world approach

+Cool base building mechanics, online multiplayer & online competition- even tho the scene is kind of dead now

+ D-Dog

CONS
---------------------
I've played all MG games since MGS, and I really loved this one. As a hardcore metal gear fan, I loved every second of it- the only con is that once it was over, I had a huge feeling that something is missing, that there was more to come. 

Unfortunately, following the Konami-Kojima fallout, it made sense why I had that feeling. I really hope it gets completed, someday, somehow. 


-It does get a bit repetitive after a while and 

-it does have unskippable entry videos that make it tedious to wait, especially if you devour the game and clock 100s of hours in a short period of time.

-unfinished

-David Hayter will ALWAYS be Snake and Big Boss. ALWAYS.

-A huge amount of lore that is shoved into tapes you have to listen- I did listen to all of them- and I was just sad this was not somehow translated into the game for additional length story-wise

- No background or spine-twisting premise for the bosses, I mean...common..they did feel too generic and just meh. even tho slightly challenging.

======================

VERDICT: You're simply not going to regret buying this if you are a die-hard fan of the series- you will have an amazing time, and you are going to absolutely love it if you're new to this MG universe. 

Definitely recommend, it's just mindblowing how good this game is, despite it's drawbacks. (and those will only affect the hardcore MG fans)

This is a very good open world stealth/action game but it is not a perfect one. I'll just list pros and cons of the single player game and then review FOB missions separately.


[b]Pros (Single Player):[/b]

- A pretty good story. I didn't like some aspects of it but overall it was well told and had interesting characters.
- Excellent open world with lots to do.
- Very good stealth aspects, it is very punishing at the start but more and more rewarding as you get better at the game.
- Decent loud action but I feel that this isn't the way this game is meant to be played.
- Lots and lots of guns, most of them are behind expensive upgrades but the point still stands.
- A vast upgrade system, there is plenty of endgame content here and plenty of options of approaching the same missions differently.
- Excellent graphics, even for 2019.
- A metric tonne of content, there is easily over a hundred hours of SP content here.


[b]Cons (Single Player)[/b]

- The helicopter ride at the start of every mission is just wasted time and could have been a skippable cut-scene.
- The second half of the game was mostly harder versions of the first half's missions which I thought was lazy.
- Some secondary mission objectives are absolutely terrible so if you are a completionist you are in for a bad time with a lot of the end game content.
- Collect-a-crap achievements which are absolutely ridiculous in their scope, again completionists are going to have a bad time with this.
- Getting around the Afghanistan map is needlessly tedious due to large sections of impassible terrain.
- Some of the endgame gun/item upgrades take a ridiculous amount of time to complete.

Overall, despite the downsides, this is an excellent game in its SP portion.

FOBs are the online portion of MGSV and this is the weakest part of the package. The amount of guards and security measures on the advanced FOBs is so heavy that even the most careful run and with plenty of experience you will likely end up in a shootout after inevitable discovery. The PvP combat in FOB's is hilariously bad and as a new player to FOB's or even one with weeks of experience you will stand absolutely zero chance against players who have grinded the endgame gear for this game. To be fair, you can just run away when someone invades your game and I highly recommend doing exactly that because PvP is a complete waste of your time. The endgame upgrades related to FOBs take an insane amount of time to complete, I've come across one that will take 10 days (no exaggeration) to complete. 

One aspect of FOBs that some will deny is the fact and it is a fact that microtransations related to FOBs (MB coins) are PtW. Well, they absolutely are pay to win. The reasons are as follows:

- Insane upgrade grind I mentioned earlier, you can skip that altogether with MB coins. 
- MB coins allow you to buy extra FOBs which will give you a massive resource and research boost.
- MB coins can buy you FOB insurance which sounds like a protection racket and that's because it is.
- MB coins also allow you to complete dispatch missions (missions where you send your minions on headhunting/resource gathering missions) which means you will be swimming in resources and high level soldiers if you can pony up real world cash.

It's not all bad, FOBs can be rewarding when you pull off that perfect stealth run but it is weakest part of the package and one that can actually negatively impact your single player experience if your resources and soldiers get stolen by another player.

This is my first MGS game, and I was hesitant to get into it considering I knew next to nothing about the story or the franchise in general. 54 hours in, and having completed only about 24% of the main story, I have one word to describe this gem. Phenomenal. The story weaves itself completely organically against the backdrop of some of the tightest gun-play and tactical operations. The base-building component is woven in beautifully with the core gameplay mechanics, and yet never impedes on the main focus of the game itself. Even though the pattern of the side-missions can get repetitive, as others may have pointed out, the absolute freedom with which to approach a situation is so liberating that it never really gets boring unlike in so many other titles. Stealth works wonderfully and the diverse pattern of enemy takedowns, interrogations, and hiding bodies (or extracting them) creates this consistent hypnotic rhythm which allows for this amazing and immersive experience. The main missions feel fresh so far and can quickly get very challenging, especially, if the focus is to get higher mission rankings. The game truly comes alive if one leans towards stealth-based and tactical strategies with the occasional gleeful killing spree on side missions. Make no mistake the gameplay is most rewarding when trying to be a ghost, or should I say, Phantom , in completion of the objectives. 
 
MGSV looks stunning, and at times while riding thru the deserts of Afghanistan, one can't but be reminded of memorable moments  from the The Witcher 3. Some have complained about the gameworld being rather barren, and the lack of NPCs but then again, this isn't an RPG. That said the sandbox style open world and the way it is populated works perfectly within the context and scope of the game.  Surprisingly for a console port, I didn't have to change a single keybinding and the controls and mapping feel transparent in their functionality (considering there are multiple possibilities of equipping support gear on the fly or accessing the iDroid for tac support). 

There are so many other details that are taken care of so well in the game (for instance the Buddy system), that go on make this such a unique and engaging experience. Highly recommend this game, particularly to those on the fence because they haven't the prior titles. Just go for it!

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain. There isn't much to say about this title that hasn't already been stated in other reviews but I do feel the need to mention a few things regardless. The overall narrative is fairly weak and incomplete and this is likely my biggest gripe with the title. The story starts out strong in the first 10 missions or so and then really begins to fizzle out 20 to 30 missions onward. Eventually you're left with the burning hulk of what could have been an interesting narrative.

Despite this, the gameplay has been nothing short of amazing. Decoys, sliding down a mountain in a cardboard box, gunplay, upgrades, MGSV really had it all in regards to the ability to have fun with the world around you and the tools you're given. There are a plethora of weapons from rifles to rocket launchers and of course you can't forget the multiple options you have in regards to nonlethal weaponry as well. You can use the weaponry and tools you've acquired to accomplish anything that's thrown at you in just about any way you could imagine. 

There is a bit of a grind involved in MGSV and while I felt it was unnecessary, I was able to get rid of the issue with mods, and yes there are a fair amount of mods available for the game as well. Just be aware that if you're going to purchase MGSV you will be purchasing it for the game mechanics and not for the story. If you're buying it for the story you may very well feel disappointed. For the price of the game vs what it has to offer I do feel this is a title I can recommend.

9 out of 10 .......................A++ open-world stealth action game.... manage a global merc operation, stockpiling resources, upgrading weapons/armor, and recruiting soldiers from the field. The stealth and combat gameplay is just flawless down to the last detail. Enemy AI is incredibly well implemented, and there is massive space for creativity and personal style in how each mission can be completed. The Fox Engine runs so well that even on my potato intel HD the world looks gorgeous and runs at a steady ~30fps, medium settings. Leaving aside the backstory from previous Metal Gears (which I am not too savvy on - last played metal gear series circa 2001 with the Sons of Liberty instalment), the story in MGS5 is, let's say, intriguing to the end, but certainly stands out as the game's weak point. As much as I was down to see how all the initial mysteries would be resolved, most of them they were fleshed out in a somewhat underwhelming way, mostly in terms of the writing and the way they were presented (e.g. via later cassette recording rather than gritty cut-scene dialog). It does feel as though the game's story narrative (with the exception of the incredible effort put into lore and backstory) has not been implemented with the same love and care that the general mechanism of gameplay has, giving weight to the rumors that Konami rushed it to production as they were breaking ties with game creator Hideo Kojima and the hefty expense bill of his team. That the game is so excellent in spite of all this is a testament to the people involved, but it's definitely a case of HOW GOOD COULD THIS HAVE BEEN??!!

After years of not knowing what "The Definitive Experience" DLC contained exactly, I decided to purchase it on the most recent sale. This Deluxe Edition includes a hidden DLC not visible on the store page (but visible in your library after purchase.) Containing the Day One / Pre-Order Edition weapons, uniform camos, and bonus staff.

There are conflicting stories and rumors that have been around since launch about buying DE over base MGSV, like not being able to use your pre-existing MGSV save on the Definitive Experience version. I think these rumors are likely true for console players with some disc releases of the game, but it is NOT true on PC.
I've avoided buying this Deluxe Edition for years because of it, turns out my pre-existing save with 800+ hours is totally safe and I can keep using it. The DE DLC is added to the game like any other DLC pack without issue or save file problems.

I did some digging to see exactly what items The DE adds to the game and was lucky enough to find an old community hub post with the list, so I'll reference that here. (Thank you to Cobra Caddie.)

Personal Ballistic Shield (Silver)*

My only question at this point is,  "Who ruined the game?"  Was it the Kojima development team, or was it Konami?  The game has everything needed to be outstanding... but there is always some corporate BS feature added in to ruin the experience. Here is my short list of such features:

- Insane crafting requirements for weapons and items:  After you get half way through the game, some of the guns and items require millions of GMP (the in-game currency) to "develop".  Who is going to re-play 18 missions just to get a dot sight upgrade on ONE gun? 
- Forced time-delays on crafting: Let's say you grind for days to gather all the necessary resources to develop a gun you want.  The game rewards you with a big "F^%$ YOU!".  You get a timer put up over the item that you wanted.  The timers range from a few minutes to WEEKS!  
- Forced gameplay styles:  Once you have grinded for days to get the required resources, then waited another week for the forced time delay to expire after leaving the game running 24/7, finally you can use your shiny new gun.  Except you can't.  If you shoot too many people in the game, your "Demon meter" fills up.  Once it gets to a certain point your character becomes PERMANENTLY covered in blood and has a huge pointy rock sticking out of his head.  
- Microtransations:  So the in-game money is called "GMP".  Except it's not the in-game money.  The real in-game money is called "MB Coins".  You earn MB coins by ... spending real life money to buy them? 
- Pay to win:  If you are willing to pay an extra $100 dollars, on top of the $60 for the game, on gun and item upgrades then you can be pretty much unstoppable in this game.    
- Near-impossible objectives:  Did you ever feel like riding around the entire country of Afghanistan looking for one prisoner hiding in a random cave?  Me neither.  That is what a lot of the game objectives are like.  
- Deceptive leveling system: If the soldiers you already have at your base are at a low level (E rank), you are only going to see low-level soldiers on the battlefield (E rank).  If you paid a bunch of extra money on microtransactions to level-up your base fast (why in the HELL would you?), and your soldiers are all high levels (S rank), then you are going to see high-level soldiers in the battlefield (S rank). Completing harder missions, or playing better have NOTHING to do with the ranking of soldiers you find. 
- Stupid Base-Building Mechanics:  The first thousand or so soldiers that join you are worthless in terms of unlocking important weapons and items.  
People who buy this game are treated like horses being led around with a carrot on a stick.  Early on in the game, a little extra grinding reaps some good rewards.  However by the middle of the game you are being led on an endless wild goose chase.  Grinding, paying more money, and accomplishing obscure, almost impossible to find objectives earns you nothing but more of the same.

Even though I'm giving this game a recommendation, it's difficult to recommend for everyone; speaking as a fan of the Metal Gear franchise, this one in particular can be a bit of a mixed bag depending on what you're looking for.

In order to better understand the story of The Phantom Pain, hereby referred to as simply MGSV, I'd strongly recommend playing Ground Zeroes first, as that serves as the prologue to MGSV; it's included with the Definitive Experience.  If you haven't already, I'd encourage playing the earlier Metal Gear games as well, such as Peace Walker and MGS3, but they aren't necessary to play in order to understand MGSV's story.

Once again, you're the legendary soldier Snake, and you're in charge of your own private military force.   It's revealed not far in the game that the army Snake raised in the previous game, Peace Walker, was effectively wiped out by agents of Cipher, an organization Snake opposed during that game, and after some time out of action, Snake must rebuild his army and strike back at the ones that took everything away from him.  

Regarding gameplay, it's essentially Peace Walker 2.0 as a lot of the same ideas and mechanics return with some refinement here.  One of your goals is to make your army stronger by recruiting people to join your staff, obtain resources and materials that you can use to develop weapons, equipment, and even expanding your base itself.  It has a bit of an open-world mentality in that you can pretty much do things your own way and are actively encouraged to try different strategies, as the enemy forces adapt to your tactics and counter them in various ways (for example, if you infiltrate facilities at night too often, they'll start carrying flashlights and night-vision googles; if you rely on headshots extensively, they'll start wearing helmets, and so on; although you'll eventually have the ability to counter these yourself by sending some of your units on deployment missions).  Given the franchise's origins, stealth is encouraged; but you can also go in guns ablazing if you really want to, especially once you've developed stronger weapons and armor for yourself to use.  The game also has a buddy system where you can deploy with one of the various buddies once you have them available; you start with just the horse, which is good for traveling to places quickly especially towards the beginning of the game, but you'll also unlock a few others that have their own specialties and uses.  I'd recommend trying them once you have them and seeing for yourself how they work and which ones best suit your particular playstyle.

The controls are fantastic, everything is easy enough to do and your character has considerably more freedom in terms of movement and control then the previous games.  MGSV also has a few features to help make it a little more accessible to players, such as reflex mode which briefly slows down your perception of time if an enemy finds you, allowing you some time to take them out before your cover is completely blown, or escape depending on your situation (if you don't want this feature on, you're free to turn it off if you wish).

One minor point of criticism I have is that some aspects of MGSV are locked online, meaning you must have an Internet connection in order to use all the features MGSV has to offer.  After you've reached a certain point, you're given the ability to build Forward Operating Bases, or FOBs for short, giving players the means of expanding their army even greater then before.  Think of FOBs as secondary bases you can build that allow you to house more staff and resources, allowing you the ability to develop more things and harvest resources faster then you would without.  This sounds great, but here's the catch; once you've made an FOB, you'll be open to attack by other players: other players in the game can infiltrate your FOBs to steal your staff and resources from you and vice versa.  Generally speaking, as long as you don't partake in such invasions yourself and have sufficient security levels prepped up, you should be left alone; although you may occasionally still get a random player that will try to invade your base to steal your stuff, and there's not much you can really do about that unfortunately.  It should be noted that, even if you do get invaded and your defense fails once in a while, you really don't lose all that much that you can't get back relatively quickly, so it's really more of a minor inconvenience at best.  Another thing that kinda sucks is that a large portion of your resources get locked online as well (to put it one way, imagine most of your resources are being stored on those FOBs), so if you lose your Internet connection for whatever reason, you won't be able to use any of those online resources at all until your connection comes back.  If you don't want [i]anything[/i] to do with this though, just don't agree to the Terms of Service before you start playing the game and you won't be taken online, although you'll also lose stuff like daily bonuses and other similar perks until you decide to agree to the ToS.

Another object of some controversy is the story itself; which I admit is a bit weaker compared to the other Metal Gear games.  Without spoiling anything, after you finish the first segment of MGSV, the story kind of drags on from there and once it starts picking back up again, the ending suddenly shows up and you'll probably be left wondering “wait, that's it?” and the ending itself may leave a bit to be desired.  Being the very last game that the creator of the franchise, Hideo Kojima, worked on before his departure from Konami and knowing that MGSV had a bit of a rocky development due to internal issues between Konami and Kojima's team, it understandably can be quite disappointing as a grand finale to the franchise as we know it, although after enough time, you may come to accept it for what it is and may even be able to appreciate the message it left after the fact.  To get the most of MGSV's story, I'd suggest listening to the optional cassette tapes you can find under the Missions tab on the iDroid.

There's another online component in the form of Metal Gear Online, some kind of PvP team-orientated multiplayer shooting game loosely based on MGSV.  Personally, I don't care for these kind of games to begin with and never bothered to try it.  As I understand it as of this writing, there's a small player base out there and it's still possible to play games, although a portion of the player base are known to use cheats and hacks which is always frustrating to potential players, but your mileage may vary.

One more matter to bring up is DLC.  If you're going with the Definitive Experience, you'll have everything that was ever released for MGSV on Steam, including the previously unavailable day-one DLC that the console versions got, which consists of a few unique weapons, items, and uniforms for your character to wear; Definitive Experience is the only way to get that content on Steam, so be aware of that.  I don't find any of these DLC to be overpowered, especially the weapons as they are just weaker versions of weapons that you could develop yourself later in the game anyway.

Overall, as I initially wrote, it's difficult to fully recommend this title; it's definitely not for everyone, although I'd recommend it to fans of the franchise in general.  MGSV easily offers the best gameplay in the whole franchise; it's so much fun sneaking around and using all sorts of different gadgets and weapons and trying different strategies for each missions (almost anything you can think of is a legit tactic to try).  For those seeking something more like the previous games with a strong story, you may be a bit disappointed, but you may be able to make something positive out of it as well.  If you're interested at all, I'd definitely suggest picking up the Definitive Experience as it's more bang for your buck then just buying the base game.

When I first got MGSV I was only interested in the creative and fun ways you can do things stealthily, but I quickly got into the story and eventually I found myself invested in it, and it is because of that, that MGSV has become one of my favorite videogames of all time. And since I've finished the story, I've decided to write a review going over the key features and explaining the goods and bads of them.


Open world:
-There are two large maps each with their own unique environments, weather patterns, and locations.
 Both maps have outposts, bases and other special locations scattered throughout them. The open world part is great 
 because it allows you to tackle missions and objectives in many, many ways. Although there are many things to in free 
 roam from completing side ops to gathering resources to just capturing outposts, I found that these activities can become 
 repetitive and not fun if you do them very often, and once you've completed the story, there isn't much else to do 
 in singleplayer.
-You can build and upgrade your very own Mother Base, with several teams and platforms with their own unique functions 
 that you can level up by building more platforms and acquiring more staff to unlock new abilities and opportunities.
-There is a HUGE amount of weapons, items, and tools you can use to help you on your many missions, though I found 
 that you don't really need all of them. I wanted to unlock everything just for the sake of completion but eventually the 
 costs become so high that replaying missions and side ops just isn't enough to maintain a stable GMP level and develop 
 new equipment.


Story:
-The story for me was probably the best part of this game and like I said before, I wasn't interested in at all when I started.
 This game has an amazing story with amazing characters (thanks primarily to Kojima) and it is because of it that this game 
 is my number 2 favorite. Some would probably say that this game doesn't have the best story in the series, and they may 
 be right, I really can't say that it does or doesn't because I haven't played any other MGS games.
-Unfortunately, the story itself is unfinished; this I'm sure many of you know already. Once you finish chapter one, you get 
 a sortof teaser for chapter two, and when I first saw that I was like: "Sh*t's about to get crazy now." But chapter two is 
 mostly just extreme replays of earlier missions with only a few new missions.
-Another con of the story is that it's not completely replay-able, sure you can do the missions again as many times as you 
 want but you wont get the full story like you did when you first played through. The only real way to replay the story is to 
 start a new game, but screw that because I don't want to go through all that open world crap just to relive the story, I just 
 don't think it's worth all that time and effort. It's truly a shame because I really like the story in this game.


Multiplayer:
-I haven't played enough of MGO to have a well informed opinion of it, but I'm going to share my opinion of it anyway.
 To me, MGO is just Konomi's attempt at GTA Online, which to Rockstar and Take 2 is just a money farm. I'm not sure 
 exactly what it is but I am determined to avoid MGO completely.


Though it has many problems, I still love this game for it's story and openworld.
In the final words of my review, I shall say: Thank you, thank you Hideo Kojima, and curse you Konomi.

Through the years, I've been looking at the MGS games with a dubious eye. I had never played any game from the franchise (except a few hours of the first modern installment of the Playstation era) and the only contact that I had with it was a few cutscenes watched on YouTube to understand what the fuss was about the "Kojima's writing genius", regurlarly praised by aficionados. Needless to say that through these videos I was not convinced, the hype seemed really exagerated.
Enter MGS V. The first hours (the introduction to the real game) were extremely cinematic in the wrong sense: maelstrom of movies influence, rigid and directive gameplay, ridiculously over the top sequences... Not a good start! 
And then, you're finally dropped in Afghanistan on your horse: the real MGS V experience can blossom. And what a beautiful, complex and generous flower! This is simply one of the best infiltration game of the modern era. With its open world settings, you are free to play it like you want thanks to the multiplicity of tools, weapons and companions and really well implemented gameplay mechanisms (horse sh*t, anyone?). The maniability of Snake is really smooth and pleasant. Even when all your nicely planned infiltration goes in the gutter, following detection by the enemy, you can shoot your way through or hide for a while rather easily. 
With a great number of missions, the game never bores you. What a pity that the end of the game seems botched (replay some of the main arc missions, what a stupid idea!), due probably to the Kojima-Konami feud. 
Nevertheless, the lasting impression that you will have will be one of a great, fun, unique and generous game!

No game has left me feeling more bittersweet than MGSV. While being one of the best games I've ever played it also includes an incomplete story that will, likely, never get the ending it deserves. Gameplay is perfect with everything feeling tight and clean for a stealth shooter game. Enemies learn your patterns and adapt to your play style. I for one kept going for headshots only for enemy soldier to start wearing helmets. However, you can still land a headshot if you aim perfectly to just hit enemies in the face and miss the helmet. Some things feel a little dumbed down, such as slowing down time right as you are discovered giving you the split second to avoid detection by killing the spotter, but much of these elements can be changed with the difficulty slider. The story is also not on the same page as previous MGS games. It falls more to the wayside and is somehow the most grounded narrative of the series. One can only guess this was a result of complaints from MGS4 and it's ridiculous amount of cutscenes. Still the game is a perfect send off for the franchise at it feels like a culmination of everything the gameplay ever wanted to be. You feel like a super stealth agent who can handle themselves in any way they see fit, including dropping a supply box on an enemies head to make them unconscious.

To sum it up: this game has its storng points, but as it is, MGSV is only a phantom of what it could have been. And sometimes, a pain.

[list]
[*] Many different ways to complete an objective in singleplayer missions.
[*] Many different tricks up your sleeves in general.
[*] The freedom of open-world gameplay is fun. Run around plundering gold and gems and stuff (and soldiers who are not worthless.)
[*] Story by the legendary Hideo Kojima (until the second half, when things start getting hazy.)
[*] NPCs have appropriate reactions to common situations, up to and including "dude, where's our truck?"
[*] Graphics on par with any AAA title.
[*] Press-X-to-not-die events are actually somewhat intuitive.
[*] You can make your helicopter play your favorite songs as you deploy on a mission.
[*] A slow trickle of MB Coins for those who refuse to buy virtual money with real money.[/list]

THE BAD:
[list]
[*][b]Context-sensitive controls[/b] are bad at guessing the context. This really hurts in a stealth game because one wrong move can ruin your stealth.
[*][b]Movement.[/b] Though somewhat justified by Snake's injuries, movement controls are clumsy and obtrusive. There is a noticeable delay between motion keys and your character's motion. Do you like to play as a swift stealthy ninja? Have fun playing as a brain-damaged pirate.
[*][b]The environment.[/b] Unclimbable 30-degree slopes. Insurmountable waist-high fences. Invisible mission area boundaries that cause you to fail the mission. Some solid objects cannot be used as cover just because.
[*][b]AI.[/b] Enemies treat armored vehicles same as infantry. Your dog learns to sniff out land mines, but never learns to avoid them. Also never learns that jumping in front of your gun while you are shooting is a bad idea. NPCs get around their shortcomings by cheating: your dog is invisible to mines, and guards can see you through walls during combat alerts. [edit] Guards in singleplayer are oblivious to their own mines. Guards in online missions are invisible to their own mines.
[*][b]Obnoxious efforts to sell you virtual currency.[/b] Past the mid-game, you can literally buy in-game multiplayer insurance by spending real money.
[*][b]The grind.[/b] Optional mission objectives may require equipment that cannot be obtained until later in the game. You will need upgraded equipment for late-game and online missions. You unlock equipment by spending resources. Said resources take a long time to amass, and can be stolen from you by other players (unless you keep buying insurance.) You will be tempted to let this game idle in the background to get through the grind faster, but...
[*][b]No volume controls[/b] aside from helicopter music. (You can still disable the game's sound from the Windows Volume Mixer panel.)
[*][b]Fake difficulty.[/b] You will unlock more powerful equipment over time. So will your opponents. Skill is still very much a factor, especially for long-time players who unlocked EVERYTHING and are competing against similar players. Equipment becomes a big factor for mid-level players. For example, during online missions, you will meet armored NPCs that shrug off shotgun blasts to the head. With skill, luck, and a lot of experience from countless failed attempts, you can sneak past all of them without getting spotted. With progress, you can unlock a special gun that bypasses all their armor.
[*][b]Fake content.[/b] During the second half of the game, only half the missions are new. The rest are old missions on hard mode. Ocean platform missions are all the same, differing only by the opponents' strength.
[*]Cannot dispose of bodies on ocean platforms. Unconscious guards can be thrown overboard to their deaths just fine, but Snake refuses to pick up dead ones.
[*][b]Most side-ops[/b] are repetitive and boring. "Kill these." "Steal those." Even if you do not bother with side-ops, you will end up doing that stuff dozens of times just to make progress to better equipment.[/list]
[edit: found these later]
[list][*][b]Late-game[/b] progression is exponentially more grindy and somewhat bit pay-to-win. The only way to unlock the equipment you need to deal with invading players, is by unlocking all four FOBs. To do so, you'll either have to buy virtual currency with real money or spend a lot of time reaping daily login bonuses. It took me a year and two months and unlock the FOBs I wanted. If you do everything perfectly, logging in every Wednesday, Saturday, and Sunday, and buy only the cheapest FOBs, you can get there in 350 days.
[*][b]Konami's own servers[/b] will occasionally disconnect you for no clear reason. In singleplayer, this is only an annoyance. Online missions, however, are automatically considered failed if Konami's servers disconnect you. Resources you spent on the mission - which can be a lot for online missions - WILL NOT be refunded.[/list]

THE UGLY:
[list]
[*][b]Venom Snake[/b], when he is covered in blood after you decide that your time is too valuable to spend on saving NPC lives (whose lives Snake would ruin anyway.)[/list]

After nearly 70 hours, I've completed the main game. And HAWT DAMN, was it great. The story is alright, it was sort of confusing as I have not played a Metal Gear game before, but I got the main idea about halfway through and the ending is "serviceable". The game play is truly what makes this game great, as it is the perfect example of what an open world game should be like (TAKE NOTES ROCKSTAR). The Fox Engine is just fantastic to play in. The gameplay mechanics are fresh and separate this game out from all others in the genre. There is an absolute stunning amount of variety to how you can play this game, most just as good as the others. Kojima really gave us something special here (a mgs game with actual gameplay and not just time filler between 2 hour cutscenes).

I also did not see much of a reason to replay the story although I can see it happening in a few years from now. Furthermore the story suffers catastrophically from the rushed second half of the game. Some character arcs end nicely, others practically disappear with no conclusion. I'm a fan of the MGS story so to me it wasn't so bad however to anyone unfamiliar with the series it will seem incomplete and confusing.

All that said I still got 180 hours and certainly don't regret any of it. It's almost a sad feeling to have no more reason to keep playing. Even worse I have a bad feeling this is the last good title that will be developed with the Fox Engine.

I became a big fan of the Metal Gear Solid games since MGS1 and to this date, I never cared for any stealth action game because the player could get away with more screwups than its counterpart. It was easier to complete the games and experience its deep, if maybe convoluted story thread.

I bought MGSV day 1 and played tons of it.... before finally putting it down and moving on to other games and clearing my backlog instead. Why?

Well, for one, an the average playthrough of previous games varied from 6-15 hours. Meanwhile, average playtimes for MGSV can vary anywhere between 35 -120+ hours and it took me at least 110 to get the true ending and I was still missing out out special "re-run" missions", side ops, loads of gear upgrades, Paz sidequest, Metal Gear Online (MGO), and Forward Operating Bases (FOBs). You definitely get your money's worth of content, but if you want to reach the end, get the true ending and have a decent base and set of gear, it will certainly take you a while to "Just beat the damn thing and find out what is going on in the Metal Gear arc".

The open world, realistic design of the game is done extremely well here, and is also one of the features I never wanted in a Metal Gear solid game personally. In previous games, you could try to get past an area or neutralize most or all the enemies and if you failed, you could go to another area and reduce the alert status after time, or deal with guards one by one. In MGSV, enemies group up, become alot more aware of their surroundings, call in supporting guards, tanks and helicopters and have better equipment to deal with you. Its done very well here, but it is not what I wanted from MGS game, which let me get away with alot more nonense so I could get to the end. S Ranks are for hardcore stealth fans, not me.

Being stealthy and non-lethal here is arguably more important here than in the other games because recruiting staff and stealing resources and equipment is key to upgrading your own gear and Mother Base, which is neccesary for story progression.

Fans had the hope that MGSV would answer most if not all of the questions still lingering about the series, since this was the last game to be produced by the series creator Hideo Kojima. Development of the game was challenged due to corporate restructuring from Konami and their removal of his name from cover art and promotional material. Its arguable that the game was formed into a live service with microtransactions thanks to Konami instead of Kojima Productions, but we may never know that answer. With all the lengthy play time that me and other players had, MGSV left many questions unanswered and even created more in which you can read articles and forum threads about for details.

Ultimately the design flow of this game and the publisher-developer relationship nightmare tarnished the production of MGSV. There were some things about MGSV that makes it my least favorite in the main line of the series. However, I almost assuredly spent more time in this game than in the entire series combined and I often question if I want to keep it installed and play it more later or consider it done (I hate how often I get detected or I mess up one small thing, I honestly wish the game was easier).

[h1]MGSV is excellent and worthy of a purchase (especially at its $20 retail price) but it has caused consternation and disappointment among fans. A 10/10 it is not, but a heavily flawed amazing game it is.[/h1]

I wish there was a neutral rating option, but there isn't, so I have to give it a thumbs down for the forced online base raiding component and mobile-game-like microtransactions.

The online base raiding component to the game was supposed to be optional, but when the time comes, the tutorial literally forces you to build a FOB, which can then be raided by other players whether you're online or not.  Once built, you cannot destroy or dismantle it.  What's more, in order to have your R&D levels high enough to research good end-game level gear for the SP campaign, you HAVE to participate in this mode.  Do you need the good end-game gear to finish the SP campaign?  Not technically, but certain weapon options only unlock with very high R&D levels that can only come from having FOBs, so you're more limited in the SP campaign if you try to ignore the online component.  All of this is just bad game design.

On the plus side, though, the game looks good, runs well, and gives you a big, open world to play in with a good deal of freedom.  You can tackle most missions in a variety of ways, and you get a large assortment of helpful gadgets in addition to your weapons in order to help you through the missions.  I was actually fairly happy with the game until I came to the part where you're forced to build an FOB.  That pretty much killed all will to play for me.

Just because the game is based on stealth doesn't mean you can't have fun going guns blazing or planning missions with a frontal assault. That's what surprised me the most, because stealth games usually punish you for going guns blazing. This game has its amazing moments with stealth, and when the time comes, the loud and proud combat is fascinating.

Metal Gear Solid 6, in some way needs to be made, it is just a fact. The fans, let alone the entire video game industry, cannot move on without another Metal Gear. Kojima and his team, or a new/just as good director on Konami needs to make a good Metal Gear Solid 6 that is just as good or even better than MGS5. The game itself is vast, expansive, and realistic, from the flora to the fauna, to the weather and the physics. It challenges, but is lenient. It establishes its rules and then lets you interpret them as you wish.

There is nothing more satisfying than successfully infiltrating a huge base, slowly working your way through the place, killing, subduing, and kidnapping as you go, knowing that every silenced bullet and every Fulton extraction is working towards a goal of being the absolute best and only of your kind. At the same time, there is a magnificent feeling to running around trigger happy with a machine gun and a rocket launcher, demolishing anything and everything that stands in your way as a friendly airstrike illuminates your field of vision with fire. 

The story never fails to surprise, entertain, and exceed expectations, and the format of the game is beautifully crafted, telling an interactive story. For a game that is relatively linear in nature, it allows you an array of options as to how you choose to play.

I bought the game on sale, shortly after it first came out, for about 30 euros, and after playing for no more than an hour or two, I was adamant that I would have happily paid the full 60. It is an experience which I would full-heartedly recommend.

People seem to almost worship Hideo Kojima for his narratives, and [i] MGS V [/i] is no exception... but I just don't get it! The whole [b] extremely tedious and drawn out [/b] introduction to this game failed to grip me in the slightest. Anyways, this goes on [b] FOR AN HOUR AND A HALF! [/b] Bloody hell! I cannot wrap my head around how far this game is up its own arse! It concludes with this chase sequence involving [i] Buff Johnny Storm on a Horse [/i] and then transitions over to the primary local: Afghanistan.

This is where my primary gripe kicks in: Afghanistan sparsely littered with Russian military outposts, against the backdrop of a sandy desert, does not make for an interesting open world! The difference is Peace Walker slaps you on the backside, gives you a cheeky wink and says "Sean, I want you to take this banana and run amok with banana hold ups galore". Phantom Pain on the other hand gives you a firm handshake and says "get to it". There are some cute Easter eggs, such as mailing yourself to outposts and the mother-base scenes like low morale / injury / Quiet rain scene / Bday / 5 days away are a nice touch, likewise toilet solder and some of the cassette players in-game effects...all of which are easily missed, but generally its light on Konami's brand of ♥♥♥ humour. You won't be snapping photos of a marine in their boxers and sexting Otacon or sending inappropriate up-skirt panty shots of a hostage which you've just went out of your way to tranq dart in the middle of a hostage situation just to send to a very enthusiastic Miller etc.

Subsistence and Extreme are two modes introduced at late end game. Subsistence is essentially going into a mission naked, acquiring everything on the battlefield with no support from mother-base. It's a nice variation on the missions which could have been used to greater effect throughout the game rather than how they briefly used it on a handful of missions.

Extreme is the hard mode, enemies tank damage and dish out more. For me this is how the base story boss battles should have played by default. With you being one shotted by sniper rounds resulting in a proper sniper boss battle, a battle of wits and Sahelanthropus menacingly stomping round the level punishing any mistakes.

Cloaked in Silence & Truth:The Man who Sold the World are the easy highlights of the game, bizarrely both are almost hidden, requiring end game interactions and requirements outwith the main "campaign" and side ops. If you haven't completed those, you haven't completed the game. Many people won't have even seen them but both close out two aspects of the story perfectly with one flipping it on its head, breaking the 4th wall. [h1]Shortly[/h1]
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is an excellent game impeded by it's own mind-numbingly padded story that resembles a reality TV show. However, it manages to overcome these flaws through lore, gameplay and graphics.

[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1]
Pros
-Very well optimized.
-Enemies have interesting designs.
-Looks great.
-Realistic, when it is.
-Cutscenes have a shaky camera, as if an actual cameraman were there recording it.
-Weird handling. To see this in action, or to have fun, get a ZHUK BR3, find a flat area and hold A or D.

Cons
-Padded story.
-Lore is difficult to understand for first-time players.
-Toxic online community.
-You are forced to build an FOB for the game's online section.
-Has many of the issues that shows like Kitchen Nightmares or reality TV shows in general tend to have. For example, clichés, unnecessary slowmos and zooming when there's a reveal, or new character.
-No anticheat.
-The game's best weapons take days to unlock and are expensive, but how convenient that you can purchase what are essentially Konami Coins to skip the wait?
-Microtransactions and pay to win. The last tiers of weapons are ridiculous.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain manages to do what most games fail at; it manages to look great while playing very smooth at the same time. It is very well optimized, and only falls below 60 FPS when the screen is bombarded with particles or in the jungled areas of Africa.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
As with all Metal Gear Solid games, you must sneak and not become spotted, however you still have a viable arsenal to use in case you get spotted.

[h1]Updates[/h1]
The only thing resembling updates are weekly new FOB events.

[h1]Online[/h1]
There is no point to playing MGSV's online portion, as the only players that play it are the fanatics who play the FOB mode, as with all games that have low online populations. Notably, the remaining fanatics are just sweats, sadly.

[b]There is no way to delete your FOB in order to remove your online progress, as keeping one is merely an unfun hassle.[/b]

[h1]Soundtrack[/h1]
Very clean with excellent tracks scattered about. Shame that some of the best tracks like Nuclear aren't ingame.


[h1]Rating[/h1]

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain, at the same time, wants to be a videogame and a TV show.  It found a balance between those two, and plays great. While the online part of MGSV:TPP is not worth your time, it's singleplayer mode is sure to soak up quite a few hours from even the newest players of the Metal Gear Solid franchise.

Despite a wall of negative pros, it still manages to be a solid game, as long as you don't touch the online portion.. at all.

Can I overlook it? Sure. The game itself, the story, the characters, it is simply an annoyance if anything. It's interesting in how the gameplay works and the story works. What was originally meant to be Hideo Kojima’s masterpiece did end up being the most polished unfinished game I’ve ever seen, which it is likely to stay for a long time. Also, I now consider Assassin’s Creed calling itself a stealth game heresy.

Graphics: Nothing to criticize here. Sure, you do find some textures that look kinda off now and then, but considering how damn detailed your character and your weapons look, that isn’t even a nuisance. Besides that, this game has some great optimization; it’s the only AAA game I can run in 4k without suffering noticeable drops in FPS.

Sound: I highly recommend playing this with surround, this way you’re able to locate enemies fairly easily, as you can hear them breathe. Other than that, the local wildlife has a sound atmosphere as well, to the point that you can hear some flies buzzing around you. Concerning the OST, you have epic soundtracks playing during important missions and sad music during tear-jerking scenes. The background music is exactly that; background music, it’s decent but adds to the atmosphere. It sure does get repetitive, but any music would do so over the course of several hours of sneaking.

Gameplay: You can finish every mission in roundabout a million different ways, with the help of several hundred gadgets at your disposal, ranging from bio-weapon-suits to anti-material rifles. All of these are developed throughout the game, on your very own paramilitary base in the Indian Ocean, eventually sporting thousands of soldiers and a size of several square miles. Stealth works logically and flawlessly most of the time. Base management only gets annoying once you have to get your new weapons by online development, which takes some days unless you pay to speed up the process.

Atmosphere: This game switches from military espionage to zombie apocalypse to fighting giant mechas within a few minutes and still manages to maintain most of its credibility. If that isn’t a sign of quality I don’t know what is. Interaction between the main characters felt a bit flat though.

Balance: The stealth gameplay itself is well balanced in most cases; in some of the main missions it’s utterly ridiculous though. While normally being tough as ♥♥♥♥ they become a joke once you found an exploit. Due to the high number of gadgets at your disposal, there’s at least one such exploit for nearly every mission in the game. Another thing is the varying difficulty of the main missions; you’d expect them to rise in difficulty with the story progressing. This isn’t the case for this game’s main missions; they regularly switch from the hardest difficulty and the longest duration to cheap as ♥♥♥♥ and not difficult at all. Given the fact that said cheap missions barely deliver anything vital to the story, I consider them filler. The missions after the main story’s ending are poorly balanced as well; it isn’t exactly hard to notice that they were never supposed to be recycled this way.

Story: While having a pretty good presentation, which is executed excitingly and dramatically, this still is the game’s weakest point. That is because you don’t get a full story; the original finale was scrapped, essentially leaving an unsatisfying ending and several plot holes. I’d normally think of something like this as unforgivable. If I would’ve known that before buying the game I wouldn’t even have bothered to buy it. If someone would’ve told me that the second half of this game’s main missions consist of replaying the former ones, I would’ve dropped it right away. So, why am I still recommending this? Because the story still managed to keep me interested and the background information made me curious enough to go through it, even though it only consisted of voices on tape, which is only slightly more entertaining than reading a Wikipedia entry and way less informative. If you want to understand everything concerning the story of this game, however, especially if you never played another Metal Gear before, you’ll have to take some hours to read through the Wikia and watch the content which was cut from the final game on Youtube.

The deciding factor whether you’ll like this game or not depends on your valuation of storytelling, if you’re all about gameplay, or just someone who cares equally for each factor of a good game, then this won’t disappoint you, given you don’t dislike stealth games in the first place. If you’re all about the story, or a fan of previous Metal Gear games, or both, this probably isn’t your case and your disappointment may vary.

I'll give this one an "Ehhh". It is a high quality game, no doubt about that and therefore deserves a thumbs up. And yet it has some serious flaws that make it a rather mediocre, maybe even bad depending on your expectations, Metal Gear Solid title.

The gameplay itself is rather fun, albeit a bit lopsided for my taste: Sneaking is pretty difficult and unrewarding and can turn the game into a frustrating experience rather quickly. That would be okay if it meant that MGSV was simply a difficult game. But it's not. Because choosing the other strategy of "just shooting everybody in the face" is very viable and with all the weaponry, equipment and companions at your disposal really easy.

The open world is great and the amount of options you have in terms of weapons, vehicles, customization, recruitment, basebuilding, research and secrets to find is huge. However, some of these things are locked until you meet requirements that are hard to see through or even find out about in the first place. In my entire playthrough of the game, I never unlocked the weapon customization feature. I only found out that such a feature exists by reading about it online. And this even applies to Story missions: I had to look up guides on how to unlock the last couple of missions because the game simply doesn't tell you how to do it. In that regard MGSV is unnecessarily obscure (and not clever or complex).

The presentation is, as you'd expect, phenomenal, but the story...is quite the opposite. Even for Metal Gear Solid standards the story is more than absurd, but one could simply accept that and call it 'creative' if it wasnt for the fact that it feels (and as far as I know actually IS) unfinished. The game ends abruptly and many of the questions that you will undoubtedly have after "finishing" it, are only explained in audiologs which unfortunately arent very engaging. 

Hence, Metal Gear Solid V only felt like one half of a very ambitious, high quality game to me and not the full game that I was hoping for.

MGSV:TPP is a combination Stealth/Management/Action game, with the Stealth being the main gameplay mechanic and the action and management portions exist to modify the stealth.

You have an open world, with a huge map (two maps), and scripted missions take place in specific smaller sections of each map. You manage a small military base, and order people to research new weapons or gadgets.

The main gameplay loop is very fun. Usually on a mission, you will navigate to an outpost, scout the outpost, take down the guards silently, and do the objective (usually destroy/capture something), and then exfiltrate.

There is great replayability for this game, because there are around 20+ big bases, and maybe 50+ small outposts, and infiltrating a base from the opposite direction will force you to change your approach.

The "multiplayer" FOB feature is OK, but not great. The MGO online is not very fun in my opinion, but it's free with the Single player.

The "buddy" system is a great mechanic, which will give you an ally with special powers.

There is also a mod called Infinite Heaven which will let you play each mission in Subsistence Mode, meaning you will start with no weapons, similar to a battle royale. Despite this, nearly every mission can be completed in this way!

Despite some of the development management issues, the gameplay here is excellent.

- The first 2-3 hrs of the game are almost 8(?) uninspired cookie cutter missions of open world stealth which become incredibly dull as they are all in the same area, with similar buildings and you have extremely limited gadgets + guns to play with
- No cover button. Oh boy this was a design choice that I found infuriating, when games like Gears of War, The Division and even Grand Theft Auto have mastered this feature over the years it is just mind-boggling that the developers of MGSV decided to remove it and opt for an auto cover system which proves to be very frustrating to learn as it seems to only work 50% of the time and will get your cover blown many times. It really is astounding that a game so fundamentally based on stealth which punishes you for being spotted would remove this fantastic feature that works so much better than any auto system.
-  Spoiler titles. Every single mission you start in this game uses the same "Directed by Hideo Kojima" title credits that appear onscreen when Boss is in the helicopter, flying to the drop zone. Why is this a problem? Well, because it lists off every single person that will be involved in the mission you are about to partake in, including a 'guest starring' section that always tells you whether you are about to encounter skull face, that you are about to fight the parasite legion, that you are about to a fighting a giant mecha etc etc. The credits even specify the mecha you about to fight, its honestly just ridiculous and completely the spoils the surprise when skullface randomly shows up in the mission or the parasite legion attack you out of nowhere. It is clear with the way the missions are scripted these encounters are meant to be random and shocking but it is spoiled at the start of the mission. Why is this in the game? If Kojima was so desperate to strike back at Konami for removing his name from box credits why couldnt he just leave the mission credits at: "Written/Directed by Hideo Kojima"?.

Pros: 
- Excellent stealth mechanics (apart from the lack of cover button) that are really fun to play with
- Realistic, Challenging Gunplay that keeps the game stressful and punishing if you decide to abandon stealth
- Decent enough AI Enemies that will investigate, flank, communicate etc etc
- Massive array of gadgets, guns, tools and vehicle to use, customize and develop for use in the open world
- 'Buddy' companion system. Really fun and actually useful (unlike FO4's companion system) companion system that actually changes the way you approach different situations in combat. It works excellently and the companion AI is decent enough that it doesnt just get you or itself killed (Like in FO4)
- Large open world with plenty of bases, outposts, checkpoints and strongholds to conduct either main missions or side ops in. Unlike other open world games with bases like JC3, or FC3/4, your capture of enemy bases is only temporary and are swiftly retaken with reinforcements by the enemy in order to keep the world hostile and full of danger, which feels much better than an empty world full of captured bases like in JC3 or FC3/4 and also keeps the map from feeling small or completed.
- Music. Almost all bases you infiltrate will have a radio/cassette player with an iconic track on cassette tape from the 1980s which you can collect and play at any time. I really loved this little feature and it allows the player to experience some really fun moments, like driving a tank through the desert at night listening to "The Final Countdown" on the way to destroying some enemies was just an awesome and quite unique experience. You can even upgrade your helicopter to have speakers which can allow for some really enjoyable experiences like flying into a heavily guarded landing zone blasting "Ride of Valkyries".
- Developing weapons. Collecting materials, upgrading staff units and developing gadgets/weapons feels satisfying and makes missions really worth completing, as you gain more toys to play with in the open world.
- Weather Effects/Day and Night cycle. Weather effects such as heavy rain, clouds and sandstorms are all fantastic and change up the gameplay effectively, forcing the player to adapt and use it to their strengths, its a very enjoyable mechanic that can change missions completely and totally wreck or bolster your strategy. Being able to choose whether to deploy in daytime or nighttime is a nice touch and both have benefits and disadvantages, the time slowly going by is also great as it feels realistic and like your time actually matters, for example if you deploy on a big base at night and spend too much time gathering intel or crawling around you can get to sunrise and become alot easier to spot.
- Basebuilding/Management. I haven't delved too deep into this yet but its easy to understand and interesting to manage different areas, staff members etc etc
- Excellent UI and Menus. The UI and Menus, (which you spend alot of time in) are well thought-out and executed, everything feels intuitive and it isnt clunky or annoying to use.
- Beautiful textures/overall graphics, game looks fantastic and motion capture is excellent.
- Optimization. Running it on ultra settings with no stuttering or fps drops, its not that taxing on my hardware although the game is 3 years old now, however its safe to say its been pretty well optimized for pc.

Overall, this game's fantastic gameplay makes up for the various problems that plague its beginning, and it massively spikes up in quality and enjoyment around level 8. Its an excellent open world stealth game that is worth playing if you can stick with it.

This is the worst port from a console I have ever had the displeasure of playing. As a fan of smooth gameplay, seamless transitions and a responsive, intuitive control schemes, the pace of this gameplay feels like a new driver who has no concept of acceleration or braking discpline while the player, a mere passenger, is experiencing this all from the total control of the trunk.

The two most torturous aspects of this game are the Delays and the Saves.
Delays: The animations and unskippable transitions are numerous and intrusive. Getting into any vehicle or on a horse has an accompanying fanfare and disorienting swooping camera so that you KNOW you JUST. got into. a VEHICLE.
Every time you want to set foot in a mission zone you have to spend 60 seconds in an unskippable helicopter scene in which you... just... sit. And watch the sky. (If you don't believe 60 seconds is a long time try slowly counting to 60 while staring at a blank wall).

Saves: this game world is elaborate and the compounds are immense. The objectives in this game are always lofty enough to be intimidating but possible enough to be encouraging. That is...until you spend 30 minutes systematically eliminating an entire base only for a single mistake to cost you your life or objective. Most devs know people mess up. Restarting a lot is part of that whole Hard Game allure. But it's not fun at all to lose that much time and effort from a single mistake. To compare: if you screw up 4 times and you have to load a few minutes back, that's ten minutes spent LEARNING how to be better. If you have to load 30 minutes back each time, not only have you wasted 2 hours of your life failing one objective, but you only learn 1 thing each time. Replaying 30 minutes of gameplay in which you made no mistakes is tedious and dull.

***TL;DR - The pace of the game is so inconsistent it feels like being throttled.***

I do recommend this game however, as I don't regret buying it. There are enough positive aspects that were well made to balance out the disastrous controls, haphazard transitions, and uninspired progress saves. I have a very strong love and strong hate opinion really. The 9/10 aspects cancelled out by the 2/10 aspects, rendered this a 5/10 game for me.

So this game is super long. Just when you think it is gonna be over, it ain't. That's not a bad thing but it takes some time to warm up to. The beginning level is way too long, way too boring and almost completely on rails. The story and vibe is very, [b]very[/b] [strike] weeby [/strike] [u] Japanese [/u]. There's some serious anime style cringe present in this game, some weird gundam style mecha robot stuff and some borderline homoerotic interactions between the protagonist and your main handicapped homies to boot. If one more person does the puts-on-aviators-glasses-shine-dramatically thing one more time I might just set my pc on fire. On top of that there's some very cringeworthy eye candy stuff where the only female "character" is essentially just there to look hot so neckbeards have something to fawn over. The lazy, nonsensical story explanation regarding her attire is equally pathetic. [spoiler] Apparently she breathes through her skin, which is why she needs to be almost naked at all times. Oh, and she photosynthesizes. Because that makes sense.[/spoiler]

Fortunately for us, the story elements and conventions that give me such extensive second hand embarrassment are mostly limited to the cutscenes (of which there are still too many). The redeeming part of this game, is in the gameplay. The stealth gameplay is super great. If you pride yourself on perfect stealth type stuff, boy, do I have a game for you. Less actiony than games like splinter cell, think more belly crawling around in the dark. The maps are open world, enormous and interesting. The missions, both main and side, are by and large a lot of fun to play with few exceptions. Customizing your home base, helicopter, buddies and gear is a lot of fun as is developing new weapons and equipment. In terms of endgame content, there is a multiplayer mode where you can infiltrate other player's bases and they can infiltrate yours. Not only can you manage your security setup and guard equipment for your various base platforms, which you construct more of over time, but you can steal resources and personnel from other players. Clearing bases and outposts quietly and kidnapping the skilled soldiers is always a blast and if you aren't feeling sneaking around every single outpost, you can always hop in a tank or ifv and roll right through.

As a whole the game is really fun if you can stomach the story. The gameplay itself is addicting, even though I've completed nearly everything I still want to finish developing every platform and every item. Definitely one to keep an eye on if it goes on sale.

In truth, I wish there was a "Mixed" option when it comes to reviewing products on Steam. Because that is what this game is in my opinion, a mixed bag. this is very much a Metal Gear Solid game in the sense that you can still go around, infiltrating bases/camps. But it doesn't hit the narrative points that previous titles had achieved. It is absolutely the weakest when it comes to not only providing the narrative, but also towards providing meaningful perspective for said narrative to exist. In theory, you could completely skip this game and you honestly wouldn't miss a whole lot. 46 missions compose the story, and most of the time the details leading up to said missions revolve around listening to cassette tapes, or by listening to support over the radio. It certainly does trim down the length of the game (where before, the details were explained in cutscenes), the issue is that it really doesn't help to provide a sense of depth or gravity to the situation. That may be a personal preference, but you also have to remember that this is the fifth game in a series where NARRATIVE DEPTH seemed to be priority one. But this isn't the only element to the game, there is also uh...A game...To this game...Anyways, now you have seemingly unlimited methods of completing tasks in this game. You can kill or tranquilize enemies (which is standard of MGS games since MGS2) but you also have additons to that system such as the fulton recovery system returning from Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker. You can drive vehicles, call in support from man's best friend, Quiet the mute sniper, or even a sort of miniature Metal Gear called a Walker Gear. Expansive gameplay is always appreciated in my book, and I admire that Kojima Productions took the task of making as many possible gameplay scenarios as possible. The game's setting comprises of (technically) three open worlds: Afghanistan, Africa, and Mother Base. You can recruit soldiers, fulton materials, vehicles, or even free roam just for the sake of free roaming. This is on one hand a unique idea since the worlds are massive in scale. However the potential is lost when you realize that it is just empty space. Occassionaly you may find soldiers out on patrol, or even some animals to rescue/fight. But %75-%90 of my experience has been traversing empty wastelands, getting from point A to point B is tedious in this game since it never varies the events that can occur between those points. Most of my playtime honestly revolved around traveling these distances, it's just driving, and driving...Also, more driving. Overall, the game is very much a mixed bag with a weak narrative, but also some fantastic means of experiencing. 

So why do I recommend Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain?

Because when you get right down to it's core, it is a fun game. There's a reason why my playtime is high (aside from the driving), it's because the game provides a fantastic experience in terms of gameplay that you really can't find anywhere else. Experiences in this game, (or methods on how to complete a task) rarely become the same between players. A lot of experiences are unique to that player BECAUSE of the variety it has with the gameplay. To give a scenario, this is my second time completing this game, the first time was on my PS3, the second time was here. Not only was my experience improved here, but it also was so varied that in a lot of ways it felt like I was playing it for the first time. Because the scenarios that you take can change that much between players and gameplay sessions. So I would absolutely recommend this game if you are looking for a game that can provide unique scenarios every time you play. Also because it is a great deal, $20 is a small price to pay to the Konami overlords for this one of a kind experience. Even better if you could get it for a cheaper price.

Metal Gear Solid 5 is a 3rd person stealth-focused infiltration game set in the 70-80s military era with some sci-fi sprinkled on top. However, right from the start, this game has mental issues; it's bipolar. Ground Zeroes is this, Phantom Pain is that. So, basic gameplay has to be split in 2...

First, let's cover Ground Zeroes.

It starts as a "playable demo" that was sold at a high price, which can be completed in about 1-2 hours, excluding any extras side-missions. These extra mission just re-uses the same map with different objectives and day/night setting.

However, I actually enjoyed my time in those 2 hours because it [i]felt[/i] like an actual Metal Gear game. Great presentation, good conversations, great stealth action. I was able to play it from start to finish without putting the controller down.

See, this demo had everything that made Metal Gear great in the first place. The story cues in and gives you motivation to persue your task. Even if it's linear or open-world, a good story makes you want to see what's next. This was the main driving force of previous MGS's.

After finishing Ground Zeroes, I was a bit bummed by the lenght, but told myself "well, Phantom Pain will probably rock".............

But then I boot up Phantom Pain...

The hospital intro was alright, nice little build up. However, I can't help to notice the bizarre/surreal presentation after leaving the bed. I wasn't sure if these soldiers were human or robots,  quickly noticing their mechanical movements and behavior.

Things happen and you escape the hospital, then follows a long cutscene. Then it hit me in the face as I started riding my horse in Afghanistan leaving Ocelot behind... Snake doesn't talk... At all. On the Muteness scale, he's worse than Tom Hardy in Mad Max. Moans and groans a lot, might say a sentence each half hour or so...

So, instead of intricate conversation exchanges that lays ground to a good story which in turn motivates you to play, you have these long monologue by each character you meet which quickly turn into a snoozefest. There is no emotional motivation coming from Snake like it used to, no chemistry between characters. You're just playing as a mute, crippled, near-brain-dead shell of a character that used to be a hero for each game. Snake yells more at his horse than he talks to others...

Phantom Pain's gameplay, unlike Ground Zeroes, shifts from a linear story-focused game to a free-roam open-world game where you have to rebuild your military empire in the likes of Peace Walker. Instead of taking missions from a static menu, you can take missions live on the field. Using your chopper and your horse, you go back and forth from your base to your next mission objective. You gain GMP (money) by completing missions and use it to expand your base, research better weapons/gears.

I do admit the gameplay is great as I enjoyed Peace Walker back then. However, PW had a great story, with some very neat QTE ideas during cutscene which made the PSP feel great for some reason. PW is one of the highest rated games for PSP, so I guess they did a great job there.

As I start clearing a few missions, I notice yet another thing that's quite irritating. Each time you start and finish a mission, each names of the characters appear on screen (Snake, Ocelot, Miller, etc) just like a TV episode, followed by the dev's names. Wether it's artistic liberty or childish corporate defiance doesn't matter, it's just irritating after a few times.

The big idea with this episodic naming thing is to annoy people like me, who used to enjoy long stretchs of gameplay with loads of conversations. Instead, this presentation style ruins any immersion the story might have, which is already hard to watch like mentioned above.

I've rescued Kaz (3rd story mission), and again, I'm treated to a long monologue with a simple one-liner from Snake. I'm not sure the game changes later, but I fear the more I'll play, the more of the same I'll see.

I'm not exactly sure to who or how I should recommend this to, since this hodgepodge of a bipolar game is a damnable mess, an under-handed bait & switch.

I rate this a solid 6/10 for gameplay, loose #ERROR#/10 for the absurd dual-game flame-out/troll.
